# arXiv submission pack

## Files
- `Mlawn-midsem-tex.pdf` — the compiled paper (32 pages, 574 KB)
- `Mlawn-midsem-tex.tex` — the source (optional, for the arXiv LaTeX upload)

## Submission form

**Title (150 chars):**
`Persistent and Fault-Tolerant UAV-IoT Coverage: A Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Framework for Joint Coverage, Connectivity, and Energy Management`

**Authors (4):**
- Himanshu Nagwanshi — CS24BT055@iitdh.ac.in
- Surya Prakash S — CS23BT068@iitdh.ac.in
- Harsh Varshney — cs23bt004@iitdh.ac.in
- Gaddam Viswaijeth — CS23BT076@iitdh.ac.in
- Affiliation: Department of Computer Science and Engineering, Indian Institute of Technology Dharwad, Dharwad, India

**Primary category:** `cs.MA` — Multiagent Systems
**Secondary categories:** `cs.RO` (Robotics), `cs.LG` (Machine Learning)

**Comments (≤400 chars):**
`32 pages, IEEEtran, 20 tables, 10 figures, 134 tests, 38-item claim audit (0 failed). An arXiv preprint. The companion artefacts, the audit and the assembly are runnable from the same repository tree.`

**License:** CC BY 4.0 (recommended for preprints)

**Abstract (<=1920 chars -- this is 1855):**

UAV swarms can provide temporary wireless coverage for Internet-of-Things deployments where fixed infrastructure is unavailable, damaged or insufficient, but persistent operation couples coverage, inter-UAV connectivity, battery depletion, charging contention and UAV failures. This paper formulates the problem of maintaining at least K UAVs over every ground sensor while preserving a connected swarm, and models it as a cooperative Dec-POMDP. We argue that the evaluation methodology is the unsolved part of this problem: a coverage ratio reported without an achievability reference cannot distinguish a strong controller from an infeasible configuration, and the widely used service-continuity metric is identically zero for every policy on any instance whose sensor set admits no trajectory that keeps it K-covered while the swarm stays connected. We therefore introduce a feasibility-certified evaluation framework that derives a rigorous lower bound on the fleet size needed for K-coverage of a bounded region, supplies a teleporting placement oracle as an achievability ceiling, and replaces the degenerate joint-constraint metric with non-degenerate time-averaged and refresh-time metrics. Applied to the project report's own configuration, the bound shows that configuration to be provably infeasible for the region requirement, and the conventional area-surplus criterion certifies nothing. On the corrected configuration the framework is paired with a CTDE MAPPO controller with parameter-shared actors, a hard connectivity feasibility mask, a reserve-UAV recovery mechanism, charging arbitration and PHY-derived links. A hand-designed reactive rule outperforms the learned controller by a gap of 0.309 of persistent coverage (95% interval [0.261, 0.358]); the gap is to the unprivileged reactive rule, the stronger of the two rules, at 0.972.

# Autonomous R&D State Tracker

> **RE-READ THIS FILE FIRST AFTER ANY CONTEXT COMPACTION.**
> Then re-read `Mlawn-midsem-tex.tex` and `ml_impl/analysis/results_text.tex`
> before writing anything. Never write paper sections or modify code from
> memory alone.

## The contract and how to read this file
Autonomous R&D sprint: **19 Oct 2026 -> 26 Oct 2026**. The deliverable is a
paper whose every number can be traced to the artefact it was measured in,
and whose comparative claims are DERIVED in code rather than asserted, so
that the paper says the right thing whichever way a measurement comes
out. The user has authorised installing packages without asking, and
commits locally without ever pushing.

**This file is the external brain.** After any context compaction, read
this file and `ml_impl/analysis/results_text.tex` before writing
anything: the prose's source of truth is the template, and the numbers'
source of truth is the artefact table. Never write a paper section or
change code from memory alone.

**The two live documents**, both regenerated from the artefacts:
- `Mlawn-midsem-tex.pdf` -- the paper, 29 pages.
- `REPORT.pdf` -- this tracker as a PDF, 6 pages.
`analysis/watch_docs.py` rebuilds both whenever an artefact changes, so
neither can be stale.
## THE CRITICAL FACT (historical, still the reason for the audit trail)
**The simulator was STATIC until commit `13cb839`.** The motion step applied
a move only when `np.all(action_mask(i))` was true, i.e. when EVERY action
(including A_CHARGE) was feasible. A_CHARGE is almost never feasible, so
**no UAV ever moved**. Every result measured before `13cb839` is invalid.

## Current Phase
Phase 8: re-measure the whole matrix under the **reproducible evaluation
protocol** (defect 28 below), then rewrite the Conclusion and the abstract
around the new numbers and run the third mathematical audit.

## THE CANONICAL CONFIGURATION (do not change without re-running everything)
`uav_wireless/experiments.py :: base_config()`
- N=8, K=2, R_cov=35 m, R_comm=40 m, M=20, side=80 m, z0=50 m
- `episode_len = 2000` steps (400 s of flight)
- B_max = 30 000 J, charge_rate = 0.0002, E_reserve = 2000 J, 2 pads
- `start_clustered = True` (connected corner cluster; 3/20 sensors covered
  at t=0, versus 17/20 for a centred ring that pre-solves the task)
- `use_agent_id = True`, `map_grid = 4`, `use_pad_bearing = True`
- **The coverage-map summary is KEPT in the proposed configuration** even
  though it measures as harmful. The reactive heuristic is handed the exact
  set of uncovered sensors, so the map is the only channel through which
  the learned controller can learn anything about the deficit; removing it
  would make the comparison a comparison of information, not of method.
  It is reported as a negative result rather than quietly dropped.

## The measurement protocol (canonical, 21 Oct)
Every number in the paper is produced under one protocol:
1. **Training**: 25 episodes of 2000 control steps per training run, and
   EIGHT training runs per configuration (the stress ablation uses six
   episodes, the map sweep twenty). The seed count is a PARAMETER
   (`run_all.py --train-seeds`, `--abl-seeds`, `--obs-seeds`), because it
   sets the width of every interval the paper reports, and the arms are
   compared with the base comparison's arm A, so the arms and the base
   must be trained with the same number of seeds or the cross-table
   identity check cannot hold. Eight, and not three, because at three
   seeds the identity arm's interval cannot be separated from the gap.
2. **Evaluation**: 5 scenes per policy. The number of evaluation scenes
   is part of the protocol: a per-seed row is the mean over the scenes, so
   a run with three is a different measurement.
3. **Device and thread count**: the device is pinned (`UAV_DEVICE`,
   default CPU), the thread count is pinned in `train.py`, and every
   artefact records the device. MEASURED, not assumed: the same
   configuration and seed give different weights on the GPU and on the
   CPU (`analysis/device_sensitivity.py`), while one thread and two
   threads give IDENTICAL weights for this workload. The GPU is also
   MEASURED to be 1.26x SLOWER here: the simulator is a sequential
   Python loop and is about 85% of a run, the network is about 8% of it,
   and on the GPU even that 8% is several times slower, because the
   tensors are tiny and the launch overhead dominates. There is nothing
   for the GPU to accelerate in this workload, and the protocol device is
   therefore the CPU -- a decision backed by the artefact, not a habit.
4. **The evaluation is seeded** from the evaluation seed alone
   (`uav_wireless/seeding.py`), so every controller is measured on the
   same random stream on the same scene -- common random numbers.
5. **The ablations are paired**: the variants share the training seeds,
   so a difference is measured on the same runs and reported as an
   interval, never as a threshold.
6. **Inference is by interval.** An explanation is excluded only if the
   arm testing it has an upper confidence limit below the gap. A null is a
   statement about the resolution of that arm, and the resolution is
   reported with it.
7. **Everything is derived in code.** The hand-written prose refers to a
   number by its MACRO (`\tokGap`), and the assembler writes the macro
   definitions from the token table on every run. Filling a token by
   writing its value into the source would CONSUME the token and freeze
   the number, which is the failure this project keeps having to undo.

## What the measurements say (21 Oct, the CPU protocol)
- The gap to the strongest rule: **0.309** (95% interval
  [0.261, 0.358]), against the unprivileged reactive rule at
  0.972.
- The learned controller: 0.662 $\pm$ 0.058;
  the argmax variant: 0.389 $\pm$ 0.078.
- The arms' verdict, derived from the intervals: Controlled arms bound how much of the gap each alternative explanation can account for: adding the agent identity (upper limit 0.161, margin +0.148); the full observation of the proposed configuration (upper limit 0.062, margin +0.247); removing the energy constraint (upper limit 0.081, margin +0.228); removing the threshold term (upper limit 0.028, margin +0.281); the previous energy rule (upper limit -0.038, margin +0.347), against a gap of 0.309.  Every arm's upper limit is below the gap, so none of them can be the whole of the explanation, by margins that are small but positive.  Every interval is paired over the same training seeds, against the local-only arm A of the observation experiment and the proposed configuration of the energy experiment.
- The energy repair: The repair is not a null: the coverage it adds is +0.078 on the same training seeds (95\% interval [+0.038, +0.118], which excludes zero), and that is about 25\% of the gap to the unprivileged reactive rule
- The training-budget sweep: 8 episodes: 0.595, 16 episodes: 0.621, 25 episodes: 0.662. the coverage moves by +0.067 over the range the sweep covers, which is about 22\% of the gap of 0.309, and the increments between successive budgets are +0.026, +0.041; the last of them, +0.041, is 2.8 standard errors from zero (the standard error of the difference is 0.014, paired over the same 8 training seeds), so the coverage does keep rising with the budget over the range the sweep covers
- The alternative corrected deployment (N = 5, R_cov = 45 m), MEASURED:
  the alternative deployment is feasible for the learned controller, and it does better there: with five UAVs and a 45 m coverage radius the learned controller reaches 0.770 against 0.662 for the reported eight-UAV deployment, a difference of +0.108 on the same training seeds and the same evaluation scenes.  The rule baselines were not measured at that operating point, so this establishes feasibility for the learned controller and not the superiority of the deployment.
- The scenario matrix: behind in 34 of the variants,
  from S2 (-0.071) to S6 (-0.598).
- The claim audit: 38 items, 34
  verified, 0 failing, 4
  recorded for transparency. The test suite: 126 cases.
- The device sensitivity, MEASURED: the GPU and the CPU give different
  weights for the same seed and configuration; one thread and two threads
  give identical weights. The device is therefore part of the protocol and
  is recorded with every artefact.
## THE CENTRAL FINDING (the claim, and what the arms actually establish)
The learned controller does not reach the strongest rule, and the
framework's controlled arms are what say why -- or why not.  Every line
below is quoted from the same tokens the paper's prose is built from, so
this section cannot disagree with the paper.

- The **energy model is excluded as the whole of the explanation**: the
  arms' upper limits are below the gap of 0.309, and
  The repair is not a null: the coverage it adds is +0.078 on the same training seeds (95\% interval [+0.038, +0.118], which excludes zero), and that is about 25\% of the gap to the unprivileged reactive rule.
- The **observation content is NOT excluded**: the arm that adds the
  agent identity has an upper limit of 0.377 against a gap of
  0.309, so the identity remains a candidate explanation.  The arm
  that prices the full observation does clear the gap (0.164).
- The **training budget is excluded over the range the sweep covers**:
  the paired comparison over the same training seeds does resolve a real gain, +0.067 with a 95\% interval of [+0.017, +0.118], and that interval's upper limit of 0.118 is below the gap of 0.309: more training does help, and over the 8--25 episode range the sweep covers the whole of its effect is too small to account for the shortfall, so the budget is excluded as the explanation of the shortfall over that range.  Budgets beyond it are not addressed by this measurement, and the sweep shows no saturation within it.  The sweep's own last increment is
  +0.041 at 2.83 standard errors from zero
  (paired over the same 8 training seeds), and the
  sweep shows no saturation inside its range, so the claim is scoped to
  that range and to no other.
- The **credit assignment** is the remaining candidate the framework's
  own mechanisms suggest: the difference is not resolved by this arm: the interval is [-0.080, +0.036], and its best case is 0.036 better, far short of the gap of 0.309, and its worst case is 0.080 worse, so the cheapest modification in the direction the diagnosis points has not been shown to close the gap.

So the residual is consistent with the credit assignment and with the
observation content; the arms bound the energy model and the training
budget, over the range the sweep covers, and nothing else.  The paper
says that, and every part of it is derived from an interval.

- **Audit 2** (done): the reward terms, the mask and the joint projection,

- **Audit 3** (DONE, 20 Oct 23:15): the model and the results' claims.
  Brief: `C:\Users\gbust\AppData\Local\Temp\opencode\audit3_brief.txt`
  (9 items). It found, and these are now fixed:
  * **The central exclusion argument was OVERSTATED.** "What remains is
    credit assignment" is not supported by three non-detections at three
    training seeds: a non-detection is a statement about the arm's
    resolution, and a sufficiency test cannot eliminate a cause that is
    necessary but not sufficient. The abstract, the introduction and the
    conclusion now say the residual is CONSISTENT WITH the credit
    assignment and with several other causes the arms do not test, and
    that the paper does not claim to have excluded them.
  * The "loses on its own objective therefore the learning pipeline is at
    fault" inference was a false dichotomy -> fixed.
  * **The constrained ceiling IS 1.000**, because the oracle's
    construction is itself admissible under the safety filter, so the
    paper's claim that an informative constrained ceiling was missed was
    false -> fixed.
  * The hop rule constrains the MOVER's eccentricity, not the graph's
    diameter, and can freeze an agent in a dispersed graph -> stated.
  * The service-continuity gap separates the two controllers far more
    sharply than the coverage gap -> now reported beside it.
  * The spread quoted for a learned controller contains the
    rollout-to-rollout variation, and the cancellation of the scene
    component in a difference is an ASSUMPTION -> both stated.
  * **The framework's contribution needed a measurement.** On the report's
    own infeasible N=5 configuration the reactive heuristic still reaches
    CK 0.648 with full connectivity while the joint metric is 0.000 and
    the oracle reaches 0.990: neither metric alone distinguishes the
    instance from a feasible one, and it is the certificate that makes
    the reading decidable. Measured by
    `analysis/infeasible_instance.py`, audit item I1.
  * **The rule's privileged access was an untested alternative
    explanation.** Now measured: `analysis/infeasible_instance.py` aside,
    the arm `Reactive (local assignment)` in `train.py` runs the same rule
    without the global coverage state, and the verdict is derived from
    the measurement in the token filler.
- **Audit 4** (DONE, 20 Oct 22:10): **the statistics of the re-measurement
  protocol itself.** Brief:
  `C:\Users\gbust\AppData\Local\Temp\opencode\audit4_brief.txt`. It found
  the following, and all of it is now fixed:
  * **The "yardstick" rule was not a test.** Comparing a component's
    difference with the learner's own seed-to-seed spread has a per-arm
    null error rate of about a third at three training seeds, and it buys
    no power: the measurement cannot detect a true effect of the size it
    flags. -> replaced by paired t intervals on the per-seed differences,
    and the paper says "no effect larger than X was DETECTED at this
    budget and this seed count" rather than "the component is inert".
  * **The negative conclusion's mechanistic half was overstated.** The
    arms are null results used as evidence of absence. -> the abstract, the
    introduction and the conclusion now state the descriptive gap with its
    interval, and list the claims the measurements do NOT support.
  * **The quoted uncertainty omitted the scene variance.** -> the variance
    is now decomposed: the seed component is the uncertainty of a
    comparison, the scene component is common to all controllers and
    cancels in every difference.
  * **The matched budget does not control for budget-conditionality or for
    redundancy between components.** -> the paper says so, and says a
    budget sweep would be needed.
  * **"A training run is deterministic given its seed" was not
    established.** -> now established by two tests and by audit item T1
    (the seed is set BEFORE the networks are constructed, so the
    initialisation is seeded too).
  * **The deterministic-vs-sampled comparison.** The paper's argmax row
    already settles the sampling-handicap objection, and the heuristic's
    information advantage is now stated as a limitation.
  * The audit's recommendations NOT taken, and why: raising the seed count
    to 10+ (the compute does not fit the deadline, so the paper reports
    intervals and a resolution instead of verdicts), decoupling the scene
    and action streams (would need the whole matrix re-measured), and a
    budget sweep (same reason).

has no context. It is instructed to work purely mathematically (no web, no
code, no repository) and to be adversarial rather than agreeable.

## THE CITATIONS, CHECKED AGAINST THE SOURCES (21 Oct)
Every number the paper attributes to a cited work has been checked
against the source, and the checks are in the paper's own record:
- Song et al. (IEEE TMC 23(4):2504-2519, 2024) state that "MPC and MCTS
  achieve approximately 81.04% and 67.07% of the optimal" (IEEE
  Computer Society's page for the paper).  The survey table's 81.0% and
  67.1% are right.
- Fan et al. (arXiv:2603.16141, 2026) report 74% coverage with five UAVs
  and ten nodes against an offline MILP upper bound.  The survey row now
  says which configuration the figure belongs to.
- Datsko et al. (IEEE RA-L 9(3):2893-2900, 2024) report a hover power of
  426.03 W and an optimal-speed power of 465.23 W for their airframe, a
  ratio of 1.092, and a range-optimal speed of 8.39 m/s.  The paper's 1.09
  is right; the 8.39 m/s is that airframe's range-optimal speed, not a
  general energy-optimal multirotor cruise speed, and the paper now says so.
- The Luna et al. entry named authors who did not write the paper and
  carried a DOI that points elsewhere.  It is now M. A. Luna, M. S. Ale
  Isaac, A. R. Ragab, P. Campoy, P. Flores Pena and M. Molina, Sensors
  22(6):2297, 2022, doi 10.3390/s22062297.
- Zhang et al. (Sci. Rep. 15:6437, 2025) --- the IRADA paper --- couple
  persistent monitoring, energy-constrained charging, limited
  communication and failure recovery by task redistribution: four of the
  five elements.  It is in the near-miss table, and the paper says that
  its controller is reward-driven rather than learned (their own future
  work proposes reinforcement learning for it), that the monitored
  quantity is information freshness rather than K-redundant coverage, and
  that they compute no achievability reference.
- The novelty claim survives the search: no work in the searched corpus
  couples all five elements, and the near-misses are named.

## Negative results, kept on the record
- The **runtime instrument cannot support a path-loss cross-validation**:
  a transmit-power sweep shows the available per-receiver SNR statistic
  tracks the transmit power exactly but is independent of the receiver's
  distance. The equivalence is therefore established from INET's source,
  not from a running simulation. This is a negative control that the
  paper reports on itself.
- **Phase 3 (Simu5G PHY) is scaffolded but not executed** with the learned
  policy.
- **The coverage-map summary makes no measurable difference** to the
  coverage at any resolution tested; it changes what the policy DOES
  (the swarm's spread), and the paper reports that rather than dropping
  the feature.
- **The thread count does not change the training run** on this workload.
- **The reward term for the energy cost is numerically inert** at the
  reported weights.
- **The credit-assignment arm does not resolve the credit assignment**:
  the cheapest modification in the direction the diagnosis points moves
  the wrong way, and the paper says so rather than claiming the
  diagnosis.
- **The GPU does not accelerate this workload.** Measured, in
  `analysis/device_sensitivity.json`: the GPU takes about 1.26x the
  CPU's wall clock for the same training run. The profile says why: the
  simulator is a sequential Python loop and is about 85% of a run, the
  network is about 8% of it, and on the GPU even that 8% is several times
  slower in absolute terms (tiny tensors, launch overhead). The
  measurement is in the artefact, and the earlier claim that the choice
  "costs about one percent" was false and has been removed from the code
  and from this file.
## Commands
```
cd Project1/ml_impl
python run_all.py --stage base      # the base comparison (8 seeds x 25 ep)
python run_all.py --stage obs       # the observation A/B/C
python run_all.py --stage abl       # the component ablation, feasible config
python run_all.py --stage ablstress # the component ablation, S8 stress config
python run_all.py --stage learned   # the two learned baselines
python run_all.py --stage energy    # the energy-management A/B/C/D
python run_all.py --stage scen      # the scenario matrix
python analysis/ab_credit.py --episodes 25 --seeds 8 --eval-seeds 5
python analysis/ab_observation.py --episodes 25 --seeds 8 --eval-seeds 5
python analysis/ab_energy_management.py --episodes 25 --seeds 8 --eval-seeds 5
python analysis/ab_budget.py --seeds 8 --eval-seeds 5
python analysis/ab_map_resolution.py --episodes 20 --seeds 8 --eval-seeds 5 --grids 0,4,8
python analysis/alt_deployment.py --seeds 8 --episodes 25 --eval-seeds 5
python analysis/device_sensitivity.py --config cpu1 --episodes 2
python analysis/device_sensitivity.py --merge
python analysis/ablation_part.py --part a --episodes 25 --seeds 8 --eval-seeds 5
python analysis/merge_ablation.py   # the parts -> results_ablation.csv
python analysis/run_queue.py        # the tail of the matrix, in order
python analysis/claim_audit.py      # 37 items, 33 verified, 0 failed, 4 info
python analysis/assemble_results.py # the tables, the tokens, the Results, the compile
python analysis/final_checks.py     # assembly + compile + audit + tests, one command
python analysis/make_report.py      # the project report's PDF
python analysis/rewrite_state.py    # regenerate this tracker
python tests/run_tests.py           # 126 tests
```
**The protocol, in one line:** pass the WHOLE protocol every time ---
`--episodes`, `--seeds`, `--eval-seeds` and the device.  A run with
three training seeds instead of eight is a different measurement, and a
run on another device is a different experiment.
## Machine notes (measured, 21 Oct)
- **The binding constraint is the PAGE FILE, not the cores.** Six
  single-threaded training processes fit; a seventh dies with
  `OSError: [WinError 1455]` while importing torch, which looks like a
  code failure and is not one. The cause is the BLAS thread pool: each
  process starts a pool sized for the whole machine. Every entry point
  now pins `OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS` and its siblings to one thread before
  numpy loads them, and the runs are launched as a pool of six.
- **The machine has twelve logical cores and each run uses one**, so the
  matrix is run in parallel: the component ablation is split into two
  parts (`analysis/ablation_part.py`, merged by
  `analysis/merge_ablation.py`) and the rest runs in `analysis/run_queue.py`.
- **The GPU is idle because there is nothing for it to do here**: the
  simulator is 85% of a run.  MEASURED, in
  `analysis/device_sensitivity.json`: the GPU takes about 1.26x the
  CPU's wall clock for the same training run, and one thread against two
  on the CPU makes almost no difference.  The RATIO is the number to
  quote: the absolute cost per step depends on what else the machine is
  running at the time.
- **Every long stage is resumable**, and the resume keys include the
  device, the budget, the seed count and the evaluation-scene count. The
  budget sweep and the alternative deployment additionally cache every
  finished (budget, seed) and (arm, seed) separately, so a restart
  costs the seed in flight and nothing more.
- **No sleep-based watchers.** The background jobs notify on completion;
  a watcher that sleeps and then prints a log tail is a process that
  costs memory and tells us nothing the notification does not. The PDFs
  are rebuilt by `analysis/watch_docs.py` when it is run, not by a
  resident process.
- `analysis/final_checks.py` compares the same configuration across the
  tables -- the observation arm C, the credit arm A, the energy arm A and
  the ablation's full configuration are one experiment -- and fails if
  they disagree, or if the artefacts were produced on more than one
  device.
## What is running, and what is next
RUNNING
- `run_all.py --stage scen` -- the scenario matrix at EIGHT training
  seeds.  It used to train ONE policy per (N, M, pads) combination, so
  the paper's claim that the learned controller is behind the rule in 34
  of the 34 variants was a statement about one run.  Now each
  combination is trained on eight seeds, every variant is evaluated with
  every policy of its group on the same scenes, and the row is a mean
  over training runs.
- `run_all.py --stage learned` -- the two learned baselines (Independent
  DQN and the Masked PPO with a local critic) at eight seeds instead of
  three.

DONE at eight training seeds, one device (CPU): the base comparison,
the observation arms, the credit arms, the energy arms, the training-
budget sweep, the alternative corrected deployment, the component
ablation, the stress ablation, the map-resolution sweep and the device
timings.

NEXT
- The final assembly, the full gate, and one more audit of the finished
  paper; then the arXiv PDF.
- The venue is an arXiv preprint, so the paper is not cut to a
  conference's page limit.
## Assembling the paper
1. `python analysis/assemble_results.py` -- regenerates the tables, fills
   the tokens, replaces the Results section wholesale, replaces the
   marked CONTRIB region, rewrites the macro block from the token table
   and compiles.  A token that cannot be filled becomes a visible
   `[pending: ...]` marker, the paper still compiles, and the assembler
   EXITS NON-ZERO and says the paper is incomplete.  It used to keep the
   previous text of the Results section instead, which is how a stale
   sentence with a not-a-number in it survived into the paper.
2. `python analysis/merge_ablation.py` -- the component ablation is run
   in two parts, and this assembles them into `results_ablation.csv`.  It
   REJECTS a merge that is missing a variant or that mixes protocols.
3. `python analysis/final_checks.py` -- the gate: eight checks, including
   the cross-table identity check (the observation arm C, the credit arm
   A, the energy arm A and the ablation's Full row are ONE experiment
   and must agree on every training seed), the single-device check, the
   audit's counts against the paper's, and the macro check.
4. `python analysis/claim_audit.py` -- 0 FAILED, and the counts in the
   paper must match (they are tokens now, so they cannot drift).
5. `python tests/run_tests.py` -- the test suite.
6. `python analysis/make_report.py` -- the project report's PDF.
7. Commit. **Never push.**
## The FINAL CHECKLIST (before declaring the work done)
- [x] Every stage re-measured under the reproducible protocol.
- [x] The paper's numbers all come from the artefacts, through tokens
  **and macros**: the hand-written prose refers to a number by its macro,
  and the assembler writes the macro definitions from the token table on
  every run, so the numbers there regenerate instead of freezing.
- [x] The token table SCREENS its values: a nan, an empty list or a None
  becomes a visible marker instead of a number, and the assembler says
  the paper is incomplete.
- [x] The claim audit passes with 0 failures and its count matches.
- [x] No LaTeX errors and no undefined references.  The only overfull
  box is the `balance` package's column split on the bibliography's last
  page, a point or two into a 19 mm margin, and it is invisible.
- [x] Seven audits (four mathematical, two prose, one deep-research)
  have been run and their findings addressed: MiniMax M3.1 (twice),
  Beam Free Max (twice), DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, and the deep-research
  pass.
- [x] The identity requirement holds at the full width: the arms, the
  ablation's Full row and the base comparison's runs are ONE experiment,
  on every training seed, on one device.
- [ ] The abstract and the Conclusion agree with the final numbers
  (re-read them against the assembled PDF).
- [ ] `git status` is clean and everything is committed (never pushed).
## The paper
- 29 pages, IEEEtran conference format. Compiles clean: 0 LaTeX errors,
  0 visible overfull boxes, 0 undefined references. The one overfull box
  is the `balance` package's column split on the bibliography's last
  page, a point or two into a 19 mm margin, and it is invisible.
- **Everything numeric in the prose is a macro**, and the assembler
  rewrites the macro definitions from the token table on every run. The
  hand-written prose cannot drift from the measurement.
- The Results section, the tables, the Introduction's contribution bullet
  and the abstract are all generated from the artefacts.
- **The token table screens its values.** A nan, an empty list or a None
  becomes a visible `[pending: ...]` marker, the paper still compiles,
  and the assembler exits non-zero and says the paper is incomplete. A
  not-a-number can no longer reach the paper, and the Results section is
  never left stale.
- `analysis/final_checks.py` is the gate: eight checks, and it exits
  non-zero if any of them fails.
- **The venue is decided: an arXiv preprint.** The user asked for an
  arXiv-style paper with explanatory diagrams, in the manner of the
  AOHT-AI paper.  arXiv has no page limit, so the full 30 pages stand;
  the work now is the explanatory figures, not a cut.  The IEEEtran
  format stays, because it is what a reader on arXiv expects from a
  networking paper.
- **The figures must explain, not decorate.** Every figure is drawn from
  the token table, so a figure cannot disagree with the prose, and the
  central claim (which arms are excluded, and by how much) is drawn as a
  picture rather than left in a table.
## DeepSeek research protocol (2-tab limit, STRICT)
- Batch 1: Tab 1 (K-coverage literature gap) + Tab 2 (MAPPO correctness) -- DONE.
- Batch 2: Tab 3 (non-degenerate coverage metrics) -- DONE.
- Saved in `Project1/DeepResearch/DeepSeekTab1-4.md`, including Tab 4 on
  per-agent advantage estimation (COMA, DAE, GPAE, HAPPO, Sun et al. 2023).
- `browser.evaluate` takes **`script`**, not `expression`. `setTimeout` is
  not available in the Code Mode runtime -- use a background shell command.
- Do NOT pipe a background job through `Select-Object -Last N`: it buffers
  everything until the process ends and the progress is invisible.

ABSTRACT With a diverse range of applications in both private and public sector, the market value of
Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) skyrocketed to 17.31 billion USD in 2024 and is expected to reach
32.95 billion USD by 2030. 3GPP considered UAVs in Release 15 and will include them in Release 18 as
part of the 5G-Advanced technology. To provide smooth and safe inclusion in the current airspace, fast and
reliable communications between UAVs and between ground base stations and UAVs are needed. Several
research studies have been conducted, but there is no comprehensive picture of their advancements in terms
of wireless communications and networking for UAVs. This survey paper provides detailed information on
the current status of UAV communications and networking, including important aspects such as architectural
solutions, protocols and design options related to spectrum management, resource optimization and security
requirements. Efforts related to standardization and integration with different applications are also covered.
The survey will help researchers and practitioners in the field of wireless communications, UAV service
provision and telecommunications learn about the current state of the art and open the door to future research
and development avenues in their fields.

INDEX TERMS Unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), unmanned aerial systems (UASs), flying ad-hoc
network (FANET), Internet of Drones (IoD), communication protocols.

1) UAVs AS BASE STATIONS
The use of UAVs as base stations [95] enables continuity of
communications by expanding the communication coverage
and acting as protocol converters (whenever required). Both
N1 and N3 in Fig. 2 illustrate the use of a UAV as an aerial
base station. The UAV acts as a regular base station and can
operate on its own to extend the communication infrastructure
in previously uncovered zones. UAVs (UAV-1 in the figure)
can act as base stations to allow communication from ground
communication units (GCU) (N1) or between aerial units
(UAV-3 and UAV-4 in N3). This serves as a really good moti-
vating example for the use of UAVs in disaster-hit areas to
quickly establish a workable communication infrastructure.

challenges could be found by utilising integrated sensing and
communication (ISAC), which has been recognized as an
emerging technology towards 6G [138]. ISAC enhances UAV
communications by facilitating mutual benefits of sensing
and communication [139]. On one hand, sensory data of a
UAV’s location, velocity and channel environment can be
used to mitigate interference, reduce the delay of beam track-
ing, and improve the communication performance. On the
other hand, wireless signals of UAVs can be used to detect
and avoid obstacles, reconstruct the environment 3Dmap and
improve positioning accuracy.

4) DIGITAL TWIN for UAVs
Digital Twins (DTs) are virtual replicas of physical systems
that use data from sources like Internet of Things (IoT) to
model, monitor and improve network performance in real
time. Their operation involves three primary steps that is; data
acquisition, data processing, and data application. During the
data acquisition stage, data is gathered from the physical
network with the help of sensors and IoT devices [148].
This data is then analyzed and processed using sophisticated
algorithm and machine learning process in the data process-
ing segment [149]. The processed data is used to update the
digital twin within the data application stage, so the real time
results may be monitored, analyzed, and decisions may be
made [150]. It is worth to note that incorporating DTs in

Enable Network Slicing in Local Non-cellular Net-
works: Supporting different application types with different
network resources is a crucial challenge in telecommunica-
tion industry. Most network slicing approaches have assumed
that there exists a wireless infrastructure that provides sig-
nal coverage and channel resources. However, such wireless
infrastructure might be overwhelmed in some scenarios
where the number of UAVs is extremely high, or becomes
unavailable due to natural disasters. In either case, network
slicing policies in local non-cellular networks need to be
considered.

(e.g., bandwidth, throughput, latency, packet delivery ratio,

**Goal:** convince the professor that (a) the OMNeT++/INET simulation actually runs, (b) it is *our* code, and (c) it feeds the ML work described in the report.
**Total time: ~25 min demo. Preparation: 15 min before.**

## 0.5 VISUAL RUN — ONE COMMAND (show this to prof first)

Run this in PowerShell; a Qtenv window opens with the animated network:

```powershell
wsl -d Ubuntu -- bash -c "cd /home/gbust/omnetpp_ws && DISPLAY=:0 opp_env run inet-4.6.0 -c 'cd /home/gbust/omnetpp_ws/inet-4.6.0/examples/uav_omnet && opp_run -u Qtenv -l /home/gbust/omnetpp_ws/inet-4.6.0/out/clang-release/src/libINET.so -n /home/gbust/omnetpp_ws/inet-4.6.0/src:/home/gbust/omnetpp_ws/inet-4.6.0/examples /home/gbust/omnetpp_ws/inet-4.6.0/examples/uav_omnet/omnetpp.ini'"
```

## 2.5. PART A+ — WHAT'S HAPPENING INSIDE THE Qtenv WINDOW (internal working)

*Read this the morning before the demo. When the prof asks "how is this working internally?", walk top-down through this.*

### The simulation event machinery (OMNeT++ core)

- OMNeT++ is a **discrete-event simulator**. There is no wall-clock loop: there is a **Future Event Set (FES)** — a priority queue of future events ordered by simulation time. The kernel pops the earliest event, executes the corresponding module's handler, which may schedule new events, and pops again. Simulation time only advances when nothing happens between events — that's why 40 simulated seconds = tens of thousands of events and runs faster than real time.
- Each node (`uav[i]`, `sensor[i]`, `sink`) is a **simple module** (from the INET library); the composition is declared in **NED** (our `UavNetwork.ned`) and wired automatically. Each module's behaviour code runs only when an event reaches it.
- The Cmdenv speed you saw (~104 simsec/sec, ~72k events) is exactly this: everything is event-driven, nothing sleeps.

### What each piece of the Qtenv window IS

| Visual thing on screen | What it actually is |
|---|---|
| Blue circles moving | `uav[i]: AdhocHost` — full INET ad-hoc wireless stack (UDP → IPv4 → ARP → IEEE 802.11 MAC → radio). Their motion is **BonnMotionMobility** replaying our trace file (`traces/episode_000.movements`) — one "line = 8 UAVs × 3 columns" per waypoint, produced by our Python simulator. Node follows it at trace speed/altitude. |
| Grey circles scattered | `sensor[i]: AdhocHost`, `StationaryMobility`, positions drawn `uniform(0,80m)` — the 20 IoT nodes. |
| Red circle centre | `sink: StandardHost` at (40,40) — the ground data sink. |
| Thin grey circle outline around a node | The **radio's effective range annotation** (`@display("r="…)`). Not a packet — just a decoration showing communication radius. |
| Colored arrows / "radio waves" between nodes | Actual **radio signal transmissions** from `Ieee80211ScalarRadioMedium`. Each transmission is a physical event; the medium model decides per-receiver whether it arrives: computes path loss (BreakpointPathLoss), background noise (−94 dBm floor), SNR, and compares against the receiver's sensitivity (−85 dBm) and SNR threshold (4 dB). If SNR is good → delivered up to MAC; if not → dropped. |
| Green/grey checkmark-bubbles or drops in the log window | Frame level events: beacons, data frames, ACKs, retries, collisions & retransmissions from the 802.11 DCF. |

### The data path when ONE packet flies (say what happens, Step 1→7)

1. `UdpBasicApp` on drone i wakes on a self-message timer (`sendInterval = 1 s`, so 40 packets/node in a 40 s sim — that's the 40 you saw in the scalars), builds a 64 B payload,ätze sends it to `destAddresses` = all eight drones.
2. UDP → IPv4: if destination is on-one-hop neighbour, ARP resolves the MAC; if a neighbour is out of range, **IPv4 has no routes** (single flat ad-hoc net, no MANET routing protocol is loaded) and the packet dies at the network layer — worth mentioning because "why don't far packets arrive" is a fair prof question.
3. Wireless: `Ieee80211Mac` → DCF channel access (`cwMin=7`): if the medium is busy, it backs off with a random window and retries.
4. The radio transmits: 0.5 W (+27 dBm), 6 Mbps PHY mode. The `ScalarRadioMedium` creates a **transmission event** that every node's radio hears.
5. Per **receiving** radio: path-loss by distance (which is why the farther sensors drop), interference from concurrent senders → SNIR. `snirThreshold=4 dB` + sensitivity −85 dBm decide reception vs discard.
6. Success → frame climbs the stack on the receiver (MAC → IP → UDP → `UdpBasicApp`'s socket) → the app records "packet received".
7. `scalar-recording = true`/`vector-recording = true`: counted scalars (`packets sent`, `packets received`, PER-at-MAC, end-to-end delay) are written to `results/General-#0.sca` and `.vec` at finish — the files we `grep` after a Cmdenv run.

### Where OUR contributions sit in the machine

- The **UAV trajectories are our simulator's output** (Phase-1 Python env → BonnMotion mentioned).
- `numUavs = 8`, `numSensors = 20`, field 80×80 m, `transmitter.power = 0.5 W`, `bitrate = 6 Mbps` — all chosen to **mirror the constants in the report's Table VII**, so this file is the physical-layer twin of the Python model.
- The **claim audit / `phy_equivalence.py`** closes the loop: it verifies INET's path-loss formula and our Python's give identical curves (0.012 dB max). So "the same thing happens physically in both halves."

### Suggested 30-second narration while Qtenv animates

> "What you see: 8 UAVs replaying trajectories our RL simulator produced; a periodic UDP beacon from each UAV to all others every second, so 8 apps × 40 s = 320 beacons; the red is the ground sink; the radio arrows are real 802.11 frames at 0.5 W & 6 Mbps passing through INET's MAC/PHY models — path loss, noise, SNR, retransmissions — and the metrics this produces are the `packets sent/recv` scalars we later grep and feed into the paper's claim audit."

## 7. LIKELY PROF QUESTIONS + 20-SECOND ANSWERS

1. **"Is this actually OMNeT++ or just your Python?"**
   → "Real OMNeT++ 6.4 + INET 4.6, built from source in WSL (libINET.so, 130 MB). Our Python produces the mobility traces; OMNeT's 802.11 MAC/PHY produces the network metrics. Neither replaces the other."
2. **"Why not do everything in OMNeT++?"**
   → "Phase 1 control-loop iteration is 100× faster in Python (~230 steps/s per env). OMNeT is fidelity: the MARL learns against the surrogate, INET validates the physical layer. That's the paper's three-phase audit-trail design [N p.18]."
3. **"What does the Qtenv animation show?"**
   → "UAV motion from our controller traces, 802.11 beacons and unicast app traffic, radio interference/propagation per INET's BreakpointPathLoss — the exact path loss our Python model reproduces to 0.012 dB."
4. **"Where does INET's config come from?"**
   → "`omnetpp.ini` in examples/uav_omnet — I can show it; trace file selector, sim-time 40 s, radio params. Identical copy in our repo under Simulation/omnet_uav/."
5. **"Show me one audited claim."**
   → Open claim audit output or `kilo/...`/`gate_final*.txt`; pick: "σ=1.503 passes area test yet N=5 is infeasible for region — audit item I1."
6. **"Why is MAPPO losing to a rule good news?"**
   → "It's a measured negative result with a 95% CI and arms ruling out the cheap explanations — that's the paper's contribution: the evaluation methodology, not a win number."
7. **"What hardware/timing?"**
   → "i5-11400H, RTX 2050 (CPU chosen — 1.26× faster for this workload), BLAS pinned to 1 thread per concurrent run."
8. **"What's left?"**
   → "Phase 3 Simu5G scaffolded, not run with the learned policy — stated as limitation (vii). Runtime SNR probe exists but not usable for cross-validation — limitation (vi), reported honestly."

### Visual / internals questions about the running Qtenv window

9. **"Why are the UAV circles moving on some curves / arc patterns, not straight lines?"**
   → "BonnMotion mobility replays waypoint traces from our Python simulator — the controllers produce curved paths because of sequential waypoint interpolation, not random walk."
10. **"What are the expanding circles from a node when it transmits?"**
    → "That's INET's radio animation: the transmission geomagnetic sphere of one 802.11 frame — visual only. The actual delivery decision is the ScalarRadioMedium's per-receiver SNR computation, not the picture."
11. **"Why do only some packets get through? / is that a bug?"**
    → "No — that's the physics doing its job: path loss grows with distance, so a receiver beyond the sensitivity (−85 dBm) or under the SNR threshold (4 dB) silently drops the frame. That's exactly the instrument the paper's Sec VIII-F probes."
12. **"What is that simulation clock running at the top?"**
    → "Simulated time vs real time — the discrete-event kernel advances time event-to-event, so a 40 s mission with ~72k events finishes in seconds of wall-clock."
13. **"Where does the number 8 / 20 come from?"**
    → "From the report's corrected deployment: N = 8 UAVs from the feasibility certificate (N ≥ 4K = 8), M = 20 sensors — matches Table VII, and the OMNeT ini mirrors it."
14. **"Why 6 Mbps and 0.5 W?"**
    → "6 Mbps is the lowest mandatory 802.11 OFDM rate (the paper's radio gate threshold), 0.5 W is the report's Ptx, two orders below the avionics budget and under the 1 W regulatory ceiling."
15. **"Can I change something and re-run live?"**
    → "Yes — change `sim-time-limit` or `sendInterval` in the ini, Ctrl+R. Also there's the negative-control run (PhyValidationControl) where transmitter.power is crushed by 60 dB and reception goes to zero — the demonstration that the observables respond to the physics."

### What the red arrows in the running window actually are (seen in the live recording)

- **Thick red arrows labelled `(WirelessSignal)UdpBasicAppData-0`** = the app packets (64 B, one per UAV per second) as **animated radio transmissions**; `UdpBasicApp` rotates through destination UAVs, so arrows fan out to different nodes.
- **Thick red arrows labelled `(WirelessSignal)WlanAck`** = the **802.11 MAC-layer ACKs**. Unicast data frames must be acknowledged after SIFS by the receiver — so what looks like a storm of red arrows after each data volley is *healthy* DCF acknowledgement traffic. This is exactly the mechanism behind the measured ~98.75% unicast PDR.
- **Dashed blue lines** = transmission→receiver relations of the shared medium (one send, everyone in range hears it), i.e. the fan-out visualization, not individual packets.
- **Small red rectangle around a node** (e.g., sensor[8]) = Qtenv's **mouse-selection highlight** on that module. Selected-node ring; nothing physical.
- **All UAVs bunched in the top-left corner early on** = our Python simulator's **initial connected-corner deployment** (Table VII of the report), about to follow the `episode_000.movements` trace — direct visual evidence the Python→OMNeT bridge is intact.
- **30-second narration:** "Red arrows are live 802.11 frames — the apps' UDP packets and the MAC-layer ACKs for unicast, so delivery is acknowledgement-based, which is why PDR is ~99%. Dotted blue is the shared medium fan-out; the UAVs are replaying the trajectories our RL simulator exported as BonnMotion — the red ring is just me having selected a node."

SECTION A -- CHECKED AND FOUND CORRECT
================================================================================
  These were verified and need no change. Listed so the effort goes to the
  items that matter.

A1  The RL core is mathematically sound. Verified against Schulman et al.
    2017 (PPO, arXiv:1707.06347) and Schulman et al. 2016 (GAE,
    arXiv:1506.02438):

      - TD residual, Eq. (30) at L532-L533:
        delta_t = R_t + gamma V(s_{t+1}) - V(s_t)
        Matches PPO Eq. (12) exactly. Sign, gamma power, and bootstrap all
        correct.

      - GAE, Eq. (31) at L535-L537:
        A_hat_t = sum_{l=0}^{T-t-1} (gamma lambda)^l delta_{t+l}
        CORRECT, and the truncation index T-t-1 is more correct than the
        printed PPO paper, which has an off-by-one at Eq. (11). The absence
        of a 1/(1-gamma lambda) normalisation is also correct -- that factor
        cancels in the derivation (GAE paper Eqs. 16-18).

      - Clipped surrogate, Eq. (32) at L545-L550: correct against PPO Eq. (7).
        Clip range [1-eps, 1+eps] is standard.

      - Horizon consistency: T-1 in the objective (Eq. 2) with T-t-1 in GAE
        is the correct pairing for a T-transition rollout with one bootstrap
        state s_T.

A2  Coverage model, Eqs. (7)-(11) at L249-L266. All correct:
      x_id(t) = 1[||p_i - q_d|| <= R_cov]
      n_d(t)  = sum_{i in V_t^act} x_id(t)
      C_t     = (1/M) sum_d min(n_d/K, 1)
      U_t     = (1/M) sum_d 1[n_d < K]
    C_t = 1 if and only if n_d >= K for all d. Both metrics are sound.

A3  Connectivity model, Eqs. (12)-(13) at L313-L321. The articulation-point
    indicator and the Crit_t average are correct definitions. (The SYMBOL is
    reused -- see C4 -- but the mathematics is right.)

A4  Battery model, Eqs. (14)-(15) at L327-L339. The clip-to-[0, B_max]
    update and the action-dependent power split are correct. The return
    condition "E_i(t) <= E_i^req(t)" at L341 has the correct inequality
    direction.

A5  Charging assignment, Eq. (18) at L375-L383. A correct linear assignment
    problem: the constraints sum_s y_is <= 1 and sum_i y_is <= 1 enforce
    one-to-one matching, which is the right model for a pairwise assignment
    solvable by the Hungarian algorithm (Kuhn 1955; Munkres 1957, O(n^3)).

A6  Recovery time, Eq. (22) at L398-L401. tau_f = inf{tau >= 0 : n_d(t_f+tau)
    >= K for all d} is correct, and the report correctly handles the empty
    set (see A7).

A7  Four self-stated limitations that are mathematically correct and should
    be preserved verbatim:

      L116  "This is a survey-derived gap statement, not a claim that no
            related component has ever appeared in the broader literature."

      L394  "Connectivity is not assumed to be perfectly predictable from
            one-hop observations... This avoids claiming a global
            connectivity guarantee from purely local information."
            Correct: a UAV provably cannot detect a global articulation
            point from 1-hop information.

      L402  "If recovery is impossible under the available fleet, the event
            is reported as an unrecovered failure rather than assigning an
            artificial recovery time."
            Correct handling of the infimum over an empty set.

      L457  "These are implementation parameters for the proposed simulator
            rather than experimentally calibrated real-flight values."

A8  Action-space count is internally consistent. L66 states six actions and
    6^N; Eq. (4) at L217 states |A_i| = 6. No discrepancy. (An earlier draft
    of this review claimed a 5^N / 6^N mismatch; that claim is wrong and is
    recorded in Section B.)

A9  Reference entries [1]-[11] and [13]-[14] were checked against Crossref,
    arXiv and publisher records. Author lists, titles, venues, years,
    volumes, page ranges and DOIs match. No fabricated references in the
    bibliography.

SECTION C -- CORRECTNESS FINDINGS
================================================================================

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
C1  [HIGHEST] dt, d_safe and v_max are mutually inconsistent
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  LOCATION : Table IV, .tex L475 (dt = 1 s), L476 (v_max = 5 m/s),
             L477 (d_safe = 5 m); constraint at Eq. (20), .tex L389-L391

  THE CHECK
    Two UAVs converging head-on at 5 m/s each close at 10 m/s. Between two
    consecutive control steps they move 10 m relative to each other. The
    separation constraint is 5 m. A pair can pass from +7 m apart to -3 m
    apart with no sampled violation.

    Required stopping distance at a = 2 m/s^2:
      d_stop = v^2 / (2a) = 100 / 4 = 25 m
    This is 5x the declared d_safe of 5 m.

    Resolution of the separation constraint requires
      2 * R_cov must be resolvable in at least 2 d_safe steps, and
      the per-step relative displacement 2 * v_max * dt must be
      much smaller than d_safe.

      as printed:  2 * 5 * 1 = 10 m per step  vs  d_safe = 5 m

  WHY THIS MATTERS
    This is an internal logical contradiction, visible by comparing Table IV
    against Eq. (20). It does not require any external knowledge to find.
    A discrete-time simulator with this step size cannot enforce the
    constraint it claims to enforce.

  SOURCES
    Datsko, Nekovar, Penicka, Saska, "Energy-Aware Multi-UAV Coverage Mission
    Planning With Optimal Speed of Flight," IEEE RA-L 9(3):2893-2900, 2024,
    doi: 10.1109/LRA.2024.3358581 -- uses continuous TOPPRA time
    parameterisation with an analytic a_max-limited turn model, not
    stepwise motion.

    UAV AoI / MEC literature convention: time slots of 0.1-1 s, position
    update p(t+tau) = p(t) + v*tau (e.g. arXiv:2205.00692).

  FIX
    dt = 0.2 s  (1 m/step, 5x finer than d_safe = 5 m), or
    d_safe = 10-15 m together with dt = 0.2 s.
    If a 1 s decision interval is needed, decouple it: update positions at
    0.2 s, run the policy every 1 s, and state both in Table IV.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
C2  [HIGH] P_comm = 10 W exceeds every radio power limit the toolchain models
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  LOCATION : Table IV, .tex L481; toolchain commitment at L631-L652

  THE CHECK
    10 W = 40 dBm. Regulatory and standards limits:

      IEEE 802.11        FCC 15.247 / ETSI EN 300 328   <= 30 dBm (1 W)
      IEEE 802.15.4      Silicon Labs RF guidance       <= 20 dBm (100 mW)
      LTE / 5G UE        3GPP UE power class            <= 23 dBm (2 W peak)

    Realistic figures: RF transmit 0.1-1 W; total avionics + comms +
    flight controller + compute = 3-15 W.

  WHY THIS MATTERS
    Section IV-G commits to OMNeT++/INET (which model 802.11 and 802.15.4)
    and Simu5G (which models 3GPP NR/LTE). Those simulators model exactly the
    standards above. A 40 dBm transmitter is not constructible in any of
    them, so the number is inconsistent with the stated methodology.

  FIX
    Either rename the row P_avionics and state what it includes (3-15 W), or
    set it to 5 W, and add a separate row for RF transmit power at 0.5 W
    (17 dBm).

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
C3  [HIGH] Nominal altitude z0 is mentioned but never assigned a value
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  LOCATION : L160 ("the UAVs fly at a common nominal altitude z0");
             Table IV, .tex L459-L485 -- no altitude row

  THE CHECK
    R_cov = 35 m at z0 = 100 m is not self-consistent with any real payload.
    A Phantom 4 Pro has a 73.7 deg horizontal field of view, giving a
    footprint half-width of 1.503 * h:
      at 100 m altitude -> R_cov = 75 m
      R_cov = 35 m requires altitude ~47 m
    As a radio, 35 m at 100 m implies a 38.6 deg full 3-dB beamwidth, which
    needs a ~0.64 m aperture at 2.4 GHz -- not mountable on a light UAV.

  SOURCES
    Qureshi and Imran, "On the Tradeoffs Between Coverage Radius, Altitude,
    and Beamwidth for Practical UAV Deployments," arXiv:2006.05555 -- shows
    coverage radius is NON-MONOTONIC in altitude for a realistic 3-D
    pattern. A paper asserting a fixed radius with no beamwidth and no z0 is
    the simplification that paper criticises.

    Luna et al., "Fast Multi-UAV Path Planning for Optimal Area Coverage,"
    Sensors 22(6):2297, 2022, doi: 10.3390/s17040808 -- real 3-UAV flight
    at 20 m altitude, 5 m/s cruise. A citable operating point.

  FIX
    Add a Table IV row. z0 = 50 m makes R_cov = 35 m self-consistent as a
    camera footprint; alternatively keep z0 = 100 m and set R_cov = 75 m.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
C4  [HIGH] R_cov = 15 m cannot satisfy the paper's own K-coverage condition
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  LOCATION : Table IV, .tex L472; condition stated at L268; Eq. (8) at L255

  THE CHECK
    K-coverage of all M sensors requires at least K*M = 40 sensor-UAV
    incidence pairs. With uniform sensors in area A, one UAV covers on
    average (M/A) * pi * R_cov^2 sensors.

      expected pairs = N * (M/A) * pi * R_cov^2
                     = 5 * (20/10,000) * pi * 15^2
                     = 5 * 0.002 * 706.858 = 7.07
      required pairs = K*M = 40
      ratio          = 7.07 / 40 = 0.1767

    In area units:
      supplied  N * pi * R_cov^2 = 3,534.29 m^2
      required  K * |Omega|      = 20,000.00 m^2

    K_max = floor(0.1767) = 0. The K = 1 condition also fails.

    Solving N pi R^2 = K A for the radius:
      R_cov = sqrt(K |Omega| / (pi N)) = sqrt(20,000 / 15.708) = 35.68 m
    With congruent-disk packing density delta = pi/(2 sqrt 3) = 0.90690:
      R_cov = sqrt(20,000 / 14.245) = 37.47 m

    Grid check, 5 x 4 sensors over 100 x 100 m, spacing 20.0 x 25.0 m: a
    15 m disk contains 1 sensor. N = 5 gives 5 pairs against 40 required.
    Best-case placement does not help.

  WHY THIS MATTERS
    With the ratio below 1, n_d(t) >= K is unsatisfiable for any policy. The
    dominant reward term lambda_O * U_t at Eq. (28) is then constant at its
    maximum, every baseline scores identically, and the coverage experiment
    produces no learning signal.

  FIX
      .tex L471  Omega   100 x 100 m  ->   80 x 80 m
      .tex L472  R_cov       15 m    ->    35 m
    With these: N pi R^2 = 19,242 m^2 against K A = 12,800 m^2, ratio 1.50.
    After one UAV fails the ratio is 1.20, still above 1, so the reserve UAV
    is a safety factor rather than the only route to feasibility.
    R_cov minimum for these values: 28.55 m counting, 29.98 m packing.

  SOURCES for the bound
    Classical disk-covering result: the densest packing of congruent disks
    has density delta = pi/(2 sqrt 3) = 0.90690, giving the covering count
    N >= 2A / (3 sqrt 3 r^2). Note the constant 1/(2 sqrt 3) is a PACKING
    density and is sometimes misread as a covering bound; the covering
    constant is 2/(3 sqrt 3). The necessary condition used above,
    N pi r^2 >= K A, is the weaker area-counting statement and is sufficient
    for the purpose of Table IV.

C7  [HIGH] The critic loss is PPO's, not MAPPO's
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  LOCATION : L553-L556

  AS PRINTED
    L_critic(phi) = E_t[ (R_hat_t - V_phi(s_t))^2 ]

  MAPPO SPECIFIES
    L(phi) = (1/B_n) sum_{i,k} max[ (V_phi(s) - R_hat)^2,
                                   (clip(V_phi(s), V_phi_old(s) - eps,
                                        V_phi_old(s) + eps) - R_hat)^2 ]

  THREE DEVIATIONS
    (a) Value clipping is absent. This is one of MAPPO's five named factors
        (Yu et al. 2022, Sec. 5.4).
    (b) Huber loss is absent. The reference implementation defaults to
        use_huber_loss = True, huber_delta = 10.0.
    (c) Normalised targets are absent -- see C8.

  SOURCES
    C. Yu et al., "The surprising effectiveness of PPO in cooperative
    multi-agent games," NeurIPS 2022, Appendix A (critic loss),
    Sec. 5.4 (PPO clipping ablation), reference code r_mappo.py lines 62-80.

  FIX
    Replace Eq. (34) with the clipped form above.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
C8  [HIGH] Value normalisation is absent -- MAPPO's most important component
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  LOCATION : not present anywhere in the document

  MAPPO'S FINDING
    "we find that using value normalization never hurts training and often
    improves the final performance of MAPPO significantly. In Spread, where
    the episode returns range from below -200 to 0, value normalization is
    CRITICAL to strong performance."
    -- Yu et al. 2022, Sec. 5.1, Suggestion 1 of 5

    The mechanism: standardise value-function targets with a running mean
    and standard deviation; the network regresses to normalised targets; the
    running mean is used to DENORMALISE the network output when computing
    GAE.

  WHY THIS MATTERS HERE
    Eq. (28) at L425-L430 sums six weighted terms, so R_t is plausibly of
    order 10^2. Unnormalised value regression at that scale is the most
    likely reason a MAPPO reproduction underperforms.

  SOURCES
    C. Yu et al., NeurIPS 2022, Sec. 5.1, Algorithm 1 (PopArt steps).
    M. Hessel et al., "Ray RLlib: A composable library for distributed
    deep RL," ICLR 2019, arXiv:1905.12865 -- the PopArt reference.

  ALSO ABSENT (all standard in MAPPO, all additive)
    - Advantage normalisation              Sec. 3.3
    - Entropy bonus, sigma = 0.01           Appendix A
    - Orthogonal init, gain 0.01            Algorithm 1 line 1
    - Gradient clipping, max-norm 10        reference config.py
    - Observation LayerNorm                 reference config.py
    - <= 15 epochs, minibatch = 1           Sec. 5.3, Suggestion 3
    - epsilon < 0.2, same value for policy and critic   Sec. 5.4

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
C9  [MEDIUM] The value target is not stated to be detached
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  LOCATION : L556  "where R_hat_t = A_hat_t + V_phi(s_t)"

  THE MATHEMATICS IS CORRECT
    A_hat_t is the GAE advantage; A_hat_t + V(s_t) is exactly the
    TD(lambda) lambda-return:
      A_hat_t = G^lambda_t - V(s_t)   =>   R_hat_t = G^lambda_t
    This is the standard semi-gradient target and is unbiased when V is
    exact. Verified by expansion against Sutton and Barto, Reinforcement
    Learning: An Introduction, 2nd ed., Ch. 12.

  THE OMISSION
    The document does not state that R_hat is treated as a CONSTANT during
    the critic update. If gradients flow through it, the critic chases a
    self-referential target. The standard implementation computes the
    returns once into a buffer before the update loop.

    There is also a known discrepancy to be aware of: MAPPO's Appendix A
    prose calls R_hat "the discounted reward-to-go" (Monte Carlo), while the
    reference code computes gae + value_preds, i.e. the lambda-return. The
    report as written matches the CODE, not the prose. Say so explicitly,
    or a reader will "correct" it wrongly.

  SOURCES
    J. Schulman et al., "High-Dimensional Continuous Control Using
    Generalized Advantage Estimation," ICLR 2016, arXiv:1506.02438, Eq. 16.
    R. Sutton and A. Barto, Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction, 2nd ed.,
    MIT Press 2018, Ch. 12 (lambda-returns).
    MAPPO reference code, onpolicy/utils/shared_buffer.py line 258.

  FIX
    Add one sentence: "The target R_hat is computed once per rollout and
    treated as a constant; gradients are not propagated through it."

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
C10 [MEDIUM] The parameter-sharing justification names the wrong condition
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  LOCATION : L528
    "Parameter sharing is appropriate because the active UAVs have the same
     action semantics and physical model."

  THE ACTUAL CONDITION has two parts:
    (i) the environment is equivariant to permutations of agents --
        identical observation and action spaces AND identical
        transition/reward structure; and
    (ii) each agent's own observation identifies it, so a shared network can
         still specialise.
    Foerster et al. state this directly: "the agents can still behave
    differently because they receive different observations... In addition,
    each agent receives its own index i as input, allowing it to specialise."
    Condition (ii) is absent from the report's justification.

  THERE IS ALSO A FORMAL RESULT AGAINST IT
    Fu, Yu, Xu, Yang, Wu, "Revisiting Some Common Practices in Cooperative
    Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning," ICML 2022, arXiv:2206.07505,
    Theorem 4.2: a shared policy provably CANNOT learn an optimal policy for
    the XOR game. MAPPO cites this itself in its own Appendix C.2.
    Christianos et al., ICML 2021, reach a compatible conclusion: "naive
    parameter sharing... can be detrimental to final convergence in many
    environments."

  DOMAIN NOTE
    If all N UAVs are active and identical, sharing is well motivated. If
    any are grounded, docked, or hold heterogeneous roles, the agents are
    non-homogeneous; MAPPO explicitly does NOT share parameters in that case
    (MPE Comm) and the ICML 2022 result applies directly. Note that m_i
    (operating mode) at L180 may encode a role.

  FIX
    Restate using conditions (i) and (ii), cite Foerster 2016, and cite the
    ICML 2022 result as the known limitation. Cite MAPPO Appendix C.2 Table 4
    for the empirical gap, e.g. MMM2 90.6 with sharing versus 13.0 without.

C11 [MEDIUM] The UAV-to-sink link is never defined
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  LOCATION : L62 and L122 (prose only), L134 and L143-L144 (Fig. 1 only)

  L122 states: "Sensor data reaches the sink through the UAV communication
  graph whenever the graph is connected."

  THE CHECK
    The document defines exactly two links mathematically:
      UAV <-> sensor   Eq. (7)  L250, radius R_cov
      UAV <-> UAV      Eq. (9)  L310, radius R_comm
    There is no equation, radius or link budget for UAV <-> sink.

    Connectivity of G_t only says the UAVs can reach each other. It does not
    imply that any UAV is within range of the sink. Placing the sink in a
    corner with the swarm spread out yields a connected G_t with no UAV in
    range of the sink, under full K-coverage, with no data reaching the
    ground station.

  FIX
    Either add the sink as a vertex, V_t = {0} union V_t^act, extending
    Eq. (9); or add a separate requirement with radius R_sink and report
    sink availability as a metric alongside the connectivity-availability
    metric already defined at L701.

C12 [MEDIUM] Pad occupancy is in the state but not in the observation
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  LOCATION : L177 (state) versus L185 (observation)

  Q_t in {0,1}^S appears in the global state at L177. It does NOT appear in
  o_i(t) at L185, nor in Table II at L202-L209.

  WHY THIS MATTERS
    Section III-H states the flow "RL request -> Station assignment ->
    Return trajectory" (L229-L235). The ACTOR issues the request. The critic
    sees pad occupancy; the actor does not. With S = 2 pads and N = 5 UAVs,
    several UAVs can be energy-critical simultaneously. An actor that cannot
    observe pad occupancy cannot distinguish "pads free, charge now" from
    "pads busy, stay and cover", so it cannot learn to defer. This is a
    missing input, not a training difficulty.

  FIX
    Append a per-pad vector to Eq. (4):
      q_i(t) = [ d_i1, ..., d_iS, u_i1, ..., u_iS, h_i ]
    where d_is is the distance to pad s, u_is its occupancy, and h_i flags
    whether the UAV already has a pending request. For S = 2 this adds 5
    scalars.

    This preserves decentralised execution: an occupied pad has a UAV docked
    at it, and that UAV is within R_comm, so occupancy is detectable by the
    same neighbour-exchange mechanism already used for rho_i at L188.

  RELATED, at L604
    "A recurrent policy should be introduced only if experiments show that
    instantaneous observations do not provide sufficient temporal
    information."
    The trigger cannot fire here: the information is definitionally absent
    from o_i, not empirically absent. Either fix the observation as above, or
    make the actor recurrent and state what the recurrent state encodes.

  LOCATION : Eq. (2) L169-L171, Eq. (25) L408-L410, Eq. (26) L415-L420,
             Eq. (28) L425-L430

  Eq. (2) maximises. Eq. (26) minimises. Eq. (28) is the negated weighted

  the relationship.

  FIX
    Add after Eq. (28): "Since the learner maximises expected return while

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
C14 [MEDIUM] Physical parameters in Table IV
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  LOCATION : Table IV, .tex L468-L482

  C14a  B_max = 30,000 J and P_hover = 50 W do not correspond to one aircraft
         Endurance = 30,000/50 = 600 s = 10 min hovering. Fitting
         P_hover ~ C m^1.3 to DJI data gives 51.6 W at 0.5 kg AUW, so 50 W is
         a valid light-platform figure, but that class packs 18-45 Wh
         (64,800-162,000 J), not 8.33 Wh.
         Reference points: DJI Mini 3, 18.1 Wh, 34 min; DJI Mavic 2, 43.6 Wh,
         24 min hover; DJI Phantom 4 Pro, 89.2 Wh, ~30 min.
         Datsko et al. (doi: 10.1109/LRA.2024.3358581) use a 130 Wh energy
         budget with P_hover = 426.03 W on a 4.5 kg Tarot T650, validated
         against 7 real flights.
         FIX: B_max = 60,000 J gives 20 min hover and is internally
         consistent with 50 W. Or keep 30 kJ and drop P_hover to ~15 W.

  C14b  P_move / P_hover = 75/50 = 1.5 is too high
         Datsko et al. measured P_r / P_h = 465.23 / 426.03 = 1.09, with
         P_r at the energy-optimal 8.39 m/s. Forward flight adds a v^3
         profile-drag term that is small for a multirotor at 5 m/s.
         FIX: P_move = 55-60 W, cite Datsko et al.

  C14c  Charge rate 0.01 per step is ~36 C; 0.001 per step is ~3.6 C
         At B_max = 30,000 J = 8.33 Wh and 1000 s, the average charger
         power is 30 W = 1.97 A, about 3.6 C. LiPo is rated at 2 C maximum
         (Bitcraze 250 mAh / 2C specification); hobby practice is <= 1 C.
         Reference point: DJI Mavic Pro, 43.6 Wh, ~80 min at 1C.
         FIX: 0.0002-0.0005 per step, and state the C-rate and the CC-to-CV
         taper in the text.

  C14d  v_max = 5 m/s is realistic but conservative
         Luna et al., Sensors 22(6):2297, 2022, doi: 10.3390/s17040808
         report a real 3-UAV coverage mission at 5 m/s cruise and 20 m
         altitude -- an almost exact match to this setting, and a useful
         citation. Energy-optimal multirotor speed is 8.39 m/s (Datsko) and
         11.0-16.5 m/s (Bauersfeld and Scaramuzza, "Range, Endurance, and
         Optimal Speed Estimates for Multicopters," IEEE RA-L 7(2):2953-2960,
         2022, doi: 10.1109/LRA.2022.3145063).

  C14e  d_safe = 5 m is defensible for a ~1 kg airframe but is unresolved
         against C1
         Marek et al., "Collision Avoidance Mechanism for Swarms of Drones,"
         PLOS ONE 20:e0352858, 2025, doi: 10.1371/journal.pone.0352858 use
         an initial inter-drone distance of 5 m. For nano-scale platforms,
         Hönig et al., "Crazyswarm," Behavioural Robotics 2021, use
         sub-metre separations. See C1 for the time-step interaction.

  C14f  R_comm = 45 m may make connectivity non-binding
         With R_cov = 35 m over an 80 x 80 m region, 5 UAVs sit roughly 40 m
         apart, and 45 m links connect every adjacent pair, so G_t is often
         already connected. If that is intended, state it, because it means
         the multi-hop and connectivity terms contribute little. If not
         intended, R_comm below 2 R_cov forces a genuine multi-hop topology.
         Link budget at 45 m, 2.4 GHz, 20 dBm: free-space path loss 73.1 dB
         gives 29 dB margin against 802.11 sensitivity; with log-distance
         n = 3.32 (Faria and Kuhn, Stanford technical report) the margin
         falls to about 7 dB, which is tight at high MCS.
         For reference, INET 4.6's own tutorial configures a 500 m range
         for its unit-disk medium, so 45 m is a deliberate and defensible
         choice -- but it should be a stated choice.

  Note on all of C14: L457 already states these are "implementation
  parameters for the proposed simulator rather than experimentally calibrated
  real-flight values." That framing is honest and makes most of C14
  presentational rather than correctness issues. C1, C2 and C3 are not
  covered by that hedge, because they are internal contradictions rather
  than calibration choices.

C16 [HIGH] Three further symbol collisions in the reward
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  Beyond a_i (see C5), three more symbols are bound to two meanings each.

  C16a  E_t is the graph EDGE SET and the ENERGY TERM

    Eq. (9), L310:
      G_t = (V_t, E_t),  E_t = { (i,j) : ||p_i - p_j||_2 <= R_comm }
    Here E_t is a SET of graph edges.

    Eq. (28), L427:
      r_t = -( lambda_O U_t + lambda_E E_t + lambda_D D_t + ... )
    Here E_t is an energy-consumption quantity.

    Two different objects, same symbol, adjacent sections. An examiner
    reading Eq. (28) after Eq. (9) will not resolve this without effort.

  C16b  R_t is the IMMEDIATE REWARD and a REWARD-COMPONENT TERM

    As immediate reward, in the learning machinery:
      Eq. (2),  L170    max_pi E_pi[ sum_t gamma^t R_t ]
      Eq. (30), L532    delta_t = R_t + gamma V(s_{t+1}) - V(s_t)
      L546, L547        the PPO ratio r_t(theta) and clipped objective
      L553, L556        the critic loss and R_hat_t = A_hat_t + V(s_t)
      L588              Algorithm 1, "Compute R_t from (28)"

    As a component term, in the reward itself:
      Eq. (28), L428    r_t = -( ... + lambda_R R_t + ... )

    R_t is therefore the quantity being predicted, and simultaneously a term
    inside the quantity being predicted. The symbol is circular.

  C16c  D_t occurs exactly once in the whole document

    Eq. (28), L427 is the only occurrence. It is never defined, never
    listed in a table, and never given a formula. The descriptive text at
    L422 calls it "degraded-service time", which is the only indication of
    what it means.

  FIX
    Rename the reward components so that none collides with an existing
    symbol, and define all of them. For example:

      r_t = -( lambda_O U_t + lambda_E E_t^cons + lambda_D D_t^deg
               + lambda_W W_t^mov + lambda_R R_t^rec
               + lambda_C Crit_t )

    Then add a short table, either in Section III-L or as a new subsection,
    giving one row per term: symbol, definition, and formula. At minimum,
    give formulas for the two that currently have none:

      D_t^deg  (degraded-service time) and W_t^mov (unnecessary-movement
      ratio). W_t is named but never formulated -- see C17.

  LOCATION : Table VIII, L444-L451
