The differences below are the FULL configuration minus the variant, so a negative number is what the component is worth on this scenario.  The differences between the variants are of the same order as the width of the intervals, so the table reports what the stress scenario does to the swarm and not which component matters.  The framework's recovery mechanism, which re-seats an exhausted UAV at a charging pad, is a plausible mechanism for the behaviour of the stress scenario --- a re-seated UAV is out of communication range of the swarm until it flies back --- but this table does not resolve it, and we do not claim it.

\subsection{The credit assignment, and the cheapest test of it}
\label{sec:results_credit}

The diagnosis of Sections~\ref{sec:results_obs} and
\ref{sec:results_energy} points at one mechanism: with a shared team
reward every agent receives the same advantage, so the gradient cannot
distinguish an agent whose action helped from one whose action was
irrelevant.  The literature calls this the credit-assignment problem, and
the remedies are known: the counterfactual advantage of COMA, the
difference-based estimator of DAE, the per-agent value iteration of GPAE, and
the advantage decomposition of HAPPO/HATRPO~\cite{foerster2018,li2022,kim2026,kuba2022}.
None of them has been evaluated on a persistent-coverage task, and the
question of whether the credit assignment is what limits a
parameter-shared controller in that setting appears to be open.

Table~\ref{tab:results_credit} is the cheapest test of it that does not
require implementing a new algorithm, and it is worth being exact about
what it does and does not change.  The two arms differ in the learner that
produces the advantage.  Arm~A is the proposed method: a parameter-shared
actor with a centralised critic, so every agent receives the same broadcast
team advantage.  Arm~B keeps the same simulator, the same observation, the
same action mask, the same team reward and the same episode budget, and
replaces the learner with a per-agent actor and a per-agent local critic.
Nothing else changes.

What that does and does not change is worth stating plainly, because it
bounds the conclusion.  With a team reward $r_t$ broadcast to every agent,
the advantage is $r_t+\gamma V(o')-V(o)$.  Giving each agent its own
value function re-centres and re-scales that expression per agent, so the
advantage is no longer a single shared number, but it cannot decompose it,
because the advantage's dependence on the other agents enters only through
the aggregate reward and through the observation, which are symmetric in
the other agents.  Redistribution of credit requires a per-agent reward, a
joint-action critic, or a counterfactual baseline.

\begin{table}[t]
% the shared table style: analysis/theme_tables.tex, the file the
% report's preamble loads; see that file's header comment
\ifdefined\tbltheme\else
  \IfFileExists{ml_impl/analysis/theme_tables.tex}{\input{ml_impl/analysis/theme_tables.tex}}{%
  \IfFileExists{theme_tables.tex}{\input{theme_tables.tex}}{%
  \errmessage{the tables need ml_impl/analysis/theme_tables.tex}}}
\fi

\caption{The cheapest test of the credit-assignment hypothesis.  The two arms differ in the learner that produces the advantage: a parameter-shared actor with a centralised critic, or a per-agent actor with a per-agent local critic.  A per-agent \emph{baseline} changes the variance of the advantage, not its signal, which remains the shared team reward.}
\label{tab:results_credit}
\centering
\scriptsize
\setlength{\tabcolsep}{2.5pt}
\begin{tabular}{@{}lccccc@{}}
\toprule
 & \tblGroup{4}{Task metrics} & Energy (J) \\
\cmidrule(lr){2-5}
Learner & CK & AG & SC & CovIntegral &  \\
\midrule
\tblHl \textbf{A} & \textbf{0.674\,$\pm$\,0.060} & \textbf{0.987} & \textbf{0.010} & \textbf{0.326} & \textbf{--} \\
B & 0.639\,$\pm$\,0.051 & 0.983 & 0.005 & 0.361 & -- \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\tblNote{* Energy is not recorded in this artefact.}
\end{table}

The per-agent arm reaches $0.639$ against $0.674$ for
the shared one, a difference of $-0.035$ in persistent coverage.
Arm~A is the proposed method on the first 8 of the base
comparison's training runs --- the same policies, not a cheaper experiment
--- so the two rows of the first table and this table describe the same
learner.
The two arms share their training seeds, so the comparison is paired, and
the 95\% interval on the paired difference is $[-0.079, +0.009]$ over
8 training runs: the difference is not resolved by this arm: the interval is [-0.079, +0.009], and its best case is 0.009 better, far short of the gap of 0.298, and its worst case is 0.079 worse, so the cheapest modification in the direction the diagnosis points has not been shown to close the gap.  The scope of that
statement is the one set out above: arm~B
supplies each agent with its own baseline and unshares the actor, and
neither of those changes the fact that the reward the gradient sees is the
same team reward for every agent.

That is a useful negative result rather than a frustrating one, for two
reasons.  It is consistent with the literature's own position: the
per-agent estimators that do change the signal are not trivial
modifications, and the closest coverage-specific evidence
\cite{sun2023} uses a per-agent difference utility rather than a per-agent
advantage estimator, so the question on a persistent-coverage task is
genuinely open.  And it narrows the search: a reader who wants to close
the gap now knows that the answer is not ``use a local critic''.

We therefore report the result as it stands: The residual is consistent with the credit assignment of a shared team reward, and the cheapest test of that diagnosis does not resolve it: the per-agent local critic's difference is -0.035 of persistent coverage (95\% interval [-0.079, +0.009]), which includes zero, the two
alternatives that the framework's other controlled arms rule out are ruled
out, and the cheapest available remedy for the credit assignment does not
close it.  The remedies that change the
signal --- a difference reward, a counterfactual baseline, a per-agent
value iteration --- are implementations of different algorithms, and we do
not claim to have implemented or evaluated them here.

\caption{The scenario matrix.  The learned controller's persistent coverage minus that of the stronger of the two rules, for every variant of every scenario.  It is behind the stronger rule in $\tokScenLosses$ of the $\tokScenVariants$ variants, by between $\tokScenSpanMin$ and $\tokScenSpanMax$ of persistent coverage, so the ordering holds in every regime the matrix tests.  The 34 cells are not 34 independent measurements: they are 32 distinct (configuration, scene) evaluations of six policy groups, each on a single scene, so the matrix is not on the same measurement basis as the five-scene gap, and a reader told only that a learned controller loses to a rule has been told the ordering and the size of the deficit but not the cause, which the arms bound without resolving.}
\label{fig:scen}
\end{figure}

Figure~\ref{fig:scen} is that matrix as a picture: one marker per variant, the difference between the learned controller and the stronger of the two rules.

Table~\ref{tab:results_scen} is the scenario matrix: it says whether the ordering survives outside the configuration it was measured on. Each row is the mean over the variants of that scenario, with the proposed
controller and the two rules evaluated on the same scenes.  The scenario
policies are trained at the base comparison's budget, and
8 policies are trained per distinct $(N, M, \text{pads})$ combination, because
the networks' input sizes depend on it; the scenarios that vary only the
geometry of the problem transfer within their combination.  Every policy
of a combination is evaluated on the same scenes, so the row is a mean
over training runs rather than a statement about one of them.  The matrix is
where the framework's value is most visible, because it shows
which regime a controller is good in rather than in which regime it was
tuned.  Counting the scenario variants in which the learned controller is
ahead, behind or level with the stronger of the two rules gives
0 ahead,
34 behind and 0 level; the largest deficit is
S6 (-0.598) and the smallest deficit is S2 (-0.080).  At the level of scenario means the learned controller is behind the stronger rule in every scenario, and behind it in 34 of the 34 variants, by between -0.598 and -0.080 of persistent coverage, so the ordering is a property of the method at this budget rather than of a particular regime, and a reader told only that a learned controller loses to a rule has been told the whole of it.

\subsection{Claim Audit and Physical-Layer Validation}
\label{sec:validation}

Every quantitative claim in this paper that is checkable is recomputed by an
automated audit from the same primitives the simulator uses
(\texttt{analysis/claim\_audit.py}). Of \tokAuditItems{} audited items,
\tokAuditPass{} are verified exactly, \tokAuditInfo{} are recorded for
transparency (battery-pack size, the power ratio, the charge C-rate, and the
density of the inter-UAV graph), and $\tokAuditFail{}$ fail. Two findings of the
audit are worth stating explicitly.

Three of the audited items are about the measurement apparatus itself, and
they are the ones a reader who has been burned by an unreproducible
pipeline should look at first.  Item R1 establishes that the evaluation of
a sampled policy is a function of (policy, scene): the sampling stream is
seeded from the evaluation seed alone, so the same policy on the same scene
gives the same number every time, and every controller is measured on the
same stream on the same scene.  Item T1 establishes that a training run is
a function of its seed, including when an evaluation is interleaved with
it, because the seed is set before the networks are constructed and so the
initialisation is seeded too.  \tokDeterminismText\ Item I1 measures the claim the framework
makes first: on the report's own infeasible configuration a rule-based
controller still reaches a respectable coverage ratio while the joint
metric is identically zero, so neither metric alone distinguishes that
instance from a feasible one, and the certificate is what makes the reading
decidable.

\emph{The area surplus is not a feasibility criterion.} The audit confirms
that $\sigma=N\pi R_{\mathrm{cov}}^{2}/(K|\Omega|)$ exceeds one for the
deployed configuration, while the corner-packing bound of
Section~\ref{sec:feasibility} shows the configuration is nonetheless
infeasible at $N=5$. The two facts are consistent precisely because $\sigma$
compares an area to an area, whereas $K$-covering a bounded region is a
covering problem.

\emph{The artefacts accompany the paper, and they are what the paper is
built from.} The simulator, the controller, the experiments and the
artefact that holds every measurement are in the repository that
accompanies this preprint, under \texttt{ml\_impl/}: the learned baselines,
the arms, the budget sweep, the ablations and the scenario matrix write
JSON or CSV artefacts, and every number in this paper that comes from a
measurement is generated from those artefacts by a single token table, so
that a number cannot be quoted here that the
artefacts do not contain.  The claim audit, the unit tests and the
assembly are runnable from the same tree, and the protocol each artefact
was measured under --- the number of training runs, the device, the
training budget and the evaluation scenes --- is recorded inside the
artefact itself where the artefact carries it: the trained CSVs carry
the number of training runs, the device and the per-seed values, and
the probe JSONs carry their own parameters.  Not every artefact carries
every field yet, and the gate now fails on a row whose device is
recorded as `?' rather than a device name.

\emph{The connectivity constraint is live in the regime the experiments use.}
An earlier version of this paper measured the density of the inter-UAV graph
on a static grid and reported that connectivity did not bind. That was the
wrong measurement: the experiments use a swarm that flies, so the quantity
that matters is the graph during the mission. Measured over a $\tokEpisodeSteps$-step
flight in the deployed regime, the mean node degree is $3.63$ of a possible
$7$, the graph is complete in only $12\%$ of steps, and nodes of degree
$\le 1$ occur in $23\%$ of UAV-steps. The $H$-step
feasibility mask and the reserve mechanism are therefore load-bearing rather
than decorative, and the audit reports the measurement rather than the
inference.

\emph{The feasibility certificate is audited, not asserted.} The audit re-derives the packing bound and its two instances: it confirms that the four corner discs are pairwise disjoint at the reported parameters and that the region therefore needs $N\ge4K=8$; it verifies the tightness construction, finding that the worst-covered point of the square lies 34.9~m from its nearest of the $4K$ disc centres, inside $R_{\mathrm{cov}}=35$\,m; and it measures the packing number of the realised sensor sets over 30 random draws, with a mean of $2.13$ and a range of $2$--$3$, which excludes $N=5$ for $4$ of the $30$ draws.  The certificate is therefore reported with the scope it actually has: unconditional for the region, and a measured minority for a random sensor layout.

\emph{The path-loss model is shared with a standards-faithful simulator.} The
Python reference PHY and INET's \texttt{BreakpointPathLoss} are the same
function: transcribing INET's implementation
(\texttt{BreakpointPathLoss.cc}) gives
$PL(d)=l_{02}+10\alpha\log_{10}(d/d_{\mathrm{bp}})$, which is exactly the
log-distance form used in Section~\ref{sec:system}. With the parameters
recorded by the OMNeT++ run ($l_{01}=l_{02}=40.04$~dB, $\alpha=2$,
$d_{\mathrm{bp}}=1$~m, background noise $-93.99$~dBm) the two agree to
\textbf{\tokPhyDelta{}~dB} over 24 (distance, exponent) combinations spanning
1--1000~m and $n\in\{2,3.5\}$ (\texttt{analysis/phy\_equivalence.py}). The
same audit confirms that the link margin at the report's two operating radii
is $+43.2$~dB (access link, 3-D slant range 61.0~m) and $+46.9$~dB
(inter-UAV link, 40.0~m), so the geometric feasibility certificate, not the
radio budget, is the binding constraint.

\emph{A control configuration was required, and it caught a real defect.} The
first OMNeT++ validation counted MAC-layer frames as the link-closure
observable and reported that links closed at every range, including 50~km.
A control run with the transmit power crushed by 60~dB returned the same
frame count, which proved that the observable was not measuring the physical
layer at all --- the identical failure mode that the professor identified in
the original abstract-disc model. The validation was therefore rebuilt around
a measurement that must respond to the transmit power, and the control
configuration is retained in the repository
(\texttt{PhyValidationControl}) so that the check is repeatable. We report
this as a methodological point rather than a result: a physical-layer claim
that has not been subjected to a negative control is not yet a measurement.

\emph{The second candidate observable, and why the runtime cross-validation
still does not exist.} The obvious way to make a runtime cross-validation is
to read the received SNR per receiver rather than a MAC-layer count, and
INET's \texttt{Radio} module does expose exactly such a statistic, the
\texttt{minSnir} histogram. We therefore built a proper negative control for
it: a transmit-power sweep in which the only quantity that changes is the
UAV's transmit power, over a 117~dB range, with receivers at 10, 30, 50 and
80~m and a UAV at 50~m altitude (\texttt{run\_phy\_probe.sh},
\texttt{analysis/phy\_runtime\_probe.py}). Table~\ref{tab:phyprobe} is the
probe.  The result is specific, and it is
reported here in full because it is the evidence for what the paper does and
does not claim.

\begin{table}[t]
\caption{OMNeT++/INET runtime probe. The only difference between the rows is
the UAV's transmit power. ``Receptions'' is the number of packets the receiver
radio delivered to the upper layer; ``$SNIR_{\mathrm{INET}}$'' is the
reported \texttt{minSnir} statistic.  A zero in the reception count means
the link is below the receiver's sensitivity threshold, so nothing is
delivered; a dash means the statistic was not reported at all, because with
no delivered packet there is no received signal to report it on.}
\label{tab:phyprobe}
\centering
\scriptsize
\begin{tabular}{@{}llccccr@{}}
\toprule
& & \multicolumn{4}{c}{Receptions at} & \\
Config & $P_{\mathrm{tx}}$ & 10 m & 30 m & 50 m & 80 m & $SNIR_{\mathrm{INET}}$ \\
\midrule
A & 0.5 W ($+27$ dBm)   & 500 & 500 & 500 & 500 & 46.96 dB \\
B & 1 mW ($0$ dBm)  & 500 & 500 & 500 & 500 & 19.97 dB \\
C & 1 $\mu$W ($-30$ dBm) & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & --- \\
D & 1 pW ($-90$ dBm) & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & --- \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

Three things follow. First, the control works: the reception count falls
from 500 to 0 as the transmit power is reduced by 117~dB, so the radio chain
is live and is genuinely being exercised. Second, the statistic tracks the
transmit power exactly --- a 27.0~dB reduction of $P_{\mathrm{tx}}$ produces
a 27.0~dB reduction of the reported SNR --- so it is not simply a frozen
constant. Third, and decisively, it does \emph{not} track the receiver
distance: the same value is reported for receivers at 10, 30, 50 and 80~m,
although the configured path loss differs by 5.3~dB between the nearest and
the farthest of them, and the link-closure threshold is the same at every
distance when the configured path loss requires it to be 13.7~dB lower at
80~m. The quantity a path-loss cross-validation needs is the SNR as a
function of distance, and that is exactly what this statistic does not
report.

The consequence for this paper is stated plainly. We therefore do
\emph{not} claim a runtime cross-validation of the physical layer. What we
do claim is the algebraic equivalence of the two path-loss functions,
established from INET's own source and its recorded parameters, to
\tokPhyDelta{}~dB. The broader methodological conclusion --- that an instrument must
be shown to respond to a control before its readings can be believed --- is
the part we would ask a reader to carry away, and the probe is included in
the repository so that the conclusion can be re-checked.

\emph{Plasticity of the learned policy.} A failure mode that does not appear
in reward curves or training loss is known in the MAPPO literature: the
accumulation of dormant neurons in shared-parameter policies, which
\cite{prime2026} report at 40--45\% for vanilla MAPPO, and which
\cite{ceilings2026} and the graph-attention line of work~\cite{shi2025} treat
as a structural limitation of MLP critics. We therefore probe the trained
shared actor directly. The probe retains the hidden-layer activations and
performs \emph{one backward pass per agent}, so that each agent's gradient
contribution to each neuron is separable; a single shared backward pass would
expose only the summed gradient and would hide exactly the per-agent effect
that \cite{prime2026} warns about. A neuron is called dormant when its mean
absolute activation falls below a fraction of the layer mean, silent when its
mean absolute gradient does, and dead when it is both.

Table~\ref{tab:dormancy} reports the result for the trained policy. The
actor has \textbf{no forward-dormant neurons} in either hidden layer at any
threshold from $10^{-3}$ to $10^{-1}$ of the layer mean (the largest
dormant fraction measured is $0.000$), and consequently no
dead neurons, in contrast to the 40--45\% dormancy reported for vanilla
MAPPO. Between $\tokDormSilentMin\%$ and $\tokDormSilentMax\%$ of the
neurons are gradient-silent, which is the expected and benign consequence
of a low-dimensional observation feeding a 128-unit layer, and no neuron is
dormant for one agent while alive for another. The probe is not decorative: a test kills half the neurons of a
hidden layer by zeroing their incoming weights and asserts that the probe
reports them as dormant, and a second test asserts that a healthy network is
not reported as dead.

\begin{table}[t]
\caption{Plasticity probe of the trained shared actor (128 units per hidden
layer). ``Dormant'' means the mean absolute activation is below the stated
fraction of the layer mean; ``silent'' is the same test on the mean absolute
per-agent gradient; ``dead'' is both.  Every entry is a measured count or a
measured fraction: the zeros say that no neuron in that layer fails the
test at that threshold, which is the result the probe was run to get.}
\label{tab:dormancy}
\centering
\scriptsize
\begin{tabular}{@{}lccccc@{}}
\toprule
Layer & $\tau$ & Dormant & Silent & Dead & Dormant for some agent only \\
\midrule
Hidden 1 & $10^{-3}$ & \tokDormALowDormant & \tokDormALowSilent & \tokDormALowDead & \tokDormASome \\
Hidden 1 & $10^{-1}$ & \tokDormAHighDormant & \tokDormAHighSilent & \tokDormAHighDead & \tokDormASome \\
Hidden 2 & $10^{-3}$ & \tokDormBLowDormant & \tokDormBLowSilent & \tokDormBLowDead & \tokDormBSome \\
Hidden 2 & $10^{-1}$ & \tokDormBHighDormant & \tokDormBHighSilent & \tokDormBHighDead & \tokDormBSome \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\section{Conclusion}
This paper defines a persistent and fault-tolerant UAV-IoT coverage problem in which the swarm must jointly manage redundant sensor coverage, inter-UAV connectivity, finite battery energy, charging contention, and UAV failures. Its central contribution is a \emph{feasibility-certified evaluation framework}: a rigorous lower bound on the fleet size required for $K$-coverage of a bounded region, a teleporting placement oracle as an achievability ceiling against which every policy is normalised, and a non-degenerate replacement for the all-constraints-simultaneously service-continuity metric.

\emph{Feasibility certificate.} The original $N=5$, $K=2$, $R_{\mathrm{cov}}=35$\,m configuration is provably infeasible for $K$-covering the region: the four corner $K$-coverage discs are pairwise disjoint, so the general packing bound $N\ge K\,P(\Omega,R_{\mathrm{cov}})$ gives $N\ge 4K=8$, and the bound is tight at these parameters. For the sensor requirement the corner argument does not transfer, and the packing bound applied to the realised sensor set excludes $N=5$ for a measured 13\% of random draws; we report that rather than the convenient unconditional claim. All trained results use the corrected, feasible configuration $N=8$, $K=2$, $R_{\mathrm{cov}}=35$\,m, for which the same construction shows that every sensor is $K$-covered for every layout. The conventional area-surplus criterion, which exceeds one for the very same configuration, does not certify feasibility, and the two facts are consistent because an area is not a covering.

\emph{What the framework exposes.} The framework is not only a certificate; it is an instrument that can tell a reader why a controller behaves as it does, and on this configuration it says something uncomfortable. A hand-designed reactive rule outperforms parameter-shared CTDE MAPPO: the gap is $\tokGap$ of persistent coverage, with a 95\% interval of $\tokGapCi$, and the learned controller is below it under either deployment mode (sampled $\tokMappoCk$, argmax $\tokArgCk$). Three candidate explanations --- the content of the observation, the energy model, and the size of the training budget --- were each tested with a single-factor intervention paired with the proposed configuration.  \tokArmsSummarySentence\ What remains is a residual that is \emph{consistent with} the credit assignment of a shared team reward (\tokCreditResidualShort), and with causes that these arms do not test: the possibility that the hand-written rule was tuned against the evaluation scenes, the limit of a decentralised policy class, and the state-dependent corrections that the safety filter and the joint projection impose on the executed trajectory.  Its privileged access to the coverage state is not among them: that is measured in the first table, and it is not the explanation. A non-detection in an arm of a given width is a statement about the resolution of that arm and not about the component, so we report the resolution of every arm, and we do not claim that the remaining components are unnecessary, that they would remain so at a larger training budget, or that the credit assignment is the whole of the explanation. We identify the remedy the residual suggests --- a per-agent signal rather than a better team signal --- and we do not claim to have implemented or evaluated it.

\emph{Scope of the physical-layer claim.} The Python reference PHY and INET's \texttt{BreakpointPathLoss} are the same function, to $\tokPhyDelta$~dB over $\tokPhyRows$ (distance, exponent) points. We deliberately do \emph{not} claim a runtime cross-validation, and the reason is measured rather than asserted: a transmit-power sweep shows that the available per-receiver SNR statistic tracks the transmit power exactly but is independent of the receiver's distance, so it cannot support a path-loss cross-validation. A physical-layer claim that has not been subjected to a negative control is not a measurement, and this is the one we would most like a reader to carry away.

\emph{Honest limitations.} (i)~All results are on $\tokEpisodeSteps$-step episodes (\tokEpisodeSeconds\,s of flight); the report's 10\,000-step target may change conclusions, and in particular the credit-assignment limitation may be partly a budget artefact; the two convergence measurements bound that possibility but do not resolve it. (ii)~The single-component arms are measured with $\tokAblNSeeds$ training seeds, and that bounds what they can resolve: their intervals have half-widths between $\tokAblResolutionMin$ and $\tokAblResolution$ of persistent coverage, and the minimum detectable effect at eighty per cent power for the widest of them is larger than its half-width; a null from an arm of that width says that no effect of that size was \emph{detected}, not that the component is unnecessary. A null result from an arm of that width says that no effect above that resolution was \emph{detected}; it does not say that the component is unnecessary. A component that is redundant with another, so that removing either alone costs nothing, is invisible to an arm of this kind, and so is a component that matters only at a larger training budget; settling either needs a budget sweep or more seeds. We run the sweep, and for the full configuration it settles the question it can reach: the budget buys $\tokBudgetSpread$ of persistent coverage over $\tokBudgetRange$ episodes, and the paired comparison over the same training seeds puts that gain at $\tokBudgetPairedCi$, an interval whose upper limit is below the gap of $\tokBudgetGap$ --- so the budget is excluded as the explanation of the shortfall, over the range the sweep covers. That is a statement about the full configuration and not about the individual components, which are each measured at the single budget the base comparison uses, and it is not a claim about budgets beyond the range the sweep covers. (iii)~The reactive heuristic is given the exact set of under-covered sensors, which corresponds to an unbounded broadcast, while the learned policy receives a fixed-size summary; part of the gap might therefore be a difference of information and not of control.  The arm reported in the first table, in which the same rule runs without the global coverage state, measures that, and the measurement does not support the caveat. (iv)~The evaluation seed determines both the scene and the action-sampling stream, so the spread reported for a controller does not separate the scene-to-scene variation from the action-sampling variation. The two are common to every controller and cancel in the comparisons this paper draws, but they both enter the absolute numbers. (v)~The comparison is not compute-matched in the sense that a hand-designed rule embeds a human's solution while the learner receives a fixed training budget, and the learned controller's margin over the other learned arms is small compared with the seed-to-seed spread, so the differences between the learned methods should be read with that spread in mind. A learning curve and a budget sweep are what would speak to the first point, and they are the two convergence measurements we report. The four candidate explanations of Section~\ref{sec:experimentaldesign} are the ones the framework's own mechanisms suggest, and they do not exhaust the possibilities; the explanation that survives them was not pre-specified, so a study that had tested a different set of arms could have reached a different conclusion. (vi)~The OMNeT++ Phase-2 scenario ran and its negative control is reported, but the runtime instrument cannot support a path-loss cross-validation, so the equivalence is established from INET's source rather than from a running simulation. (vii)~Phase-3 (Simu5G PHY) is scaffolded but not executed with the learned policy. (viii)~The joint connectivity projection leaves no hole: in a probe that drives the swarm with \tokConnPolicy{}, $\tokConnSteps$ transitions into a disconnected graph occurred, all $\tokConnAsc$ of them after a UAV left the active set, $\tokConnTele$ after a teleport and $\tokConnUnexplained$ unexplained, so \tokConnAllLeaving.  The probe drives the swarm with the stored policies, so it speaks for the deployed controller on those runs; it does not speak for a policy trained with a different observation or a different budget, and the projection's own revision count on the deployed configuration is $\tokProjRevisions$ per episode. The per-agent mask proved sufficient on the configurations tested, and the ablation measures the components' effects rather than asserting them. (ix)~The degenerate service-continuity metric is retained for comparison but supplemented by the non-degenerate alternatives.

\section*{0. One-line summary (pehle yeh padh, 30 sec)}
UAV swarm ek area mein IoT sensors ko K-cover karta hai, battery finite, drones fail ho sakte hain, swarm connected rehna chahiye. Humne MAPPO (multi-agent RL) banaya, but ek hand-written rule ne usse $0.298$ zyada coverage diya (gap). Paper ka real contribution = feasibility-certified evaluation framework jo batata hai ki koi config possible hai ya nahi, aur reported number meaningful hai ya nahi. Negative result honestly reported with controlled arms + 38-item audit + OMNeT negative control. Methodology contribution, not algorithm win.

% ============================================================
% PART A: OLD REPORT
% ============================================================
\section{PART A --- OLD MIDSEM REPORT (kya tha, kya bolta tha, har section)}

\subsection{A.1 Old report ka framing (10 pages, proposal)}
Old report title: "Persistent and Fault-Tolerant UAV-IoT Coverage: A Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Framework for Joint Coverage, Connectivity, and Energy Management." Authors same (Himanshu, Surya, Harsh, Gaddam). It was a \textbf{proposal}, not a results paper. Abstract says: "Numerical performance claims are intentionally deferred until the proposed experiments are completed." Contributions: (1) unified system model, (2) CTDE MAPPO framework with masks + reserve, (3) literature synthesis, (4) benchmark/metric protocol. No results, no feasibility check, no audit, no OMNeT execution. 10 pages, ~5 figures, 14 references. Tone: optimistic, "we propose, we will do."

\subsection{A.2 Old report ka system model (Section III) --- har equation}
\textbf{Params (Table VI):} N=5 active UAVs, 1 reserve, M=20 sensors, 80x80 m, Rcov=35 m, Rcomm=40 m, z0=50 m, K=2, dt=0.2s, vmax=5 m/s, dsafe=5 m, Bmax=30000 J, Phover=50 W, Pmove=75 W, Pelec=5 W, Ptx=0.5 W, charge increment 0.0002, T=10000 steps (2000 s).\\
\textbf{Dec-POMDP:} G=<N,S,{Ai},{Oi},T,R,gamma>. Global state st = (pi,vi,bi,mi,Fi) for all UAVs + sensors + Qt. Local obs oi = [pi, vi, bi, Ni, Clocal\_i, rho\_i, tau\_return, Epad\_i] (8 features). Action space: 6 actions (Hover, +/-x, +/-y, Charge). Joint action 6N. K-coverage: nd(t) = number of active UAVs covering sensor d. Ct = (1/M) sum min(nd/K,1). Ut = under-coverage rate. Connectivity: graph Gt, connected if one component. Articulation point indicator kappa\_i. Crit = avg kappa. Battery: E(t+1) = clip(E - P*dt + Pch*dt). Return threshold Ereq = Epad + Erejoin + Ereserve. Mandatory return when E <= Ereq. Charging: Hungarian assignment, cost = alpha*dist + beta*queue + mu*urgency. Safety: speed, workspace, separation. Mask if violates. Failure/recovery: reserve UAV activated, recovery time tau\_f. Reward: rt = -[lambdaO*Ut + lambdaE*Econs + lambdaD*Ddeg + lambdaW*Wmov + lambdaR*Rrec + lambdaC*Critt]. Weights: lambdaO=1.00, lambdaE=0.10, lambdaD=0.50, lambdaW=0.05, lambdaR=0.30, lambdaC=0.20. Feasibility (old): area counting N*pi*R*R >= K*A → Rcov >= sqrt(KA/piN) = 28.5 m; packing correction → 30.0 m. Both satisfied by 35 m. Surplus sigma = N*pi*R*R/(K*A) = 1.50. "Leaves margin for single-UAV failure (sigma=1.20 after failure)." Bound necessary not sufficient.

\subsection{A.3 Old report ka ML algorithm (Section IV)}
CTDE MAPPO: parameter-shared actor, centralized critic. GAE, clipped PPO, critic MSE loss. Action feasibility mask: workspace, speed, separation, charge validity, connectivity-preservation. Failure-aware execution: remove failed UAV, activate reserve, update obs. Training protocol: randomize sensors, positions, batteries, pads, failure times; curriculum (no failures → single → contention). Hyperparameters: gamma=0.99, epsilon=0.20, GAE lambda=0.95. Implementation plan: Phase 1 Python (geometric, K-coverage, connectivity, battery, charging, failure, heuristic, MAPPO), Phase 2 OMNeT++/INET (wireless, network metrics), Phase 3 Simu5G (PHY-aware). Same actor interface across phases.

\subsection{A.4 Old report ka comparison + metrics + scenarios (Sections V-VII)}
Comparison models: Fixed formation+threshold recharge, Greedy lowest-battery, Reactive reconfiguration, MAD-DDQN, POGS-QMIX, MAHPPO-AM, Vanilla MAPPO. Metrics (Table IX): CK, under-coverage, connectivity availability, fragility, service continuity, outage severity, reserve utilization, recovery, energy, charging, movement, safety, scalability, stability. Scenarios S1-S8: sensor density, fleet size, battery, pads, Rcomm, Rcov, failure time/location, combined stress. Conclusion: defines problem, proposes MAPPO+mask+arbitration+reserve. "No performance advantage claimed before experiments." Literature survey: 10 core papers + 4 recent. Gap: no single framework couples all 5 elements.

\subsection{A.5 Old report ka literature survey}
10 core papers in Table I: [1] energy-efficient coverage DRL, [2] multi-ABS placement DDQN, [4] MAD-DDQN energy, [5] decentralized biconnectivity, [6] fault-tolerant ad hoc, [7] recharging coordination, [8] persistent aerial service, [9] fault-tolerant MARL exploration, [10] robust UAV coverage DRL, [14] energy-aware persistent coverage POGS-QMIX. Gap statement: no single framework models all 5 elements (K-coverage, connectivity criticality, battery+charging, failure recovery, decentralized execution). MAPPO cited separately [3].

% ============================================================
% PART B: WHAT CHANGED AND WHY
% ============================================================
\section{PART B --- What changed in new report and WHY}

\subsection{B.1 Config changes}
\begin{itemize}
\item N: 5 → 8. WHY: feasibility certificate proves N=5 infeasible for region (N≥4K=8). Old area-surplus test was wrong.
\item Episode: 10000 → 2000 steps. WHY: at 400 steps pack never depleted → charging/reserve never fired → three proposed mechanisms never exercised. Sweep shows 2000 steps is where energy binds (213 returns, 0.4 stranding/ep) while mission achievable.
\item Initial deployment: unspecified → connected corner cluster (3/20 sensors). WHY: centred ring already covers 17/20 → CK≥0.85 for do-nothing controller; clustered makes comparison decidable. Pre-deployed kept as S9.
\end{itemize}

\subsection{B.2 Reward changes}
\begin{itemize}
\item 6 → 7 terms: added λB (Bt = mean fractional shortfall below return threshold). WHY: consumption-only signal gives no reason to turn back (flight to pad = 0.0016 of pack vs late team-level consequence).
\item Weights: λD 0.50→2.00, λC 0.20→0.50. WHY: energy term numerically inert (≤5e-5 vs coverage ~1); degraded-service and connectivity must not drown under coverage signal. New ordering: λD ≥ λO ≥ λC ≥ λR > λE ≥ λW.
\end{itemize}

\subsection{B.3 Observation changes (8 → 11 features)}
\begin{itemize}
\item Added one-hot identity 1i. WHY: parameter sharing needs symmetry breaking; without it, shared policy collapses to single action, swarm rigid body (measured: 1.84/8 distinct actions, spread 11.3m = cluster radius).
\item Added pad bearing d-hat-pad. WHY: old obs carried energy cost to pad but not direction; policy cannot express return.
\item Added G×G deficit summary Mdef (G=4). WHY: agent knows how many it covers, not where deficiency is. Measured: no coverage difference (null, reported) but behaviour changes (spread 9.0→10.6m).
\end{itemize}

\subsection{B.4 Mask changes}
\begin{itemize}
\item Generic connectivity mask → H=3 eccentricity lookahead + joint projection. WHY: individually legal moves can jointly disconnect; projection reverts all to previous config. Also analysis of what rule does/doesn't prevent (ring example: valid topology rejected). Measured: 0.10/16000 actions unexecuted.
\item Energy mask repair: old admitted departures with flat battery → stranding 5.7/8. New requires E\_i ≥ E\_pad + E\_reserve after the move, one-sided (already-low UAV may still move toward pad). Stranding 5.7→0.4.
\end{itemize}

\subsection{B.5 New methodology (not in old report)}
\begin{itemize}
\item Feasibility certificate (packing bound N≥4K=8). Old used area-surplus (wrong).
\item Teleporting oracle (achievability ceiling 1.000 at N=8).
\item Degeneracy theorem for SC (F=empty → SC=0 ∀π).
\item Non-degenerate metrics (deficit + max refresh time).
\item Claim audit (38 items, 0 fail).
\item Determinism protocol (device + thread count part of protocol).
\item Negative control for PHY (60 dB crush → same frame count → instrument fake).
\item Plasticity probe (0\% dormant vs 40-45\%).
\item Exhaustion vs failure distinction.
\end{itemize}

\subsection{B.6 New implementation fixes (old equations got wrong in practice)}
\begin{itemize}
\item Termination vs truncation: old treated end-of-mission as terminal → GAE bootstrapped from zero → biased advantages. Fix: separate flags, tests pin it.
\item Value normalisation: old asserted present but missing. Fix: running EMA stats, un-normalise at 3 consumer points (TD residual, GAE, bootstrap). One accessor + tests.
\item Motion step bug: first Phase-1 sim passed all equations/tests but motion step never applied moves → spread never changed. Found by behavioural diagnostic, not tests/loss.
\item Frame count instrument: MAC frames responded to Ptx? No → 60 dB control caught it.
\end{itemize}

\subsection{B.7 New literature positioning}
\begin{itemize}
\item Old: 14 refs, 1 table, generic gap.
\item New: 44+ refs, Table I (focused survey) + Table II (near-misses: Trotta [15], IRADA [44], Scherer/Rinner [16], Hartuv [17], Shi [18]) with exactly what each lacks.
\item Dedicated subsection on closest prior work for evaluation philosophy ([38] drone-mesh ceilings, [39] CS-FUB, [40], [35]/[41] MILP).
\item Bounded-absence claims: no infeasibility certificate for persistent coverage in corpus; no paper names degenerate binary metric. Stated as bounded search, not universal.
\item Credit-assignment line: COMA, DAE, GPAE, HAPPO/HATRPO, wonderful-life-utility [26].
\end{itemize}

\subsection{B.8 New results (none in old report)}
\begin{itemize}
\item Base comparison: Fixed 0.372 / Greedy 0.784 / Reactive 0.953 / Reactive-local 0.972 / Indep DQN 0.381 / Masked PPO 0.625 / MAPPO 0.674±0.060 / argmax 0.418 / oracle 1.000.
\item Gap 0.298 (CI [0.248,0.349]).
\item Controlled arms (5) with CIs all below gap.
\item Budget sweep 8/16/25 → 0.588/0.624/0.674.
\item Component ablation (base + stress S8).
\item Observation experiment (3 arms).
\item Credit assignment test (-0.035).
\item Scenario matrix (9 scenarios, 34/34 variants behind).
\item Plasticity probe (0\% dormant).
\end{itemize}

% ============================================================
% PART C: NEW REPORT (section by section)
% ============================================================
\section{PART C --- NEW REPORT (section by section, what it says)}

\subsection{C.1 Abstract (p.1)}
UAV swarms provide temporary coverage where fixed infra unavailable. Persistent operation couples coverage, connectivity, battery, charging, failures. Formulates maintaining ≥K UAVs over every sensor while preserving connected swarm. Dec-POMDP. Argues evaluation methodology is the unsolved part: coverage ratio without achievability reference can't distinguish strong controller from infeasible config; service-continuity metric identically zero on infeasible instances. Introduces feasibility-certified framework: (i) rigorous lower bound on fleet size, (ii) teleporting placement oracle as ceiling, (iii) non-degenerate time-averaged + refresh-time metrics. Applied to project's own config: provably infeasible for region + minority of random sensor layouts; area-surplus certifies nothing. On corrected config: MAPPO with mask, reserve, arbitration, PHY-derived links. Hand-designed rule outperforms by 0.298 (CI [0.248,0.349]). Figure 1 is the argument in one picture. Arms bound how much each explanation accounts for (all upper limits below gap, smallest 0.161). Residual consistent with credit assignment; cheapest test (-0.035) doesn't resolve. Physical-model, feasibility, protocol, determinism claims recomputed by automated audit (38 items, 0 failing); audit doesn't cover Section VIII results. Every measurement number generated from artefact. Path-loss expression shown algebraically equivalent to independent standards-faithful simulator (constant 0.012 dB offset) with transmit-power negative control.

\subsection{C.2 Introduction (pp.1-2)}
Motivation (IoT in remote/disaster areas), persistent redundancy requirement, conflicts, joint action space 6N, MARL/CTDE/MAPPO suitability. Research question: can decentralized MAPPO maintain K-coverage + connectivity + energy + charging + failure recovery, and can performance be certified against rigorous achievability bound? 11 contributions listed (model, certificate, ceiling, negative result, MAPPO framework, PHY-derived links, non-degenerate protocol, observation-content spec, corrected deployments, negative-control methodology, literature synthesis).

\subsection{C.3 Literature survey (pp.2-6)}
Focused survey of 10 core papers (Table I) + near-misses (Table II: Trotta, IRADA, Scherer/Rinner, Hartuv, Shi, Qiu, Liu). Gap: no work couples all 5 elements with learned decentralized policy. Adjacent work on evaluation philosophy ([35],[41] MILP refs, [40] feasibility construct, [39] CS-FUB, [38] drone-mesh ceilings). Three absences: no infeasibility certificate for persistent coverage; no paper names degenerate binary metric; credit-assignment line (COMA, DAE, GPAE, HAPPO, wonderful-life-utility). Bounded search, not universal absence.

\subsection{C.4 System model (pp.6-14)}
Architecture (N active + 1 reserve + M sensors + sink + S pads). Dec-POMDP. Global state, local obs (11 features). Action space 6. K-coverage with radio gate (Eq. 19). Feasibility certificate (packing bound). Connectivity model (graph, articulation points). Radio model (Al-Hourani, path loss, MCS gate). Battery model (with exhaustion distinction). Charging arbitration. Safety constraints (energy mask one-sided). Failure/recovery (exhaustion vs failure). Primary objective + reward (7 terms, weights). Parameter settings (N=8, T=2000, clustered deployment). Scope (abstracts fading dynamics, obstacles, wind, aging, GPS denial, sensor failures, multi-failure).

\subsection{C.5 ML algorithm (pp.14-18)}
CTDE MAPPO (shared actor, centralized critic). Value normalisation (EMA, un-normalise at 3 points). Credit assignment analysis (shared team reward → same advantage; per-agent value doesn't repair; redistribution needs per-agent reward/joint-action critic/counterfactual baseline). Truncation vs termination bootstrap fix. Masking at logit level (H=3 eccentricity + joint projection, analysis of what it does/doesn't). Failure-aware execution. Training protocol. Hyperparameters. Implementation plan as audit trail (Phase 1-2 executed, Phase 3 scaffolded). Two cost confessions (motion step bug, frame-count instrument).

\subsection{C.6 Comparison models (pp.18-19)}
Fixed, Greedy, Reactive, Reactive-local, Independent DQN, Masked PPO local critic, POGS-QMIX (cited, not re-implemented), Vanilla MAPPO. "Evaluated" column. All on same scenes/seeds/constraints. Adaptations documented.

\subsection{C.7 Metrics (pp.19-20)}
CK, under-coverage, connectivity availability, fragility, SC (degenerate, retained for comparison), time-averaged deficit, max refresh time, outage severity, reserve utilization, recovery, energy, charging, movement, safety, scalability, stability. Which reported and which not (3 not reported: outage severity during recovery, recovery time distribution, inference-time scaling; collision/out-of-bounds prevented not measured).

\subsection{C.8 Scenarios (pp.20)}
S1-S9 (added S9 initial deployment). Each has two variants, every variant run. Evaluation protocol stated exactly (sampling seeded from eval seed; (policy,scene) function; seed-to-seed vs scene-to-scene variation reported separately; paired arms; resolution reported).

\subsection{C.9 Results (pp.20-31)}
Base comparison, gap 0.298, privilege test, SC separation, energy/stranding, connectivity accounting, budget sweep, observation experiment, energy arms, component ablation (base + stress), credit assignment, scenario matrix (34/34), claim audit, PHY validation (equivalence + negative control), plasticity probe.

\subsection{C.10 Conclusion (pp.30-31)}
Central contribution = feasibility-certified evaluation framework. Feasibility certificate (N≥4K=8, tight, sensor-set probabilistic). What framework exposes (negative result 0.298, arms bound explanations, residual consistent with credit assignment). Scope of physical-layer claim (algebraic equivalence 0.012 dB, no runtime cross-validation). Honest limitations (ix). Remedies suggested (per-agent signal) not implemented.

\subsection{C.11 References (pp.32-33)}
44+ references including near-misses and credit-assignment line.

% ============================================================
% PART D: GLOSSARY
% ============================================================
\section{PART D --- Glossary (34 terms)}
\begin{description}[style=nextline,leftmargin=1.2em]
\item[Feasibility certificate] Proof that a config can K-cover region. Packing bound N≥4K=8.
\item[Teleporting oracle] Upper bound on coverage (drones placed anywhere, no motion/energy).
\item[Service continuity (SC)] Binary metric, degenerate on infeasible configs.
\item[Dec-POMDP] Cooperative multi-agent problem with partial obs.
\item[CTDE MAPPO] Centralized training, decentralized execution, shared actor.
\item[Feasibility mask] Safety filter: bounds, speed, separation, charge, connectivity.
\item[Charging arbitration] Hungarian assignment of drones to pads.
\item[Reserve UAV] Backup drone on failure.
\item[Credit assignment] Shared reward → same advantage → who helped? Unresolved.
\item[Stranding] UAV empties pack away from pad → removed from active set.
\item[Exhaustion vs failure] Exhaustion = out of service, not failed; reserve can re-seat.
\item[Radio gate] Coverage/adjacency only if link carries ≥6.5 Mbit/s.
\item[Claim audit] 38 items recomputed from artefacts, 0 fail.
\item[OMNeT++/INET] Network simulator, Phase 2, 802.11 MAC/PHY.
\item[BonnMotion] Mobility trace format (.movements).
\item[Packing number P(A,R)] Max points in A pairwise >2R apart.
\item[Area surplus sigma] NπR²/(KA); passes but certifies nothing.
\item[GAE] Generalized advantage estimate.
\item[PPO clipping] Limits policy update ratio.
\item[H-step lookahead] Connectivity check H hops.
\item[Joint projection] Reverts all moves if jointly disconnecting.
\item[Entropy collapse] Policy loses exploration (ep 675 in long run).
\item[BC init] Behaviour cloning init (97\% acc) for residual MAPPO.
\item[Residual MAPPO] BC init + PPO fine-tune (CK 0.819 after 3 ep).
\item[Stress regimes] single\_pad, small\_battery, low\_comm, failure, multi\_failure.
\item[Headroom gate] ceiling - best rule ≥ 0.10.
\item[IQM] Interquartile mean (rliable stats).
\item[NED] OMNeT network description language.
\item[Cmdenv/Qtenv] OMNeT command-line / GUI run modes.
\item[BreakpointPathLoss] INET path-loss model.
\item[Al-Hourani] LoS probability model for air-to-ground.
\item[MCS table] 802.11 OFDM modulation/coding rates.
\item[SNIR] Signal-to-noise-plus-interference ratio.
\item[Stranded UAV] Out of service (empty pack away from pad).
\end{description}

\end{document}

\markboth{Energy-Flow Feasibility for Persistent K-Coverage}{Nagwanshi \textit{et al.}: Energy-Flow Feasibility}

\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
UAV swarms can provide temporary wireless coverage for Internet-of-Things deployments where fixed infrastructure is unavailable, damaged or insufficient, but persistent operation couples coverage, inter-UAV connectivity, battery depletion, charging contention and UAV failures. This paper formulates the problem of maintaining at least $K$ UAVs over every ground sensor while preserving a connected swarm, and models it as a cooperative Decentralized Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (Dec-POMDP). We argue that the evaluation methodology is the unsolved part of this problem: a coverage ratio reported without an achievability reference cannot distinguish a strong controller from an infeasible configuration, and the widely used service-continuity metric is identically zero for every policy on any instance whose sensor set admits no trajectory that keeps it $K$-covered while the swarm stays connected. We therefore introduce a \emph{feasibility-certified evaluation framework} that derives a rigorous lower bound on the fleet size needed for $K$-coverage of a bounded region, supplies a teleporting placement oracle that certifies the instance is coverable, at the reported configuration the ceiling is 1.000, so it normalises to the identity and its only information is that the instance is coverable at all, and replaces the degenerate joint-constraint metric with non-degenerate time-averaged and refresh-time metrics. Applied to the project report's own configuration, the bound shows that configuration to be provably infeasible for the region requirement and for a measured minority of random sensor layouts, and the conventional area-surplus criterion certifies nothing.

On the corrected configuration the framework is paired with a centralized-training decentralized-execution MAPPO controller with parameter-shared actors, a hard connectivity feasibility mask, a reserve-UAV recovery mechanism, charging arbitration and PHY-derived links.  Every controller, learned or hand-written, is frozen and rolled out on the same \tokRuleScenes{} held-out scenes (Section~\ref{sec:protocol}).  The strongest hand-written rule, the unprivileged local-assignment reactive rule, reaches $\tokRuleReactiveLocalCK$; MAPPO with the corrected implementation and an observation that reports the bearing of the nearest under-covered sensors reaches $\tokEgoShapeCK$ over \tokEgoShapeN{} training seeds (95\% interval \tokEgoShapeCi).  The difference, learner minus rule, is \tokLearnerMinusRule{} (95\% interval \tokLearnerMinusRuleCi), and \tokGapVerdict.  An earlier version of this work reported a gap of $0.298$ against the strongest rule; the cause and the correction are documented in Appendix~\ref{sec:second_sprint}, and the corrected number is the one reported here.  The paper's physical-model, feasibility, protocol and determinism claims are recomputed by an automated claim audit (\tokAuditItems{} items, \tokAuditFail{} failing), which does not audit the results of Section~VIII, and every number that comes from a measurement is generated from the artefact it is measured in, and the path-loss expression of the physical-layer model is shown to be algebraically the one an independent standards-faithful simulator evaluates, a constant $\tokPhyDelta$~dB offset at every distance and exponent tested, with a transmit-power negative control that shows why only the algebraic equivalence is claimed.
\end{abstract}

\begin{IEEEkeywords}
UAV-IoT networks, persistent coverage, fault tolerance, multi-agent reinforcement learning, MAPPO, Dec-POMDP, connectivity maintenance, feasibility bounds, evaluation methodology.
\end{IEEEkeywords}

\section{Introduction}
The Internet of Things (IoT) increasingly operates in environments such as agricultural fields, disaster-affected regions, industrial sites, and remote monitoring areas where fixed communication infrastructure may be sparse or temporarily unavailable. UAVs can provide rapidly deployable aerial communication or sensing support because their positions can be changed in response to the spatial distribution of demand. Energy-efficient UAV control has therefore been studied for communication coverage, fairness, and connectivity, while aerial-base-station placement has been formulated as a learning-based spatial optimization problem \cite{liu2018,qiu2019}.

The practical difficulty changes substantially when the network must remain operational for a long mission rather than only achieve good coverage at one instant. The supplied project model considers $N$ UAVs operating over $M$ ground sensors, finite batteries, communication links between neighboring UAVs, a limited number of charging pads, and the possibility that an active UAV fails during the mission. The central requirement is persistent redundancy: every sensor should remain within coverage range of at least $K$ active UAVs. At the same time, the UAV communication graph should remain connected so that information can be forwarded through the swarm to a ground station or data sink.

These requirements conflict. A UAV that moves toward an uncovered sensor may leave a coverage gap elsewhere. A UAV that returns to charge may be the only communication bridge between two groups of UAVs. A failure removes both its coverage contribution and its communication links, requiring the remaining swarm to reconfigure. Charging is also a shared resource: several UAVs can become energy-critical simultaneously while only a small number of pads are available. Persistent service therefore requires a joint decision process rather than a sequence of unrelated coverage and charging heuristics.

A centralized controller faces a rapidly growing joint action space. In the proposed discrete action model, each UAV selects one of six actions: hover, move in one of four cardinal directions, or charge. The joint action space consequently contains $6^N$ combinations. This growth does not by itself make centralized learning impossible for every small swarm, but it makes explicit joint-action enumeration and centralized policy design progressively less attractive as $N$ increases. A decentralized execution architecture is therefore desirable for scalability and fault containment.

Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) provides a natural framework for this setting. CTDE allows a centralized critic to use information unavailable to the individual UAV during training while retaining decentralized policies during deployment. MAPPO is particularly suitable because it combines centralized value estimation during training with a policy-gradient actor that can be executed independently by each agent.

The research question addressed in this work is: \emph{Can a decentralized MAPPO policy maintain persistent $K$-coverage and swarm connectivity while coordinating finite battery usage, charging, and single-UAV failure recovery, and can its performance be certified against a rigorous achievability bound rather than reported as an unscaled coverage ratio?}

This paper contributes a \emph{feasibility-certified evaluation framework} for persistent $K$-coverage UAV networks, which extends the recent feasibility-ceiling idea (\cite{ceilings2026}) from 1-coverage drone interception to persistent $K$-coverage by adding the point-set packing lower bound $N \ge K\,P(A,R_{\mathrm{cov}})$, the energy-flow bound of Section~\ref{sec:energyflow}, and the non-degenerate metrics below.  Instead of reporting coverage numbers with no achievability reference, which is what the existing literature does, and which is meaningless when the configuration is infeasible, the framework (i) derives a rigorous lower bound on the number of UAVs required for $K$-coverage of a bounded region, (ii) uses a teleporting placement oracle as an achievability ceiling against which any policy is normalised, and (iii) replaces the degenerate ``all constraints satisfied simultaneously'' service-continuity metric with non-degenerate time-averaged and refresh-time metrics.  The framework is the difference between a number and a measurement.

The framework earns its keep in a second way that is easy to overlook, and which this paper demonstrates rather than asserts.  A framework that says whether a coverage number is meaningful also says \emph{why} a controller produces the number it does, because the same reference points, the ceiling, the non-degenerate metrics, and the controlled ablations, apply to the controller and not only to the configuration.  Applied to a controlled experimental setup, the first version of this work reported that a hand-designed reactive rule outperforms parameter-shared CTDE MAPPO on this task, and it bounded the reason with controlled arms.  That number is retracted in Appendix~\ref{sec:second_sprint}: it came from a learner whose entropy bonus was sign-flipped and whose update ran 25 gradient steps per run, and from a protocol that compared a policy in training against a rule at rest.  Under the corrected protocol the learner is ahead of the strongest rule by \tokLearnerMinusRule{} (95\% interval \tokLearnerMinusRuleCi), and \tokGapVerdict.  Reporting that sequence, the failure, its cause, and the correction, is more useful to a reader than a favourable number whose provenance has not been examined.

The contributions are:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item A unified system model coupling persistent $K$-coverage, inter-UAV connectivity, finite battery energy, charging contention, and UAV failure recovery.
    \item A \emph{feasibility certificate}: a rigorous covering bound on the number of UAVs required for $K$-coverage, in the general form $N \ge K\,P(A,R_{\mathrm{cov}})$, where $P$ is the packing number of the set to be covered.  Its region instance is $N \ge 4K$ and is \emph{tight} at the reported parameters; its sensor-set instance is computed per layout, and it excludes the reported $N=5$ configuration for a measured 13\% of random draws.  The bound identifies the instances on which no controller can achieve the requirement, and the joint service-continuity metric is identically zero for every policy on the instances where that is so, which is why it must be replaced.
    \item An \emph{achievability ceiling}: a teleporting placement oracle that upper-bounds any policy's coverage, separating ``the policy is weak'' from ``the task is infeasible'' and normalising reported performance as achieved divided by oracle.  The separation is measured rather than asserted: on the report's own infeasible $N=5$ configuration a rule-based controller still reaches a respectable coverage ratio with full connectivity while the joint metric is identically zero, so neither metric alone distinguishes that instance from a feasible one, and it is the certificate that makes the reading decidable (Section~\ref{sec:results}).
    \item A \emph{measured result}: on the configuration the paper's own certificate declares feasible, the learner is ahead of the strongest rule by \tokLearnerMinusRule{} of persistent coverage (95\% interval \tokLearnerMinusRuleCi), and \tokGapVerdict.  The earlier measurement, its cause, and the correction are in Appendix~\ref{sec:second_sprint}.
    \item A CTDE MAPPO framework with parameter-shared decentralized actors, a centralized training critic, hard action feasibility masks with an $H$-step connectivity lookahead, and an explicit reserve-UAV recovery mechanism.
    \item PHY-derived links, the Al-Hourani LoS probability, a log-distance path loss with shadowing, and an IEEE 802.11 OFDM MCS table, that \emph{gate} the abstract coverage and communication discs rather than replacing them, so that a UAV counts as covering a sensor or as adjacent to another UAV only when the link carries a usable service rate, together with a measured validity condition showing when the disc approximation is the binding constraint and when it is not.
    \item A non-degenerate evaluation protocol (time-averaged spatial integral of persistent coverage error, maximum refresh time, and $k$-coverage probability) replacing the degenerate all-simultaneous-constraint service-continuity metric.
%% BEGIN CONTRIB
    \item A \emph{measured specification of what a shared policy's observation must contain}: an ego-centric summary of the coverage deficit, unit bearings and normalised distances to the $k=3$ nearest under-covered sensors, plus a neighbour-repulsion vector, is what the evaluated controller receives, and it is sufficient: replacing it by the exact global under-covered set costs $-0.090$ (Table~\ref{tab:knobs}), so more information hurts at this budget, and the one-hot identity and pad bearing of the earlier design are not part of the evaluated configuration.
    \item Corrected deployment parameters ($N=8$, $K=2$, $R_{\mathrm{cov}}=35\,\mathrm{m}$, or $N=5$, $K=2$, $R_{\mathrm{cov}}=45\,\mathrm{m}$) derived from the feasibility certificate, replacing the infeasible $N=5$, $K=2$, $R_{\mathrm{cov}}=35\,\mathrm{m}$ baseline.  The earlier comparison of the two deployments was measured with the pre-correction learner and is not claimed; the certificate itself, which is the point of the item, is unchanged by the learner.
    \item An evaluation protocol that treats a physical-layer claim as requiring a negative control, and reports a measured instance in which the available instrument could not support the claim it was being used for.
    \item A focused literature synthesis showing the difference between existing coverage, connectivity, recharge-scheduling, and fault-tolerant approaches and the combined problem considered here.
\end{enumerate}

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section~II presents the literature survey and the research gap. Section~III defines the system architecture and mathematical model, including the feasibility certificate. Section~IV presents the proposed MAPPO algorithm. Section~V specifies the comparison models, Section~VI the performance metrics and the evaluation protocol, and Section~VII the experimental design matrix. Section~VIII reports the results and the claim audit, Section~IX concludes the paper, and the Appendix details the protocol correction and re-measurement.

\section{Literature Survey}
\label{sec:litsurvey}
The survey is restricted to work that is directly related to at least one of four components of the target problem: UAV coverage/control, inter-agent connectivity, persistent energy-aware operation, or fault-tolerant swarm recovery. The ten core papers in Table~\ref{tab:survey} are discussed comparatively rather than as isolated summaries. MAPPO is cited separately as the underlying learning method \cite{yu2022}.

\cite{liu2018} & Energy-efficient and fair UAV communication coverage. & DRL-based UAV control. & Jointly considers coverage, fairness, connectivity, and energy efficiency. & Does not model explicit UAV-failure recovery, charging-pad contention, or a persistent $K$-coverage SLA. & Baseline for coverage--connectivity--energy trade-offs. \\
\cite{qiu2019} & Multi-aerial-base-station placement with irregular 3D coverage. & Prioritized-replay DDQN and two-level placement. & Uses a spatial representation to improve multi-ABS placement under terrain/blockage effects. & Primarily a placement problem; no persistent battery lifecycle or swarm fault recovery. & Motivates learning-based spatial control and size-invariant state representations. \\
\cite{omoniwa2022} & Energy-efficiency optimization for multiple UAVs serving static/mobile users. & Cooperative MAD-DDQN. & Jointly optimizes 3D trajectories and user service while accounting for interference. & Energy efficiency is central; persistent $K$-coverage, charging coordination, and failure recovery are not jointly modelled. & Strong value-based MARL benchmark. \\

\cite{basu2004} & Fault-tolerant ad hoc robot networks. & Movement-control and topology-repair algorithms. & Formalizes self-forming, self-healing, and self-organizing communication networks after node loss. & Focuses on network topology rather than persistent sensor coverage and battery-aware learning. & Provides the network-level motivation for failure recovery. \\
\cite{mathew2015} & Recharging coordination for persistent multi-robot missions. & Combinatorial rendezvous planning with mobile charging robots. & Couples charging schedules with persistent task execution and routing constraints. & Charging is the main focus; UAV coverage/connectivity/failure are not unified in the same learned controller. & Supports explicit charging-resource modelling. \\
\cite{arribas2023} & Persistent aerial service under limited flight and recharge times. & HORR and PHeRR scheduling schemes. & Provides fleet-size and recharge scheduling models for persistent service under energy constraints. & Service locations are scheduled rather than dynamically reconfigured after UAV failure. & Direct motivation for finite-energy persistent operation. \\
\cite{trotta2018} & Joint coverage, connectivity, and charging for distributed UAV networks. & Centralised optimal positioning + distributed game-theoretic scheduling + bio-inspired positioning. & Couples coverage, connectivity, and charging with rigorous performance bounds. & No failure model, no reserve UAV, no $K$-multiplicity, no learned policy. & Closest prior work on the joint problem; cited to delimit the gap. \\
\cite{jiang2024} & Fault-tolerant multi-UAV exploration with changing UAV health. & Fault-tolerant MARL with temporal information and health/topology inputs. & Allows UAV health degradation and faults during the mission and learns cooperative recovery behavior. & Exploration is the task; persistent sensor $K$-coverage and charging-pad contention are outside the main formulation. & Closest fault-aware MARL direction. \\
\cite{khan2025} & Robust UAV wireless coverage using multi-agent deep RL. & Centralized and decentralized deep Q-learning variants with a shared network. & Studies decentralized autonomous UAV coverage and compares centralized and decentralized control. & Focuses on coverage rather than explicit persistent redundancy, graph fault tolerance, and charging. & Recent decentralized coverage-learning benchmark. \\

\cite{mei2026} & Energy-aware persistent multi-UAV coverage with outage history. & POGS-QMIX with priority/outage guidance and return-energy masking. & Explicitly combines persistent coverage, outage memory, battery limits, and periodic recharging. & Uses a centralized online coordination layer and does not directly target articulation-point preservation plus reserve-UAV failure recovery in the same formulation. & Recent persistent-coverage benchmark and a key comparison model. \\
