================================================================================
PATH: Simulation/UAV_IoT_Demo/src/uav_iot_demo/ChargingStation.cc
================================================================================
#include "ChargingStation.h"

namespace uav_iot_demo {

Define_Module(ChargingStation);

void ChargingStation::initialize()
{
    stationId = par("stationId").intValue();
    maxConcurrentCharges = par("maxConcurrentCharges").intValue();
    currentCharges = 0;
    chargingPower = par("chargingPower").doubleValue();

    chargingStartedSignal = registerSignal("chargingStarted");
    chargingCompletedSignal = registerSignal("chargingCompleted");
    queueLengthSignal = registerSignal("queueLength");

    EV_INFO << "ChargingStation [" << stationId << "] initialized - max concurrent: "
            << maxConcurrentCharges << endl;

    emit(queueLengthSignal, 0.0);
}

void ChargingStation::handleMessage(cMessage *msg)
{
    std::string msgName = msg->getName();

    if (msgName.find("chargingRequest") != std::string::npos) {
        if (currentCharges < maxConcurrentCharges) {
            currentCharges++;
            EV_INFO << "ChargingStation [" << stationId << "] accepted UAV - "
                    << currentCharges << "/" << maxConcurrentCharges << " slots used" << endl;

            emit(chargingStartedSignal, 1.0);
            emit(queueLengthSignal, (double)currentCharges);

            cMessage *response = new cMessage("chargingResponse_start");
            send(response, "chargingPort");
        } else {
            EV_WARN << "ChargingStation [" << stationId << "] queue full - rejecting request" << endl;
            emit(queueLengthSignal, (double)currentCharges);

            cMessage *response = new cMessage("chargingResponse_busy");
            send(response, "chargingPort");
        }
    }
    else if (msgName.find("chargingComplete") != std::string::npos) {
        if (currentCharges > 0) currentCharges--;

        EV_INFO << "ChargingStation [" << stationId << "] UAV complete - "
                << currentCharges << "/" << maxConcurrentCharges << " slots used" << endl;

        emit(chargingCompletedSignal, 1.0);
        emit(queueLengthSignal, (double)currentCharges);
    }

    delete msg;
}

void ChargingStation::finish()
{
    EV_INFO << "ChargingStation [" << stationId << "] final state - "
            << currentCharges << " active charges" << endl;
}

} // namespace uav_iot_demo

#ifndef __UAV_IOT_DEMO_CHARGINGSTATION_H_
#define __UAV_IOT_DEMO_CHARGINGSTATION_H_

#include <omnetpp.h>
#include <vector>

using namespace omnetpp;

namespace uav_iot_demo {

class ChargingStation : public cSimpleModule
{
  private:
    int stationId;
    int maxConcurrentCharges;
    int currentCharges;
    double chargingPower;

    simsignal_t chargingStartedSignal;
    simsignal_t chargingCompletedSignal;
    simsignal_t queueLengthSignal;

  protected:
    virtual void initialize() override;
    virtual void handleMessage(cMessage *msg) override;
    virtual void finish() override;

  public:
    virtual ~ChargingStation() {}
};

} // namespace uav_iot_demo

#endif

package uav_iot_demo;

simple ChargingStation
{
    parameters:
        @class(ChargingStation);
        int stationId = 0;
        int maxConcurrentCharges = 2;
        double chargingPower = 50.0;
        int currentCharges = 0;

        @signal(chargingStarted);
        @signal(chargingCompleted);
        @signal(queueLength);
        @statistic(queueLength;record=count,vector);
    gates:
        inout chargingPort;
}

    int id;
    double battery;
    double posX;

    std::string status;

class MlBridge : public cSimpleModule
{
  private:
    std::string host;
    int port;
    double stateInterval;
    int sockFd;
    bool connected;

    cMessage *stateTimer = nullptr;

    simsignal_t stateSentSignal;
    simsignal_t actionReceivedSignal;

  protected:
    virtual void initialize() override;
    virtual void handleMessage(cMessage *msg) override;
    virtual void finish() override;

    bool connectToPython();
    void disconnectFromPython();
    std::string collectState();
    void sendState(const std::string& json);
    std::string receiveAction();

================================================================================
PATH: Simulation/UAV_IoT_Demo/src/uav_iot_demo/UAVBattery.cc
================================================================================
#include "UAVBattery.h"

namespace uav_iot_demo {

Define_Module(UAVBattery);

UAVBattery::~UAVBattery()
{
    cancelAndDelete(dischargeTimer);
}

void UAVBattery::initialize()
{
    currentEnergy = par("initialEnergy").doubleValue();
    energyCapacity = par("energyCapacity").doubleValue();
    dischargeRate = par("dischargeRate").doubleValue();
    idleDischargeRate = par("idleDischargeRate").doubleValue();
    chargeRate = par("chargeRate").doubleValue();
    lowBatteryThreshold = par("lowBatteryThreshold").doubleValue();
    criticalBatteryThreshold = par("criticalBatteryThreshold").doubleValue();
    isCharging = par("isCharging").boolValue();
    uavId = par("uavId").stdstringValue();

    batteryLevelSignal = registerSignal("batteryLevel");
    batteryStatusSignal = registerSignal("batteryStatus");
    batteryDrainedSignal = registerSignal("batteryDrained");
    batteryChargedSignal = registerSignal("batteryCharged");

    EV_INFO << "UAVBattery [" << uavId << "] initialized with " << currentEnergy << " J" << endl;

    emit(batteryLevelSignal, getBatteryPercentage());
    emit(batteryStatusSignal, isCharging ? 1.0 : 0.0);

    if (!isCharging) {
        dischargeTimer = new cMessage("dischargeTimer");
        scheduleAt(simTime() + 1.0, dischargeTimer);
    }
}

void UAVBattery::handleMessage(cMessage *msg)
{
    if (msg == dischargeTimer) {
        if (!isCharging) {
            discharge();
            scheduleAt(simTime() + 1.0, dischargeTimer);
        }
    }
    else if (msg->isSelfMessage()) {
        // Handle charging completion
        if (isCharging) {
            startCharging();
        }
    }
    else {
        // Message from gate - check if it is a charge command
        std::string msgName = msg->getName();
        if (msgName.find("charge") != std::string::npos) {
            if (msgName.find("start") != std::string::npos) {
                startCharging();
            } else if (msgName.find("stop") != std::string::npos) {
                stopCharging();
            }
        }
        delete msg;
    }
}

void UAVBattery::discharge()
{
    if (currentEnergy > 0) {
        currentEnergy -= dischargeRate;
        if (currentEnergy < 0) currentEnergy = 0;

        EV_INFO << "UAVBattery [" << uavId << "] discharging: " << currentEnergy << " J ("
                << getBatteryPercentage() << "%)" << endl;

        emit(batteryLevelSignal, getBatteryPercentage());

        if (getBatteryPercentage() <= criticalBatteryThreshold) {
            EV_WARN << "UAVBattery [" << uavId << "] CRITICAL battery level!" << endl;
            emit(batteryStatusSignal, -1.0); // Critical
            emit(batteryDrainedSignal, 1.0);
        } else if (getBatteryPercentage() <= lowBatteryThreshold) {
            EV_WARN << "UAVBattery [" << uavId << "] LOW battery level - return to base!" << endl;
            emit(batteryStatusSignal, -2.0); // Low - return to base
        } else {
            emit(batteryStatusSignal, 0.0); // Normal discharge
        }
    }
}

void UAVBattery::startCharging()
{
    isCharging = true;
    if (dischargeTimer && dischargeTimer->isScheduled()) {
        cancelEvent(dischargeTimer);
    }

    double energyNeeded = energyCapacity - currentEnergy;
    double chargeTime = energyNeeded / chargeRate;

    EV_INFO << "UAVBattery [" << uavId << "] charging - " << chargeTime << "s to full" << endl;
    emit(batteryStatusSignal, 1.0); // Charging

    currentEnergy += chargeRate;
    if (currentEnergy > energyCapacity) currentEnergy = energyCapacity;

    emit(batteryLevelSignal, getBatteryPercentage());
    emit(batteryChargedSignal, currentEnergy);

    if (currentEnergy >= energyCapacity) {
        stopCharging();
    }
}

void UAVBattery::stopCharging()
{
    isCharging = false;
    EV_INFO << "UAVBattery [" << uavId << "] charging stopped - " << currentEnergy << " J" << endl;

    emit(batteryStatusSignal, 0.0);
    emit(batteryLevelSignal, getBatteryPercentage());

    if (!dischargeTimer) {
        dischargeTimer = new cMessage("dischargeTimer");
    }
    scheduleAt(simTime() + 1.0, dischargeTimer);
}

double UAVBattery::getBatteryPercentage() const
{
    return (currentEnergy / energyCapacity) * 100.0;
}

void UAVBattery::updateBatteryLevel(double delta)
{
    currentEnergy += delta;
    if (currentEnergy > energyCapacity) currentEnergy = energyCapacity;
    if (currentEnergy < 0) currentEnergy = 0;
    emit(batteryLevelSignal, getBatteryPercentage());
}

void UAVBattery::finish()
{
    EV_INFO << "UAVBattery [" << uavId << "] final energy: " << currentEnergy << " J ("
            << getBatteryPercentage() << "%)" << endl;
}

} // namespace uav_iot_demo

#ifndef __UAV_IOT_DEMO_UAVBATTERY_H_

#include <omnetpp.h>

using namespace omnetpp;

namespace uav_iot_demo {

class UAVBattery : public cSimpleModule
{
  private:
    double currentEnergy;
    double energyCapacity;
    double dischargeRate;
    double idleDischargeRate;
    double chargeRate;
    double lowBatteryThreshold;
    double criticalBatteryThreshold;
    bool isCharging;
    std::string uavId;

    cMessage *dischargeTimer = nullptr;

    simsignal_t batteryLevelSignal;
    simsignal_t batteryStatusSignal;
    simsignal_t batteryDrainedSignal;
    simsignal_t batteryChargedSignal;

  protected:
    virtual void initialize() override;
    virtual void handleMessage(cMessage *msg) override;
    virtual void finish() override;

    void startCharging();
    void stopCharging();
    void discharge();
    void updateBatteryLevel(double delta);
    double getBatteryPercentage() const;

  public:
    virtual ~UAVBattery();
};

package uav_iot_demo;

simple UAVBattery
{
    parameters:
        @class(UAVBattery);
        double initialEnergy = 100;
        double energyCapacity = 100;
        double dischargeRate = 0.5;
        double idleDischargeRate = 0.1;
        double chargeRate = 2.0;
        double lowBatteryThreshold = 20.0;
        double criticalBatteryThreshold = 10.0;
        bool isCharging = false;
        string uavId = "";

        @signal(batteryLevel);
        @signal(batteryStatus);
        @signal(batteryDrained);
        @signal(batteryCharged);
        @statistic(batteryLevel;record=count,vector);
        @statistic(batteryStatus;record=count,vector);
    gates:
        inout charge;
}

package uav_iot_demo;

import inet.networklayer.configurator.ipv4.Ipv4NetworkConfigurator;
import inet.node.inet.Router;
import inet.node.inet.StandardHost;
import simu5g.common.binder.Binder;
import simu5g.common.carrierAggregation.CarrierAggregation;
import simu5g.nodes.gNodeB;
import simu5g.nodes.NrUe;
import simu5g.nodes.Upf;
import simu5g.world.radio.LteChannelControl;

network UAVIoTNetwork
{
    parameters:
        int numUAVs = 3;
        int numIoTNodes = 5;
        @display("bgb=1000,700");

    submodules:
        channelControl: LteChannelControl {
            @display("p=50,50;is=s");
        }
        configurator: Ipv4NetworkConfigurator {
            @display("p=50,100");
        }
        binder: Binder {
            @display("p=50,150;is=s");
        }
        carrierAggregation: CarrierAggregation {
            @display("p=50,200;is=s");
        }
        server: StandardHost {
            @display("p=200,100;i=device/server");
        }
        router: Router {
            @display("p=350,100;i=device/smallrouter");
        }
        upf: Upf {
            @display("p=500,100");
        }
        gnb: gNodeB {
            @display("p=650,200;is=vl");
        }
        ue[numUAVs]: NrUe {
            @display("p=650,350");
        }
        iotNode[numIoTNodes]: StandardHost {
            @display("p=200,350;i=app/sensor");
        }

    connections:
        server.pppg++ <--> Eth10G <--> router.pppg++;
        router.pppg++ <--> Eth10G <--> upf.filterGate;
        upf.pppg++ <--> Eth10G <--> gnb.ppp;
        for i = 0..numIoTNodes-1 {
            iotNode[i].pppg++ <--> Eth10G <--> router.pppg++;
        }
}

================================================================================
PATH: Simulation/omnet_uav2/UavPair.ned
================================================================================
import inet.networklayer.configurator.ipv4.Ipv4NetworkConfigurator;
import inet.node.inet.AdhocHost;
import inet.physicallayer.wireless.ieee80211.packetlevel.Ieee80211ScalarRadioMedium;

//
// Two-node link probe.
//
// Design notes, because both choices were forced by measured failures:
//
// 1. Every degree of freedom is a NETWORK-LEVEL parameter, and every one is
//    prefixed "sim" so it cannot shadow the submodule parameter it feeds.
//    Submodule patterns such as "**.uav[*].mobility.traceFile" do not match
//    through the module vector and are silently ignored by OMNeT++, so an
//    earlier sweep replayed one default trace at fourteen "distances" and
//    reported a flat 0.995 PDR out to 4 km.  A parameter that refers to itself
//    ("mobility.traceFile = traceFile") is also an error, hence the prefix.
//
// 2. Geometry is a 3-D BonnMotion trace (t x y z tuples), so altitude is real
//    and the analysis script derives distances from the same numbers the
//    simulator reads.
//
// Traffic is uav[0] -> uav[1] and uav[1] -> uav[0]: one delivery counter per
// direction, no contention, nothing else on the channel.
//
network UavPair
{
    parameters:
        string simTrace = default("traces/pair.movements");
        double simTxPower @unit(W) = default(0.1W);
        double simSensitivity @unit(dBm) = default(-85dBm);
        double simSnir @unit(dB) = default(4dB);
        double simInterval @unit(s) = default(0.1s);
        double simBitrate @unit(bps) = default(6Mbps);
        double simSigma = default(6);  // dB, plain double: LogNormalShadowing.sigma has no unit
        double simNoise @unit(dBm) = default(-94dBm);
        @display("bgb=800,800");

    submodules:
        configurator: Ipv4NetworkConfigurator {
            parameters:
                config = xml("<config><interface hosts='**' address='10.0.0.x' netmask='255.255.255.0'/></config>");
                @display("p=50,50;is=s");
        }
        radioMedium: Ieee80211ScalarRadioMedium {
            parameters:
                // Free space plus log-normal shadowing: the deterministic model
                // gives a step-function PDR(d), which is not a channel anyone can
                // fit a delivery model to.  sigma = 0 reproduces the step and is
                // kept as the control.
                pathLoss.typename = "inet.physicallayer.wireless.common.pathloss.LogNormalShadowing";
                pathLoss.sigma = parent.simSigma;
                // Match the Python simulator's noise floor (-174 dBm/Hz + 7 dB NF
                // over 20 MHz = -94 dBm); INET's default is -110 dBm, 16 dB quieter,
                // which would inflate every SNIR and flatter the link.
                backgroundNoise.power = parent.simNoise;
                @display("p=50,150");
        }
        uav[2]: AdhocHost {
            parameters:
                @display("r=,,#0080ff");
                mobility.typename = "BonnMotionMobility";
                mobility.traceFile = parent.simTrace;
                mobility.is3D = true;
                mobility.nodeId = index;

                numApps = 1;
                app[0].typename = "UdpBasicApp";
                app[0].destAddresses = index == 0 ? "uav[1]" : "uav[0]";
                app[0].destPort = 1000;
                app[0].messageLength = 64B;
                app[0].sendInterval = parent.simInterval;
                app[0].startTime = uniform(0s, parent.simInterval);
                app[0].localPort = 1000;

                wlan[0].bitrate = parent.simBitrate;
                wlan[0].mac.dcf.channelAccess.cwMin = 7;
                wlan[0].radio.transmitter.power = parent.simTxPower;
                wlan[0].radio.receiver.sensitivity = parent.simSensitivity;
                wlan[0].radio.receiver.snirThreshold = parent.simSnir;
        }
}


================================================================================
PATH: Simulation/omnet_uav2/UavSwarm.ned
================================================================================
import inet.networklayer.configurator.ipv4.Ipv4NetworkConfigurator;
import inet.node.inet.AdhocHost;
import inet.physicallayer.wireless.ieee80211.packetlevel.Ieee80211ScalarRadioMedium;

//
// Contention probe.
//
// All "sim"-prefixed network parameters, for the reasons documented in
// UavPair.ned: submodule patterns that pass through a module vector are
// silently ignored, and a parameter that refers to itself is an error.
//
// Every node transmits to uav[0], except uav[0] which transmits to uav[1].
// So uav[0] is both a contender and the measurement point: its
// "packets received" divided by the sum of everybody's "packets sent" is the
// aggregate delivery ratio under MAC contention at a known node density.
//
// Geometry comes from a 3-D BonnMotion trace supplied by the caller.
//
network UavSwarm
{
    parameters:
        int simNumUavs = default(8);
        string simTrace = default("traces/swarm.movements");
        double simTxPower @unit(W) = default(0.1W);
        double simSensitivity @unit(dBm) = default(-85dBm);
        double simSnir @unit(dB) = default(4dB);
        double simInterval @unit(s) = default(0.1s);
        double simBitrate @unit(bps) = default(6Mbps);
        double simSigma = default(6);  // dB, plain double: LogNormalShadowing.sigma has no unit
        double simNoise @unit(dBm) = default(-94dBm);
        @display("bgb=1000,1000");

    submodules:
        configurator: Ipv4NetworkConfigurator {
            parameters:
                config = xml("<config><interface hosts='**' address='10.0.0.x' netmask='255.255.255.0'/></config>");
                @display("p=50,50;is=s");
        }
        radioMedium: Ieee80211ScalarRadioMedium {
            parameters:
                pathLoss.typename = "inet.physicallayer.wireless.common.pathloss.LogNormalShadowing";
                pathLoss.sigma = parent.simSigma;
                backgroundNoise.power = parent.simNoise;
                @display("p=50,150");
        }
        uav[simNumUavs]: AdhocHost {
            parameters:
                @display("r=,,#0080ff");
                mobility.typename = "BonnMotionMobility";
                mobility.traceFile = parent.simTrace;
                mobility.is3D = true;
                mobility.nodeId = index;

                numApps = 1;
                app[0].typename = "UdpBasicApp";
                app[0].destAddresses = index == 0 ? "uav[1]" : "uav[0]";
                app[0].destPort = 1000;
                app[0].messageLength = 64B;
                app[0].sendInterval = parent.simInterval;
                app[0].startTime = uniform(0s, parent.simInterval);
                app[0].localPort = 1000;

                wlan[0].bitrate = parent.simBitrate;
                wlan[0].mac.dcf.channelAccess.cwMin = 7;
                wlan[0].radio.transmitter.power = parent.simTxPower;
                wlan[0].radio.receiver.sensitivity = parent.simSensitivity;
                wlan[0].radio.receiver.snirThreshold = parent.simSnir;
        }
}

PATH: ai_feedback_on_Midsem_report_tex.txt
================================================================================
I reviewed the uploaded report in detail and cross-checked the core novelty claims against related UAV/MARL/coverage literature. My honest assessment is:

This is not “just a standard MAPPO UAV project.” The strongest part is genuinely research-like: your feasibility-certified evaluation framework.
But the MAPPO controller itself is not yet a strong algorithmic contribution, because your own experiments show a hand-designed reactive rule beats it badly. The work is most defensible as a methodological / evaluation-framework paper with a negative MARL result, not as “we propose a superior learned UAV controller.”

Below is a deep technical review.

1. High-level verdict
What you did well
Your report has several unusually strong aspects for an R&D/student project:

You discovered that the original configuration was infeasible.
The observation that the conventional area-surplus criterion passes while the corner-packing bound rejects the configuration is important. This is one of the best parts of the work.

You separated “controller failure” from “task infeasibility.”
Many UAV/RL papers report coverage ratios without proving that full coverage was ever achievable. Your oracle/certificate idea directly addresses that weakness.

You reported a negative result honestly.
You did not hide that the reactive rule beats MAPPO. That is scientifically stronger than forcing a weak learning result to look good.

You added serious audit/reproducibility machinery.
Automated claim audits, deterministic seed handling, path-loss checks, and negative controls are far above typical course-project quality.

You correctly identify credit assignment as a likely bottleneck.
The result that a shared team reward may fail in persistent multi-UAV coverage is plausible and connects to known MARL credit-assignment issues. COMA, for example, was explicitly motivated by multi-agent credit assignment and uses a counterfactual baseline to isolate an agent’s contribution Source.

What is weak or risky
The novelty is overclaimed in places.
The packing bound itself is not a new mathematical invention; it is a standard covering/packing lower-bound idea. Your innovation is its application as an evaluation certificate for UAV-IoT persistent K-coverage, not the lemma itself.

The MAPPO result is too undertrained to support broad claims.
25 episodes / 8 seeds is not enough to conclude “MAPPO is bad for this problem.” You can conclude: under this implementation, training budget, reward, observation, and architecture, MAPPO underperformed a reactive rule.

The “decentralized execution” claim is weakened by the global safety/action mask.
If the connectivity mask uses global true state at execution time, then the actor is decentralized but the system is not fully decentralized. You should call it:
“decentralized actor with centralized safety-filter / supervisor.”

The reactive heuristic may not be a fair opponent unless carefully described.
If it uses exact coverage deficits, exact sensor states, or global geometry, then it may be more privileged than the learned policy. Your “local assignment” version helps, but reviewers will still ask whether the heuristic gets cleaner information than MAPPO.

The physical model is over-detailed relative to how much it affects the result.
Your own audit says the link margin is huge, so the PHY is not the binding constraint. That is fine, but then avoid implying that PHY realism is central to the result.

2. Is this innovation or already discovered?
Short answer
Partly innovation, partly recombination, partly rediscovery.

The pieces individually already exist:

UAV coverage with energy-aware DRL already exists.
Persistent UAV coverage with recharging already exists.
Action masking in RL already exists and is formally studied; invalid action masking is known to be a valid technique in policy-gradient algorithms Source.
MAPPO is a known cooperative MARL baseline and has been shown to work well on standard multi-agent benchmarks Source.
Joint UAV coverage, connectivity, and charging existed before your work; Trotta et al. propose centralized and distributed strategies for stationary UAV coverage, connectivity, and energy replenishment Source.
K-coverage and recharging in UAV-IoT networks is also studied; Song et al. explicitly address assigning UAVs for K-coverage and recharging in IoT networks Source.
Persistent multi-UAV coverage with priority, outage memory, finite battery, recharging, and MARL is close to your topic; a recent POGS-QMIX paper studies persistent geometric multi-UAV service coverage with finite battery and recharging, using priority/outage guidance and return-energy masks Source.
Where your work is more original
Your strongest originality is not “we use MAPPO for UAVs.” That is not enough.

Your strongest originality is:

A feasibility-certified evaluation protocol for persistent redundant UAV coverage, combining a packing-number lower bound, a teleporting oracle ceiling, and non-degenerate metrics to avoid misreading infeasible experiments.

That is a legitimate research angle.

However, phrase it carefully:

Do not say: “We invented packing-based feasibility.”
Do say: “We integrate a packing-based infeasibility certificate into the evaluation protocol for persistent K-coverage UAV-IoT experiments, and show that a commonly used area-surplus criterion can be misleading.”
That is much more defensible.

3. Strongest parts of the report
3.1 Feasibility certificate is genuinely valuable
Your argument:

Then any K-cover requires:

This is correct as a lower bound. The logic is simple and strong: if two points are more than 2R apart, one coverage disk cannot cover both; therefore each packed point needs K distinct disks.

For your square region:

This directly exposes the problem with the old N=5,K=2,R=35 configuration. That is a meaningful finding.

3.2 You correctly criticize area-surplus
The area-surplus criterion:

can be necessary-ish for region coverage but is not sufficient. Your example is good:

Yet the region cannot be K-covered because the corners require 8 UAVs.
This is an excellent teaching example. Keep it.

3.3 Your metric criticism is good
The “service continuity” metric becomes uninformative when no feasible configuration exists. If the feasible set is empty, every policy gets zero, so the metric cannot distinguish:

terrible controller,
almost-correct controller,
impossible task.
Your use of graded metrics like persistent coverage, under-coverage rate, and refresh time is correct.

But see the logical caveat in Section 5 below.

“A standard CTDE MAPPO setup did not solve this persistent redundant UAV coverage problem as well as a simple reactive rule.”

That is useful if framed correctly.

4. Main technical mistakes / weaknesses
4.1 You should not present MAPPO as the successful proposed solution
Right now the report sometimes sounds like:

“We propose a MAPPO controller for persistent coverage.”

But your results say:

“MAPPO loses badly to the reactive rule.”

So the paper’s framing should change.

Better framing:

“We propose a feasibility-certified evaluation framework and use it to audit a CTDE MAPPO controller. The audit reveals that, on the corrected feasible configuration, a hand-designed reactive rule substantially outperforms MAPPO.”

This is much stronger and more honest.

4.2 Training budget is too small for a strong MARL conclusion
A reviewer will attack this immediately.

You report roughly 8 training seeds and 25 episodes. For MAPPO, that is very small. MAPPO papers usually train over large numbers of environment steps and perform careful hyperparameter tuning. The original MAPPO work reports strong results across standard cooperative benchmarks, but that strength depends on careful implementation and sufficient training Source.

So your conclusion should be limited:

Bad claim:

“MAPPO cannot solve persistent UAV-IoT coverage.”

Better claim:

“Under the tested observation, reward, masking, and training budget, our MAPPO implementation does not match a reactive rule.”

Even better:

“This motivates future work on per-agent credit assignment, stronger architectures, curriculum learning, and centralized/MPC baselines.”

4.3 The reactive rule may be unfairly strong
The reactive rule seems to know where under-covered sensors are and moves toward them. That is exactly the high-level structure the learned policy struggles to discover.

If the heuristic uses global sensor coverage state, while MAPPO receives a compressed deficit grid, then the comparison is not purely “learning vs rule.” It is partly:

exact symbolic state access,
handcrafted assignment,
privileged geometry,
deterministic reactive behavior,
versus a learned decentralized policy with partial observation.

Your local-assignment reactive variant helps a lot, especially because it still performs extremely well. But you need to be very explicit:

What information does the reactive rule receive?
Is it the same information as MAPPO?
Does it use true per-sensor n 
d
​
 (t)?
Does it know all sensor positions?
Does it know global UAV positions?
Does it use centralized assignment?
If yes, call it a strong oracle-like heuristic baseline, not a fair decentralized peer.

4.4 “Decentralized execution” is overstated
Your actor may be decentralized, but the safety filter/mask appears to use the simulator’s true global state to reject actions that would disconnect the swarm.

That means execution is not purely decentralized.

Better terminology:

“CTDE actor with centralized safety-filtered execution.”

or

“Decentralized policy executed under a centralized feasibility shield.”

This matters. A reviewer could say: if the mask needs global connectivity, then your deployed system still requires a central supervisor.

4.5 The connectivity model ignores sink connectivity
You say that if the UAV graph is connected, sensor data can reach the sink, but later admit that the sink is not a vertex and is assumed to remain within communication range of at least one UAV.

That is a significant modeling assumption.

For a UAV-IoT communication network, the relevant graph should probably include:

UAV nodes,
sink/base-station node,
maybe sensor-to-UAV access links.
Then require the active UAV graph plus sink to be connected. Otherwise you can have a connected UAV swarm that is disconnected from the base station.

Fix:

G 
t
​
 =(V 
UAV
​
 ∪{sink},E 
UAV−UAV
​
 ∪E 
UAV−sink
​
 )
Then evaluate sink reachability explicitly.

4.6 The physical-layer model is mostly non-binding
You include Al-Hourani LoS probability, path loss, 802.11 MCS gating, OMNeT++/INET audit, etc. The Al-Hourani model is a known air-to-ground model for optimizing LAP/UAV altitude for coverage Source. 3GPP TR 36.777 is also a standard reference for enhanced LTE support for aerial vehicles Source.

But your own audit shows huge link margins, so the radio model does not materially affect the central result. That is not bad, but the narrative should say:

“At the chosen parameters, the radio gate is present but non-binding; geometry and fleet feasibility dominate.”

Otherwise it feels like physical-layer realism is being used rhetorically more than scientifically.

4.7 Energy/charging assumptions are not realistic enough
You correctly admit that the charging rate is about 3.6C and is a modeling assumption. That is good.

But then you should avoid claiming realism. Say:

“The energy model is a stress-test abstraction designed to make charging contention occur within a tractable episode, not a calibrated battery model.”

Also, if the episode is 400s and hover endurance is 600s, the battery stress depends heavily on movement duty cycle and charge rate. A reviewer may ask: are you studying persistent operation, or just a short stress episode?

You can defend it, but you need to make the scope modest.

4.8 You need stronger baselines
The baselines are decent for a project, but not enough for a paper-level claim.

You should add or discuss:

Centralized MPC / greedy assignment baseline
A centralized controller that directly optimizes current deficit, connectivity, and energy.

MILP or CP-SAT placement/repositioning oracle for small cases
This would provide a stronger upper bound than a teleporting placement oracle.

QMIX / VDN / QTRAN-style baselines
Persistent multi-UAV coverage with energy and outage guidance has been studied with QMIX-style value factorization; the POGS-QMIX work is especially close Source.

COMA / counterfactual advantage baseline
Since you diagnose credit assignment, you should test at least one method designed for credit assignment. COMA explicitly addresses multi-agent credit assignment using a counterfactual baseline Source.

Graph neural network / attention policy
UAV swarms have permutation and spatial structure. A shared MLP with one-hot identity may be weaker than a graph/equivariant policy. Recent UAV swarm coverage work explicitly uses symmetry-informed MARL for communication coverage Source.

4.9 The claim audit sounds stronger than it is
You say 38 items, 0 failing. But your abstract also says the audit does not audit Section VIII results.

That can confuse readers.

Be precise:

“The audit verifies model, protocol, physical-layer algebra, feasibility, and determinism claims. It does not independently validate the statistical performance conclusions of Section VIII beyond recomputing artifact-generated numbers.”

Otherwise it sounds like the audit proves the experimental claims are scientifically correct, when it mostly proves that numbers are reproducibly generated.

5. Mathematical/logical issues to fix
5.1 Service-continuity statement needs precision
You write something like:

SC(π)=0 for every policy π⟺F=∅
The spirit is right, but the logic needs care.

If F

=∅, a bad policy may still never visit F, so SC(π)=0 for that policy. You partly clarify this, but the equation can still be misread.

Better:

F=∅⇒SC(π)=0∀π
and

π
max
​
 SC(π)>0⇒F

=∅
But the reverse depends on reachability, motion constraints, energy, initial state, and horizon. A feasible static configuration does not automatically imply a feasible trajectory from the initial cluster under battery/connectivity constraints.

So write:

“If the feasible set is empty, the binary service-continuity metric is identically zero for all policies. Conversely, observing zero service continuity does not prove infeasibility, because a poor policy on a feasible instance may also score zero.”

That is logically safer.

5.2 Teleporting oracle is an upper bound only for coverage, not full service
You already mention this, but it should be emphasized.

A teleporting static placement oracle upper-bounds instantaneous coverage. It does not necessarily upper-bound:

recovery time,
energy-feasible persistence,
connectivity-maintaining trajectories,
charging contention,
service continuity over a trajectory.
So call it:

“coverage achievability ceiling”

not:

“overall task optimum.”

5.3 Region coverage vs sensor-set coverage must be kept separate
This is one of the most important distinctions.

Your original N=5 configuration is provably infeasible for covering the entire region. But your actual experiments evaluate 20 discrete sensors. For a discrete random sensor set, N=5 may often be feasible.

You do acknowledge this, which is good. Keep hammering it:

Region certificate: N=5 impossible.
Sensor-set certificate: depends on actual layout.
Your random-draw result: N=5 excluded for 13% of 30 layouts.
Do not conflate these.

5.4 Tightness construction needs all constraints
You say N=8 is exactly sufficient for region K-coverage. Geometrically, yes.

But your full system also has:

safety distance,
communication range,
radio gate,
no-articulation / H-hop mask,
starting cluster,
finite battery,
charging,
reserve behavior.
So distinguish:

“Geometrically tight for static region K-coverage.”

from:

“Dynamically achievable under the simulator.”

You claim the audit checks connected placement and safety-mask admissibility. Good. Make that explicit immediately after the tightness claim.

6. Literature positioning: what is already known?
Already known / not novel
MAPPO itself
MAPPO is not your contribution. It is a known algorithm. The standard reference shows PPO-style methods can be strong in cooperative multi-agent benchmarks Source.

Action masking
Action masking is not novel. It has been formally studied in policy-gradient algorithms and shown to produce valid gradients under the masking setup Source.

Time-limit truncation handling
Your distinction between termination and truncation is correct, but not novel. Pardo et al. discuss why bootstrapping should be handled carefully when episodes end because of time limits Source.

UAV coverage + charging
Trotta et al. already jointly consider coverage, connectivity, and charging strategies for distributed UAV networks, including centralized optimal and distributed scheduling/positioning approaches Source.

K-coverage + recharging
Song et al. study methods to assign UAVs for K-coverage and recharging in IoT networks Source.

Persistent energy-aware multi-UAV coverage with MARL
Recent work such as POGS-QMIX studies persistent geometric multi-UAV service coverage with finite batteries, recharging, outage memory, return-energy action masks, multi-seed evaluation, and sensitivity studies Source.

What may be novel
Your novelty is the combination of evaluation devices:

packing-based infeasibility certificate,
corrected feasible configuration,
teleporting coverage oracle,
non-degenerate metrics,
explicit demonstration that area-surplus and binary service-continuity can mislead,
audit-backed negative result for MAPPO.
That is a valid niche.

But do not claim you are the first to do coverage, charging, connectivity, failure, and MARL unless your literature search is very strong. Phrase it as:

“We are not aware of prior work combining these five elements with a feasibility-certified evaluation protocol.”

That is safer.

7. Paper-writing issues
7.1 The report is too defensive
The writing repeatedly says things like:

“we do not claim…”
“the framework earns its keep…”
“the difference between a number and a measurement”
“the cheapest test does not resolve it”
“this is not cosmetic”
This is intellectually honest, but the tone can become argumentative. Academic writing should be calmer.

Replace:

“The framework is the difference between a number and a measurement.”

with:

“The framework provides the feasibility context needed to interpret reported coverage values.”

Replace:

“The area-surplus criterion certifies nothing.”

with:

“The area-surplus criterion is not sufficient for pointwise K-coverage.”

7.2 Too many contributions
You list 11 contributions. That is too many.

Compress to 4–5:

Unified UAV-IoT persistent K-coverage model with energy, connectivity, charging, and failure recovery.
Feasibility-certified evaluation framework using packing lower bound and teleporting coverage oracle.
CTDE MAPPO controller with safety mask, charging arbitration, and reserve recovery.
Non-degenerate evaluation protocol and reproducible audit.
Negative empirical result: reactive rule outperforms MAPPO; ablations diagnose possible causes.
7.3 Avoid “we proved” for empirical things
Use:

“measured,”
“observed,”
“under the tested setting,”
“consistent with,”
“does not rule out.”
You already often do this, but keep it consistent.

8. Experimental concerns
8.1 Eight seeds is okay for a project, weak for strong claims
The main gap is large enough that 8 seeds may be persuasive. But ablations with intervals crossing zero should be treated as inconclusive.

For example:

identity: +0.008, CI crosses zero,
local critic: -0.035, CI crosses zero,
threshold term: interval crosses zero.
Conclusion should be:

“Not resolved at this budget.”

not:

“does not matter.”

8.2 The budget sweep does not exclude training budget
You say training from 8 to 25 episodes improves C 
K
​
  by +0.086, which accounts for only 29% of the gap.

That does not prove a larger budget cannot close the gap. Learning curves can be nonlinear. It only says:

“Within the tested budget range, increased training did not close the gap.”

8.3 Need hyperparameter tuning fairness
Did MAPPO get tuned as heavily as the reactive rule? If not, reviewers may say the comparison is unfair.

At minimum, report:

actor/critic network sizes,
learning rate,
entropy coefficient,
rollout length,
minibatches,
PPO epochs,
reward normalization,
value normalization,
gradient clipping,
action mask implementation,
number of environment steps,
number of policy updates.
You likely already have much of this; make it easy to find.

8.4 Need wall-clock / sample-compute cost
If reactive rule has no training cost and beats MAPPO, that is a useful engineering result. But report:

training time,
inference time,
simulation speed,
number of environment transitions.
9. What you should change before submitting
Must fix
Reframe the paper around evaluation methodology, not MAPPO success.
Soften novelty claims.
Clarify decentralized execution vs centralized safety filter.
Separate region feasibility from sensor-set feasibility everywhere.
Fix service-continuity logic.
State that the teleporting oracle is a coverage ceiling, not full task optimum.
Reduce contribution list to 4–5 items.
Explicitly define what information each baseline receives.
Add stronger limitations around training budget and seed count.
Add sink connectivity or clearly mark it as a simplifying assumption.
Should add if possible
One credit-assignment baseline: COMA, difference reward, HAPPO/HATRPO, or counterfactual advantage.
One graph/equivariant policy baseline.
One centralized MPC/assignment heuristic.
A longer MAPPO training run, even if only for 2–3 seeds, to show whether learning curves plateau.
A table comparing information access for each method.
Example table:

Method	Uses global sensor positions?	Uses exact under-covered set?	Uses global UAV graph?	Learns?	Decentralized actor?	Centralized safety?
MAPPO	partial/broadcast	compressed	mask only	yes	yes	yes
Reactive-global	yes	yes	yes	no	no	yes
Reactive-local	local	local	maybe	no	maybe	yes
This would make the fairness issue transparent.

10. My final judgment
Is your project valid R&D?
Yes. Definitely.

Is it publishable as currently framed?
Probably not yet, because the claims are too broad and the MAPPO result is weak.

Could it become a good paper?
Yes, if you frame it as:

“Feasibility-certified evaluation for persistent redundant UAV-IoT coverage: why naive coverage metrics mislead, and what a MAPPO negative result teaches us.”

That is much stronger than:

“A MAPPO framework for fault-tolerant UAV-IoT coverage.”

What is the actual contribution?
Your actual contribution is:

You built a rigorous evaluation and auditing framework that reveals when UAV coverage experiments are infeasible or misleading, and you used it to show that a standard MAPPO controller underperforms a reactive rule on a corrected feasible persistent K-coverage task.

That is real research value.

What is not yet proven?
You have not proven:

that MAPPO cannot solve the task,
that your learned controller is competitive,
that credit assignment is definitely the cause,
that your physical model materially changes the conclusion,
that your approach is fully decentralized,
that no prior work has combined similar elements.
Best one-sentence summary
This is a strong evaluation-methodology project with an honest negative MARL result; its main innovation is the feasibility-certified measurement framework, not the MAPPO controller.

PATH: alert.py

"""Loud repeating alarm to wake the user."""
import winsound, sys, time

def beep(freq, ms):
    winsound.Beep(freq, ms)

print('playing alert...')
sys.stdout.flush()

# classic wake-up alarm: 4 bursts, each 3 tones, twice
for burst in range(3):
    for f in (1800, 1400, 1800):
        beep(f, 260)
    time.sleep(0.35)

# second pattern, lower and longer, more penetrating
for burst in range(2):
    for f in (2000, 1600, 2000, 1600):
        beep(f, 320)
    time.sleep(0.5)

# final long tone
beep(2200, 1200)

print('done')

# CLAIMS LEDGER

Every claim the paper makes, its evidence file, and its status (supported / weak / retracted).

## Status legend
- supported: evidence exists and is reproducible
- weak: evidence exists but is underpowered or hedged
- retracted: claim withdrawn pending re-measurement

# Current Findings (2026-10-31, pre-residual)

## Completed experiments
- G3: 25/25 MAPPO seeds across 5 stress regimes (failure, multi_failure, single_pad, small_battery, low_comm)
- C3 credit: 10/10 seeds (single_pad, small_battery, team vs c3)
- Residual MAPPO: 2/5 seeds (seed2 running)

## Key results

### MAPPO stress regimes (team reward, 5 seeds each, 200 ep x 2000 steps)
| Regime | CK mean | sd | entropy | headroom | vs reactive |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| single_pad | 0.615 | 0.125 | 1.266 | 0.385 | -0.125 |
| small_battery | 0.371 | 0.083 | 0.810 | 0.629 | -0.346 |
| low_comm | 0.377 | 0.061 | 1.175 | 0.623 | -0.299 |
| failure | 0.630 | 0.136 | 1.369 | 0.370 | -0.086 |
| multi_failure | 0.713 | 0.139 | 1.206 | 0.287 | -0.003 |

### C3 credit vs team (paired, 5 seeds)
- single_pad: delta +0.013 (p=0.66, not significant). C3 slightly better.
- small_battery: delta -0.024 (p=0.68, not significant). C3 slightly worse.
- Conclusion: C3 credit does NOT significantly improve over team reward. Negative result.

### Entropy stability
- All stress regimes: stable entropy (no collapse). min_ent ranges 0.31-0.99.
- Nominal MAPPO collapsed at ep 675 (entropy -> 0). Stress regimes fix this.

### Headroom gate
- All 5 regimes PASS (headroom >= 0.10, range 0.287-0.629).

### Network certificate (INET, supported)
- Free-space range knee: 1762 m. At 80 m mission scale, PDR = 0.9975.
- Contention: PDR 0.998 at N=16. Network is NOT the binding constraint.
- Channel model: PDR(d) = 1 - Phi((sens - (Tx-PL(d)))/sigma), sigma=6 dB.

### Residual MAPPO (partial, 2/5 seeds)
- Smoke test: CK=0.792 vs MAPPO 0.378 after 3 ep (promising).
- Full results pending (seed2 running, seeds 3-4 queued).

### rliable aggregates (MAPPO team across 5 regimes as tasks, n=25)
- mean=0.541 [0.477, 0.613], IQM=0.525 [0.437, 0.620], median=0.503

## Implications for paper
1. C3 contribution is weak (not significant). Consider reframing as "credit assignment explored, no significant gain."
2. Stress regimes are the real contribution: prevent collapse, improve CK.
3. Residual MAPPO (BC init) may be the headline result if full runs confirm smoke test.
4. Network certificate (C1) is solid and novel.
5. C4 (fair evaluation) is the methodology contribution.

# FIRST-PRINCIPLES ANALYSIS OF THE INNOVATION PORTFOLIO

Mode: FULL (novel problem, high cost of error, architecture decision)

## Stage 1 - Reframe
Goal: publish a research paper. The current report is a methodological paper
(certification + corrected protocol). To be research-level publishable it needs
an ALGORITHMIC contribution that (a) is novel, (b) has measurable impact,
(c) is tested under the certified protocol.

## Stage 2 - Expose assumptions
- ASSUMPTION: the learner fails on small_battery because it never saw depletion
  (cost to test: low - curriculum experiment running).
- ASSUMPTION: the learner fails on clustered because it can't perceive the full
  swarm (cost: medium - needs attention, not yet implemented).
- ASSUMPTION: energy-aware shaping will help small_battery without hurting
  nominal (cost: low - experiment running).
- ASSUMPTION: difference credit helps (cost: low - diff2 running, preliminary
  +0.007).
- ASSUMPTION: the "learning does not help" thesis is still defensible on at
  least one regime (currently small_battery -0.064, clustered -0.038).
- UNKNOWN: whether any single innovation closes both failure modes.

## Stage 3 - Ground truths (irreducible constraints)
1. Physics: a UAV at 1m/s over 80m field, 2000 steps = 400s, battery depletes
   only under stress (B_max=15kJ). Energy is NOT the binding constraint on
   nominal; it IS on small_battery (B_max=15kJ, E_reserve=1kJ).
2. Information: the policy is shared and decentralized; it sees only local obs.
   The global state (which sensors are uncovered) is available only via the
   critic during training. The reactive rule gets the EXACT deficit set.
3. Feasibility: N>=4K=8 is the hard lower bound; the oracle is 1.000.
4. Compute: 200 episodes x 2000 steps ~ 50 min per seed on CPU. 3 seeds per
   config is the minimum for a citable mean.

## Stage 4 - Invert (what guarantees failure)
- Training on nominal only -> zero-shot failure on stress regimes (already
  observed: small_battery -0.064).
- Not reporting the random baseline on the SAME config -> "below random"
  false claim (already retracted).
- Comparing train-CK to eval-CK -> false comparisons (already fixed).
- Claiming a gain that doesn't exclude zero -> reviewer rejection.
- A single "does learning beat the rule" number hides regime dependence.

## Stage 5 - Reconstruct (candidate approaches)
Approach A: "Certification + corrected protocol" (current paper). Methodological.
  Novelty: medium. Publishability: needs a venue that values methodology (e.g.,
  IEEE TMC, IEEE IoT Journal). Risk: reviewers ask "where's the algorithm?"

Approach B: "Energy-aware curriculum MARL" (innovations 1+2+4). Algorithmic.
  Novelty: medium-high (curriculum over battery stress is uncommon).
  Testable: yes, running now. Risk: may not close small_battery.

Approach C: "Graph-attention MARL with feasibility-aware planning" (innovations
  6+10). Algorithmic. Novelty: high. Testable: needs implementation (1-2 days).
  Risk: implementation complexity, may not improve.

Approach D: "Hybrid belief + attention" (innovations 6+7 from HBRL paper).
  Novelty: high. Testable: needs LGCP + attention (2-3 days). Risk: too much.

## Stage 6 - Verify
Falsifier for Approach B: if curriculum+energy shaping does NOT improve
small_battery (still -0.06), then the "energy management" hypothesis is wrong
and we need a different mechanism (e.g., explicit recharge planning).

Cheapest empirical check: the running experiment (3 seeds, ~2.5h). If it
fails, pivot to Approach C.

Reversibility: all experiments are additive (new config flags, new .pt files);
nothing is deleted. Checkpoints preserved.

## Stage 7 - Artifact
Decision: run Approach B first (in flight). If it closes small_battery, combine
with diff credit (already +0.007) and test the combined config on all
regimes. If it fails, pivot to Approach C (graph attention) for the spread
start regime.

The publishable story either way:
- If B works: "MARL beats tuned rules on persistent UAV coverage once
  correctly trained, and the certification framework tells you which regimes
  still fail."
- If B fails: "even corrected, learning fails on energy management; the
  certificate identifies the regime and the mechanism (no depletion in
  training)."
Both are honest, novel, and use the certificate as the contribution.
EOF

# G1 Memo — Budget Truth Test (2026-10-25)

## Question
Does the existing MAPPO converge at a larger budget, and what do the converged results mean for the thesis?

## Setup
- 5 seeds (0-4), 200 episodes x 2000 steps = 400k env steps/seed (~8x the midsem's 50k).
- Old nominal regime (N=5, M=20, side=80, R_cov=35, R_comm=40, K=2, 2 pads, no failures).
- Device: CPU. BLAS pinned to 1 thread.
- Training time: ~63 min/seed (5 seeds in parallel ~63 min total).

## Results
| Seed | Final CK | Last-10 mean CK | Min (all) | Max (all) |
|------|----------|-----------------|-----------|-----------|
| 0    | 0.5078   | 0.6070          | 0.3976    | 0.8259    |
| 1    | 0.6750   | 0.6968          | 0.2424    | 0.8973    |
| 2    | 0.3678   | 0.4913          | 0.2467    | 0.8674    |
| 3    | 0.3324   | 0.4533          | 0.2293    | 0.5977    |
| 4    | 0.3352   | 0.4736          | 0.2796    | 0.6688    |
| Mean | 0.4436   | 0.5444          | —         | —         |
| SD   | 0.1479   | 0.1251          | —         | —         |

Reactive rule (unprivileged): 0.972 (deterministic). Oracle ceiling: 1.000.

## Findings
1. **MAPPO does NOT converge at 400k steps.** Last-10 CK ranges 0.45-0.70 across seeds with high variance. The learning curve oscillates wildly (min 0.23, max 0.90 within a single seed). No seed shows a clear plateau.
2. **The midsem's 0.674 (single seed, 25 ep = 50k steps) was a lucky seed.** At 400k steps with 5 seeds, the mean is 0.44 — much worse and highly variable. The original "0.298 gap" is meaningless.
3. **Headroom gate (R6): ceiling - best rule = 1.000 - 0.972 = 0.028 < 0.10.** The nominal regime FAILS the headroom gate. No "main" result can be reported in this regime. Need stress regimes (R6) to create headroom.
4. **High variance across seeds** (sd 0.15 on final CK) indicates the training is unstable — possibly due to the team reward, the observation, or insufficient exploration. This is consistent with the credit-assignment hypothesis but not proof.

## Implications for the thesis
- The original thesis (network-in-the-loop) is UNAFFECTED by this — C1/C2/C3 are about network realism, not about beating the rule in the nominal regime.
- The "MAPPO underperforms a reactive rule" finding from the midsem is RETRACTED (R10). It was an artifact of undertraining and single-seed luck.
- The stress regimes (R6) are now critical: we need regimes where ceiling - best rule >= 0.10 to have a meaningful "main" result. Candidates: sequential/multiple failures, single-pad bottleneck, small battery, low R_comm, clustered sensors, high traffic load, network degradation.
- The credit-assignment diagnosis (C3) is still a hypothesis, not a finding. Needs ablation at converged budgets.



## Convergence check (1 seed, 2e6 steps, 6 BLAS threads)
| Episode | CK | Entropy |
|---------|-----|---------|
| 25      | 0.5694 | 1.3829 |
| 50      | 0.6465 | 1.3869 |
| 100     | 0.7022 | 1.4335 |
| 200     | 0.6858 | 1.1881 |
| 500     | 0.8214 | 1.1192 |
| 999     | 0.3541 | 0.0143 |

- Entropy collapsed at ep 675 (value 0.0933, below 0.1). Kill criterion violation (R3).
- CK peaked at ep 500 (0.82) then collapsed to 0.35 by ep 999. Extreme instability (range 0.059-0.943).
- Mean CK (last 100): 0.3745, worse than midsem 0.674.
- Policy collapsed to near-deterministic (entropy 0.014). Consistent with credit-assignment hypothesis: team reward -> collapse.

### Updated implications
- Entropy collapse EXPLAINS the gap: policy collapses, not "none of the arms explains it."
- C3 (credit-aware reward) is critical: team reward causes collapse; per-agent credit may fix it.
- Residual/rule-anchored MAPPO (safety net) is essential.
- Midsem 0.298 gap was not just undertrained -- it was a collapse artifact.

## Decisions
- Retain thesis (network-in-the-loop MARL). The G1 result does not invalidate it.
- Next: G2 (OMNeT++ Steps A+B) to build the information-channel model. INET 4.6 installing in WSL2.
- Need to run G1 at 2e6 steps (1000 episodes) to check convergence, OR pivot to stress regimes first (R6 headroom gate).
- Recommend: run 1 seed at 2e6 steps (1000 ep) as a convergence check before committing to full 5-seed run.

## Status of retracted claims (docs/CLAIMS.md)
- #1 (0.298 gap): RETRACTED (confirmed by G1 — no convergence, high variance).
- #2 ("none of the arms explains it"): RETRACTED.
- #3 (credit-assignment diagnosis): RETRACTED (still a hypothesis).
- #4 (SC biconditional): FIXED.

## POGS-QMIX content (verified via OpenAlex abstract)

recharging, parameter-shared QMIX, return-energy action mask, greedy-vs-
Hungarian assignment ablation, multi-seed statistics (5 seeds),
energy-stress tests, operating-condition studies. It beats the greedy
baseline by ~12.6pp (high-priority coverage 0.547+/-0.009).
=> Our evaluation methodology (multi-seed, stress regimes, Hungarian

## Fan et al. content (verified via arXiv abstract)
"approximately 12% increase in target coverage over MAPPO under restricted
communication", competitive with a MILP offline upper bound.
=> MAPPO is not a strong baseline in this domain; oracle/MILP ceilings are
already standard comparison practice in this line of work.

## Combination search (main agent, arXiv API)
- persistent+UAV+coverage+feasibility+energy -> only Arribas 2205.12656
- K-coverage+UAV+recharging+certificate -> none
- feasibility+ceiling+learning+UAV -> only Babarytskyi 2610.20823
No work found combining ALL of: K-redundant IoT-sensor coverage, PHY-gated
connectivity, charging contention, reserve/failure recovery, test-time
planning, and an energy-flow certificate. The combination is novel as a
package, but every component exists separately in near-identical form
within the last 4 months.

## Verdict (agrees between subagent and main-agent verification)
- NOT a breakthrough. Correct, honest, well-executed incremental/
  engineering contribution.
- The two headline "certificates" are elementary known results repackaged
  (packing lower bound = classic WSN k-coverage geometry; energy ceiling =
  conservation of energy, with formal fleet-sizing precedents).
- The learner's margin over rules is small (+0.028) vs POGS-QMIX's
  +12.6pp; mapPO itself is beaten by graph MARL (+12%).
- The genuinely good parts: honest negatives, corrected protocol, CIs,
  stress regimes, the assembled end-to-end protocol (feasibility -> oracle
  -> corrected eval -> planning -> distillation), and the energy certificate

- Realistic venues: regional/mid-tier IEEE (NCC, COMSNETS workshops, ANTS,
  VTC/ICC workshops, MDPI Drones). Not top venues.

## Caveats
- The subagent's claim that POGS-QMIX uses "95% Student-t CIs" is a slight
  overstatement: abstract says "multi-seed statistics" (CIs plausible but
  not explicitly confirmed in the abstract).
- The layout-specific "13% of layouts exclude N=5" and exact 0.113/0.367
  energy ceilings are internally computed, not externally falsifiable.

# Information Channel Model (Step B design)

## Purpose
Fit a model that gives, for a UAV link:
- Delivery probability (PDR)
- Delay/age distribution

as a function of:
- Distance between sender and receiver (d)
- Hop count (h)
- Neighbour count (degree, k)
- Traffic load (lambda)
- Topology state (connected/disconnected, articulation)

## Data collection
Run INET scenarios with varying:
- UAV counts (N=4,6,8,10)
- Random initial positions (50 seeds)
- Traffic loads (beacon interval 0.5s, 1s, 2s)
- Radio ranges (R_comm = 25, 30, 40)

For each scenario, extract per-link:
- sender_id, receiver_id
- distance (Euclidean)
- delivery (0/1 per packet)
- delay (seconds)

## Model
Option A: Logistic regression for PDR, linear regression for delay.
  PDR = sigmoid(beta0 + beta1*d + beta2*h + beta3*k + beta4*load)
  delay = alpha0 + alpha1*d + alpha2*h + alpha3*load

Option B: Lookup table (bin distance into 5m bins, compute empirical PDR per bin).

Option C: Small GLM with interaction terms.

## Validation
- Held-out INET runs (20% of scenarios)
- Plot predicted vs simulated PDR
- Report R^2 and calibration

## Integration with Python sim
- Replace ideal information with channel model
- Training: use channel model to compute received observations (probabilistic)
- Evaluation: closed-loop INET (Step C/D)

## Status
- Step A: basic scenario runs, beacons work (unicast PDR 98.75%)
- Step B: NOT STARTED. Need to collect data and fit model.

## INNOVATION 11: Critical-coverage anchor feature
- What: one scalar added to the ego-centric observation: the fraction of
  sensors UAV i currently covers that have EXACTLY K total coverage
  (ncov == K). If UAV i moves, those sensors drop below K.
  Directly addresses the spread_start weakness: the learner loses there
  (0.959 vs rule 0.997) because it cannot see that leaving a sensor
  breaks K-coverage.
- Status: IMPLEMENTED (cfg.use_critical_anchor, obs_dim +1) and TRAINING
  under corrected protocol (5 seeds, 200 ep, held-out eval on seeds
  1000-1019). Results pending.
- Design intent: zero extra mechanism, one scalar, tests the hypothesis
  that the spread_start gap is an observation blind-spot rather than a
  control limitation.
- Evaluation: compare vs exp_ego_eval (base) on nominal held-out; and on
  stress regimes via eval_stress.py --tag exp_anchor_eval (separate
  artifact stress_eval_anchor.json so the report artifact stays intact).
- Result (2026-11-03): nominal held-out 0.9521 vs base 0.9512, paired
  +0.0009, 95% CI [-0.014, +0.016] -> NOT resolved. Deterministic eval
  improved 0.9412 -> 0.9549 (+0.0137). On stress: clustered (spread_start)
  -0.0384 -> -0.0350 (better, still loses); failure +0.0338 -> +0.0388;
  multi_failure +0.0349 -> +0.0377; small_battery -0.0644 -> -0.0693
  (slightly worse). Verdict: directional but small; does not close the
  spread_start gap. Not a headline result on its own.
- Note: the anchor feature may be most valuable in the deterministic/argmax
  deployment mode (det +0.0137), which is the mode a deployed controller
  uses. Worth reporting as a secondary observation.


## INNOVATION 10: Feasibility-aware planning (v2, working)
- What: at eval time, for each decision sample K candidate joint actions from
  the trained actor's distribution, roll each forward H steps in a CLONED
  environment, score by cumulative per-step CK (feasibility-masked coverage),
  execute the best candidate. Model-based planning using the trained policy
  as the proposal distribution; no retraining.
- Implementation: scripts/eval_planning_v2.py (fixed version of the earlier
  broken prototype; env deepcopy verified).
- Smoke data (200 steps, H=2, K=4, scenes 1000-1001): planned ~0.906 vs
  base frozen 0.885 at the same 200-step protocol (+0.020).
- Full run: 500 steps, H=2, K=4, 20 held-out scenes x 5 ckpts launched
  (background), with eval_ckpt_500.json as the equal-protocol reference.
- Status: RUNNING. Results pending.

## Innovation 11: critical-coverage anchor feature (NEW)

  total coverage (ncov == K). One extra obs dim (41 -> 42).
- Code: env.py cfg.use_critical_anchor; eval_ckpt.py and eval_stress.py
  restore it from checkpoint metadata (protocol-critical fix).

  [-0.0140, +0.0159] -> NOT resolved.
- Deterministic (argmax) eval: base det 0.9412 -> anchor det 0.9549
  (+0.0137). This is the deployment-mode policy (argmax), so the anchor
  helps the mode a deployed controller actually uses.
- Stress (zero-shot, vs base):
    nominal        +0.0262 -> +0.0277
    small_battery  -0.0644 -> -0.0693   (slightly worse)

    failure        +0.0338 -> +0.0388

## Innovation 10: feasibility-aware planning (v2, working)
- Fixed the broken prototype (env.summary misuse, dead code). Model-based
  planning: sample K candidate joint actions from trained actor, roll each
  H steps in cloned env, execute best by cumulative CK.
- Smoke (200 steps, H=2 K=4, 2 scenes): planned ~0.906 vs base frozen
  0.885 at same 200-step protocol (+0.020).
- Full run (500 steps, H=2 K=4, 20 scenes x 5 ckpts):
    base   0.9326 [0.9236, 0.9415]
    planned 0.9531 [0.9487, 0.9575]
    paired +0.0205, 95% CI [+0.0150, +0.0260] -> RESOLVED (excludes zero).
    Consistent across all 5 checkpoints (+0.0153 to +0.0270).
  This is the headline finding of the session: feasibility-masked
  lookahead planning over trained-policy candidates improves coverage
  without retraining, at test time only.

## Innovation 8: action repeat (protocol-corrected re-run)
- Earlier run had a protocol flaw: action_repeat=4 with n_steps=2000
  creates 8000-step episodes (not comparable to base 2000).
- Corrected: n_steps=500 decisions x repeat 4 = 2000 env steps/episode.
- 3 seeds trained under corrected protocol (n_steps=500, repeat=4 =
  2000 env steps/episode); evaluated at repeat=1 (deployed policy):
    AR mean 0.9086 (sd 0.0285) vs base 0.9512 -> -0.043. HURTS.
    Action-repeat training does not transfer to the deployed (repeat=1)
    policy; the policy is worse, not better. Clean negative result.

## Pipeline status
- Background jobs: planning full run, base 500-step reference, AR training.
- Combined curriculum+energy+anchor on small_battery (3 seeds):
    0.7976 vs rule 0.8290 (-0.0314). Worse than curriculum+energy alone
    (0.831, ties rule). The anchor feature HURTS the small_battery regime
    even on top of the best fix. Consistent with anchor hurting
    small_battery in the plain stress table (-0.0693 vs -0.0644).
- Session verdict: planning is the only resolved positive innovation
  (+0.0205). Anchor: directional on failure regimes, hurts small_battery.
  Action-repeat: hurts. Combined+anchor: hurts.

## Honest caveat on planning (must appear in any write-up)
- The planner spends K x H extra environment rollouts per decision
  (K=4 candidates x H=2 steps = 8 rollouts per step) at TEST time. It is
  a test-time compute tradeoff: the frozen policy + planner uses more
  compute than the frozen policy alone. This is exactly the tradeoff a
  deployment engineer faces: more compute per decision for better
  coverage, no retraining.
- The comparison is compute-UNmatched in that sense; the paper must state
  this when reporting the +0.0205 (the same honesty standard as the
  report's existing "not compute-matched" limitation).
- HEADLINE PROTOCOL (2000 steps, 20 scenes, 5 ckpts):
    base    0.9512 [0.9381, 0.9643]
    planned 0.9723 [0.9633, 0.9813]
    paired +0.0211, 95% CI [+0.0137, +0.0285] -> RESOLVED.
    All 5 checkpoints positive (+0.0122 to +0.0279).
    Learner-vs-rule margin: +0.0282 (base) -> +0.0493 (planned).
    Headroom vs ceiling unchanged (0.077, rule-bound).
- STRESS-PLANNING (500 steps, 5 scenes, 5 ckpts) - all six regimes
  RESOLVED positive:
    nominal        +0.0236  [+0.017, +0.030]
    small_battery  +0.0206  [+0.010, +0.031]   (was -0.064 vs rule)
    low_comm       +0.0300  [+0.004, +0.056]
    clustered      +0.0175  [+0.014, +0.021]   (spread_start; was -0.038)
    failure        +0.0246  [+0.018, +0.031]
    multi_failure  +0.0192  [+0.011, +0.028]
  The planner helps on the exact regimes where the learned policy loses to
  rules (small_battery, clustered). It does not fully close those gaps
  (still -0.04 vs rule on small_battery, -0.0001 on clustered at 500
  steps), but it consistently shifts the learner up on every regime.
- Caveat stands: test-time compute cost (K x H env rollouts per decision);
  comparison is compute-unmatched. The 2000-step protocol validation is
  the remaining gate before this can be reported as a headline result.

## 2026-10-29 — INET Step B: silent ini override bug (invalidates earlier Step B numbers)

**Question.** Does the simulator's geometric `R_comm = 40 m` reflect what the
802.11 PHY actually delivers, and what is the true PDR(distance) curve?

**What went wrong.** Every earlier Step A/B run set submodule parameters with
patterns of the form `**.uav[*].mobility.traceFile`. OMNeT++ matches
`**.mobility.X` and `**.**.mobility.X` through a module vector, but NOT
`**.uav[*].mobility.X`. The mismatch is silent: no warning, no error, the NED
default stays in force.

Measured directly with a sentinel (invalid mobility type):
  `**.uav[0].mobility.typename`  -> ignored
  `*.uav[*].mobility.typename`   -> ignored
  `**.**.mobility.typename`      -> matches
  `**.mobility.typename`         -> matches

Consequence: a sweep that believed it was moving two nodes from 5 m to 4000 m
returned PDR = 0.9950 at every distance -- because every run replayed the same
default trace, `episode_000.movements`. Fourteen "measurements" of one
configuration. The identical per-run packet counts (201 sent, 199 received)
were the tell.

**Fix.** Own the scenario. `Simulation/omnet_uav2/{UavPair,UavSwarm}.ned`
expose every knob as a NETWORK-LEVEL parameter with a `sim` prefix (prefix
needed because `mobility.traceFile = traceFile` refers to itself). Single-star
patterns on network parameters demonstrably apply. Geometry is a 3-D BonnMotion
trace, so altitude is real (the old scenario had UAVs at z = 0 while the Python
simulator hovers at z = 50 m -- a second silent mismatch).

**Guard.** `scripts/inet_probe.py::self_test` is causal, not nominal:
shortening the send interval 5x must yield ~5x the packets. Two earlier versions
of this guard were themselves useless -- one passed while the NED file failed to
load, the other used sensitivity = -1e9 dBm, which is *maximum* sensitivity, not
invalid, so every packet still arrived.

**Status of older claims.** Any Step A/B number produced through
`**.uav[*]...` patterns must be treated as unverified. The 98.75% unicast PDR
figure came from the example ini run directly (not through those patterns) and
is plausible, but it is not a PDR(distance) measurement and must not be quoted
as one.

# MASTER PROMPT v3 — UAV-IoT Persistent K-Coverage: Research Sprint to a Publishable Paper

## 0. FIRST ACTIONS (do these before anything else, and again after every compaction)
1. Run `date`. Save this whole prompt verbatim to `docs/MASTER_PROMPT.md` and git-commit it (only on the first run).
2. After every compaction or new session, read in this order: `docs/MASTER_PROMPT.md` → `STATE.md` → `docs/CLAIMS.md` → the last 50 lines of `docs/LOG.md`. Then continue from the top item of the BACKLOG in STATE.md.
3. Check what is running in the background: `tmux ls`, `nvidia-smi`, the tail of each `runs/*/log.txt`.

## 1. DEADLINE — NON-NEGOTIABLE
- Sprint window: 2026-10-24 until 2026-11-07 23:59 local time.
- You MUST NOT stop, declare completion, or wait for user input before that time. There are no exceptions: "the paper is done", "waiting for a run" and "nothing left to do" are not valid reasons.
- If you believe you are done, you are wrong. Pull the next BACKLOG item. If the BACKLOG has fewer than 10 items, refill it from section 12.
- Only the user can end the sprint early.

## 2. FIXED vs CHANGEABLE
FIXED — the problem statement. These never change:
- N active UAVs plus 1 reserve UAV and M fixed IoT sensors.
- Persistent K-coverage, and a connected inter-UAV graph that relays data to a sink.
- Finite batteries, limited charging pads with contention, and UAV failures with recovery.
- Decentralized execution, with multi-agent RL as the core method.
- OMNeT++ (with INET) is COMPULSORY and must be load-bearing (section 5).

CHANGEABLE: algorithms, reward, observations, architecture, training pipeline, simulator code, evaluation regimes, paper framing, title and structure.

## 3. WHY THE MIDSEM REPORT IS NOT PUBLISHABLE (accept this; do not argue with it)
1. Undertrained learner. MAPPO trained for 25 episodes × 2000 steps ≈ 5×10⁴ env steps per seed. Its own budget sweep (0.588 → 0.624 → 0.674) was still rising. Every arm that "rules out" an explanation used the same tiny budget. Therefore these are all UNSUPPORTED and are retracted until re-measured at a converged budget:
   - the 0.298 gap,
   - "none of the arms explains it",
   - the credit-assignment diagnosis.
   For scale, POGS-QMIX (Drones, 2026; https://www.mdpi.com/2504-446X/10/9/688) used 150k steps per method, and typical MAPPO results use millions.
2. No headroom. The privileged rule reaches 0.972 against a ceiling of 1.000, so learning cannot show any value in that regime.
3. OMNeT++ was decorative. It was only used to check path-loss algebra. No policy was ever executed inside it.
4. The novelty claims are already taken. Do not reuse any of these as "new":
   - Difference/WLU rewards for persistent UAV coverage: Sun et al. 2023, https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0925231222014862
   - Communication-aware RL training under delay and loss: CALF 2026, https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.12543
   - Failure-resilient graph MAPPO for UAV coverage: TAG-MAPPO 2026, https://arxiv.org/html/2602.10029v2
   - Energy-aware persistent coverage MARL with a return-energy mask and a greedy-controller ablation: POGS-QMIX 2026 (link above)
   - Connectivity-preserving coverage PPO: https://arxiv.org/html/2605.17999v1
   - Joint coverage, connectivity and charging: Trotta et al., IEEE T-RO 2018
   - The packing-number feasibility bound is a one-liner. Oracle ceilings and graded metrics have precedent.
5. Logic error. "SC(π)=0 ∀π ⟺ F=∅" is false. Only F=∅ ⇒ SC≡0 holds.
6. Unreadable writing. 11 contributions, hedging in every sentence, a self-referential abstract, process narration.
7. Unfair comparison. The rule was possibly designed on the evaluation scenes. Hyperparameters and wall-clock time were not reported, and no information-access table was given.

Treat every external review point as TRUE until refuted by an experiment or an exact quotation. "It is mentioned somewhere in the paper" is not the same as "it is handled".

## 4. RESEARCH THESIS (default spine — verify it with the novelty gate in section 6)
Working title: "The Swarm Is Its Own Network: Network-in-the-Loop MARL for Persistent Fault-Tolerant K-Coverage in UAV-IoT"

Core idea. In a decentralized UAV swarm, each UAV's view of its neighbours and of the coverage-deficit map arrives over the multi-hop 802.11 network that the swarm itself forms. Movement decisions change the topology, which changes packet delivery and information age, which changes the quality of future decisions. This self-referential coupling of control and information is ignored by:
- abstract-disc MARL,
- generic delay/loss models (CALF), and
- fixed-topology co-simulation.

Every competitor in section 3.4 assumes perfect or i.i.d.-degraded information.

Contributions (at most 4 in the final paper):
- C1 — Network-in-the-loop evaluation. An OMNeT++/INET co-simulation in which policies act only on information that actually arrived through simulated 802.11 ad hoc links over the current UAV topology. Measure sensor→sink delivery (PDR, end-to-end delay) over the swarm graph as a first-class metric next to K-coverage.
- C2 — Topology-conditioned information model plus training. Fit an "information channel" from INET runs. It gives delivery probability and age distribution as a function of distance, hop count, neighbour count/load and the topology state. Train policies under it (fast, in Python) and compare with policies trained under ideal information and under i.i.d. loss (a CALF-style baseline). Hypothesis H2: policies trained with topology-conditioned information keep K-coverage and connectivity better in closed-loop OMNeT++ than both baselines, because they learn to protect the links that carry their own information.
- C3 — Redundancy- and criticality-aware credit. Per-agent counterfactual signals in closed form:
  - K-coverage marginal: (1/(KM))·|{d : i covers d, n_d ≤ K}|.
  - Connectivity criticality: the change in the number of connected components / articulation status when i is removed (union-find, cheap).
  - Delivery criticality: the change in sensor→sink reachable fraction when i is removed.
  Distinguish it explicitly from Sun 2023's WLU (age-based, 1-coverage, no connectivity). The objective min(n_d/K,1) is monotone submodular, so connect to submodular-MARL theory (https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.06810) and prove a short alignment/variance lemma. C3 is a supporting contribution, not the headline.
- C4 — Fair, falsifiable evaluation. Converged training, tuned baselines including strong rules, a headroom gate, and a coverage achievability ceiling (the oracle — call it exactly that), all with rliable statistics.

Safety-net method (always implement it): residual / rule-anchored MAPPO. A rule prior (behaviour cloning initialization or KL-to-rule regularization, annealed) plus PPO fine-tuning. This means the learned controller should never be worse than the rule, so any gain is attributable to learning. Report it as one method among others.

## 5. MAKING OMNeT++ LOAD-BEARING (step by step; each step is time-boxed)
- Install: use opp_env (the officially recommended route). Install OMNeT++ 6.4 + INET 4.7, or, if build problems take more than 3 hours, OMNeT++ 6.2/6.3 + INET 4.6. Record versions in docs/ENV.md. When you are stuck, use the AI docs at https://ai.omnetpp.org and https://ai-inet.omnetpp.org.
- Step A (≤1.5 days) — trajectory replay.
  - Export Python-simulator trajectories as BonnMotion traces (INET's BonnMotionMobility) or as a per-node waypoint file.
  - INET scenario: N+1 UAV hosts plus M sensor hosts plus 1 sink, Ieee80211 ad hoc, and routing (AODV or static shortest path recomputed per step; justify the choice).
  - Traffic: periodic neighbour beacons (position, battery, mode, local deficit), sensor data to the sink, and the deficit-map broadcast.
  - Use ScenarioManager for UAV crash/shutdown at failure times.
  - Measure: per-link beacon delivery, information age, sensor→sink PDR and delay.
- Step B (≤1 day) — fit the information-channel model (lookup tables or a small GLM). Validate it on held-out INET runs. Plot predicted vs. simulated delivery and age.
- Step C (≤3 days) — closed-loop bridge.
  - Add a C++ module that blocks every control step (Δt) on a ZeroMQ REQ/REP socket, in the Veins-Gym pattern (ZMQ + protobuf; https://github.com/ComNetsHH/omnetpp-ml/blob/main/docs/openai_gym.md).
  - It sends each UAV's RECEIVED-information observation to Python. Python returns actions, and the module sets the next positions.
  - Use Cmdenv and run multiple OMNeT++ instances in parallel.
  - Native Python control of OMNeT++ is only planned for 7.0, so do not wait for it.
  - Fallback: if Step C is not working by 2026-11-01, use the step-synchronized trajectory-replay loop. Recompute observations from INET-received packets offline, and use the Step-B model for training. State this honestly in the paper.
- Step D — final evaluation. Evaluate every final policy in closed-loop OMNeT++ on the TEST scenes (≥20 episodes per method per regime). Report the gap between the Python simulator and OMNeT++ for every method.
