These requirements conflict. A UAV that moves toward an
uncovered sensor may leave a coverage gap elsewhere. A
UAV that returns to charge may be the only communication
bridge between two groups of UAVs. A failure removes
both its coverage contribution and its communication links,
requiring the remaining swarm to reconfigure. Charging is
also a shared resource: several UAVs can become energy-
critical simultaneously while only a small number of pads are
available. Persistent service therefore requires a joint decision
process rather than a sequence of unrelated coverage and
charging heuristics.
A centralized controller faces a rapidly growing joint action
space. In the proposed discrete action model, each UAV selects
one of six actions: hover, move in one of four cardinal
directions, or charge. The joint action space consequently
contains 6N combinations. This growth does not by itself
make centralized learning impossible for every small swarm,
but it makes explicit joint-action enumeration and centralized
policy design progressively less attractive as N increases. A
decentralized execution architecture is therefore desirable for
scalability and fault containment.
Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) provides a
natural framework for this setting. CTDE allows a central-
ized critic to use information unavailable to the individual
UAV during training while retaining decentralized policies
during deployment. MAPPO is particularly suitable because
it combines centralized value estimation during training with
a policy-gradient actor that can be executed independently by
each agent.
The research question addressed in this work is: Can a
decentralized MAPPO policy maintain persistent K-coverage
and swarm connectivity while coordinating finite battery us-
age, charging, and single-UAV failure recovery, and can
its performance be certified against a rigorous achievability
bound rather than reported as an unscaled coverage ratio?
The central invention of this work is a feasibility-certified
evaluation framework for persistent K-coverage UAV net-
works. Instead of reporting coverage numbers with no
achievability reference—which is what the existing litera-
ture does, and which is meaningless when the configuration
is infeasible—the framework (i) derives a rigorous lower
bound on the number of UAVs required for K-coverage of a
bounded region, (ii) uses a teleporting placement oracle as an
achievability ceiling against which any policy is normalised,
and (iii) replaces the degenerate “all constraints satisfied
simultaneously” service-continuity metric with non-degenerate
time-averaged and refresh-time metrics. The framework is the
difference between a number and a measurement.
The framework earns its keep in a second way that is easy
to overlook, and which this paper demonstrates rather than
asserts. A framework that says whether a coverage number is
meaningful also says why a controller produces the number
it does, because the same reference points — the ceiling, the
non-degenerate metrics, and the controlled ablations — apply
to the controller and not only to the configuration. Applied
to a controlled experimental setup, the framework shows that
a hand-designed reactive rule outperforms parameter-shared
CTDE MAPPO on this task, and it bounds the reason with
controlled arms. Controlled arms bound how much of the
gap each alternative explanation can account for: adding the
agent identity (upper limit 0.137, margin +0.161); the full
observation of the proposed configuration (upper limit 0.102,
margin +0.196); removing the energy constraint (upper limit
0.075, margin +0.223); removing the threshold term (upper
limit 0.011, margin +0.287); the previous energy rule (upper
limit 0.015, margin +0.283), against a gap of 0.298. Every


=== PAGE 3 ===
arm’s upper limit is below the gap, so none of them can be
the whole of the explanation, by margins that are small but
positive. Every interval is paired over the same training seeds,
against the local-only arm A of the observation experiment and
the proposed configuration of the energy experiment and the
proposed configuration of the credit experiment. The credit
assignment of a shared team reward is the explanation the
residual is consistent with, and the cheapest test of it does
not resolve it . Reporting that result, with the experiments that
support it and the resolution at which each arm was measured,
is more useful to a reader than a favourable number whose
provenance has not been examined.
The contributions are:
1) A unified system model coupling persistent K-coverage,
inter-UAV connectivity, finite battery energy, charging
contention, and UAV failure recovery.
2) A feasibility certificate: a rigorous covering bound on the
number of UAVs required for K-coverage, in the general
form N ≥K P(A, Rcov), where P is the packing
number of the set to be covered. Its region instance
is N ≥4K and is tight at the reported parameters;
its sensor-set instance is computed per layout, and
it excludes the reported N = 5 configuration for a
measured 13% of random draws. The bound identifies
the instances on which no controller can achieve the
requirement, and the joint service-continuity metric is
identically zero for every policy on the instances where
that is so, which is why it must be replaced.
3) An achievability ceiling: a teleporting placement oracle
that upper-bounds any policy’s coverage, separating “the
policy is weak” from “the task is infeasible” and nor-
malising reported performance as achieved divided by
oracle. The separation is measured rather than asserted:
on the report’s own infeasible N = 5 configuration a
rule-based controller still reaches a respectable coverage
ratio with full connectivity while the joint metric is
identically zero, so neither metric alone distinguishes
that instance from a feasible one, and it is the certificate
that makes the reading decidable (Section VIII).
4) A measured negative result: on the configuration
the paper’s own certificate declares feasible, a hand-
designed reactive rule outperforms parameter-shared
CTDE MAPPO by 0.298 of persistent coverage (95%
interval [0.248, 0.349]), and the four single-factor arms
bound how much of that gap each of them can account
for.
5) A CTDE MAPPO framework with parameter-shared
decentralized actors, a centralized training critic, hard
action feasibility masks with an H-step connectivity
lookahead, and an explicit reserve-UAV recovery mech-
anism.
6) PHY-derived links — the Al-Hourani LoS probability,
a log-distance path loss with shadowing, and an IEEE
802.11 OFDM MCS table — that gate the abstract
coverage and communication discs rather than replacing
them, so that a UAV counts as covering a sensor or as
adjacent to another UAV only when the link carries a
usable service rate, together with a measured validity
condition showing when the disc approximation is the
binding constraint and when it is not.
7) A non-degenerate evaluation protocol (time-averaged
spatial integral of persistent coverage error, maxi-
mum refresh time, and k-coverage probability) replac-
ing the degenerate all-simultaneous-constraint service-
continuity metric.
8) A measured specification of what a shared policy’s
observation must contain: the agent’s own identity and
a bearing to the charging pad are the two terms the
controlled comparisons examine, and at 8 training seeds
they do not settle the question about the coverage. In
the component ablation, the identity changes persistent
coverage by +0.008, an interval [-0.121, +0.137] that
includes zero, so at this budget what it demonstrably
buys is the ability to specialise, and without it the
deterministic policy nearly collapses to a single action
and the swarm barely disperses. A broadcast summary
of where the coverage deficit is was added a priori and
measured to make no difference to the coverage at any
resolution tested, while it does change what the policy
does; it is reported rather than quietly dropped.
9) Corrected deployment parameters (N = 8, K = 2,
Rcov = 35 m, or N = 5, K = 2, Rcov = 45 m) derived
from the feasibility certificate, replacing the infeasible
N = 5, K = 2, Rcov = 35 m baseline, and both of
them MEASURED under the protocol below rather than
argued: the alternative deployment is feasible for the
learned controller and it does better there, by +0.083
of persistent coverage.
10) An evaluation protocol that treats a physical-layer claim
as requiring a negative control, and reports a measured
instance in which the available instrument could not
support the claim it was being used for.
11) A focused literature synthesis showing the differ-
ence between existing coverage, connectivity, recharge-
scheduling, and fault-tolerant approaches and the com-
bined problem considered here.
The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Sec-
tion II presents the literature survey and the research gap.
Section III defines the system architecture and mathematical
model, including the feasibility certificate. Section IV presents
the proposed MAPPO algorithm. Section V specifies the
comparison models, Section VI the performance metrics and
the evaluation protocol, and Section VII the experimental
design matrix. Section VIII reports the results and the claim
audit, and Section IX concludes the paper.
II. LITERATURE SURVEY
The survey is restricted to work that is directly related to
at least one of four components of the target problem: UAV
coverage/control, inter-agent connectivity, persistent energy-
aware operation, or fault-tolerant swarm recovery. The ten


=== PAGE 4 ===
core papers in Table I are discussed comparatively rather
than as isolated summaries. MAPPO is cited separately as the
underlying learning method [3].
A further recent line of work integrates communication and
control directly within MARL. MAPPO itself is adopted from
Yu et al. [3]. Sun et al. formulate joint resource allocation and
3D trajectory control and use action masking for constrained
hybrid actions [11]. Carvalho and Aguiar address decen-
tralized multi-agent coverage path planning with parameter
sharing, CTDE, safety filtering, and zero-shot generalization
[13]. Zhuang Chen et al. formulate UAV trajectory design
for emergency communication as a constrained MDP and
explicitly account for energy and turning behavior [12]. These
works reinforce the practicality of CTDE, action masking, and
structured rewards, but their primary objectives differ from
persistent redundant coverage with explicit failure recovery.
A. Research Gap
The literature can be grouped into complementary but
incomplete directions, and Table I lists the focused survey
while Table II lists the near-misses — the works that already
combine two or more of the elements this paper targets, and
the works a reader is most likely to raise when judging the
novelty claim. Energy-efficient coverage works jointly address
coverage and energy, and some include connectivity, but they
generally do not treat UAV failure and limited charging infras-
tructure as first-class elements of the same control problem [1],
[4]. Connectivity research provides decentralized graph condi-
tions and topology-repair mechanisms, but does not integrate
persistent sensor coverage and energy-aware learning [5], [6].
Persistent-service studies explicitly model recharge schedules
and energy limitations, yet typically assume fixed service
locations and a planned fleet or replacement process rather
than autonomous failure-driven reconfiguration [7], [8]. Recent
fault-tolerant MARL and persistent-coverage MARL move
closer to the target setting, but address different combinations
of health state, outage memory, target assignment, or coverage
objectives [9], [14].
Each of the five elements (i)–(v) has been studied in
combination with others — one work in Table II combines four
of them — and the near-misses are named explicitly so that the
claim can be checked. Trotta et al. [15] couple coverage, con-
nectivity and charging with rigorous performance bounds, but
have no failure model, no reserve UAV, no K-multiplicity and
no learned policy. Scherer and Rinner [16] couple persistent
surveillance, energy and communication constraints, but not
fleet-level failure recovery or decentralised execution. Hartuv
et al. [17] size a spare-drone fleet under energy constraints,
without coverage multiplicity or connectivity criticality. Zhang
et al. [44] come closest of all: their IRADA couples persistent
monitoring, energy-constrained charging, limited communi-
cation and failure recovery by task redistribution, which is
four of the five elements — and the controller that does it
is reward-driven rather than learned, their own future work
proposing reinforcement learning for it. Shi et al. [18] pro-
vide the closest published competitor, a symmetry-informed
decentralised swarm controller for communication coverage,
without a persistent K-coverage SLA, charging contention, or
reserve-UAV recovery. Qiu et al. [29] optimise aerial base-
station placement, which is a placement problem rather than
a persistent-control problem, and Liu et al. [1] provide the
energy-efficient coverage baseline that the others build on.
We are therefore not aware of work coupling all five
elements, and specifically not of any doing so with a learned
decentralised policy executed under centralized training with
decentralized execution (CTDE). This is a survey-derived gap
statement over the works listed in Table I and the near-misses
discussed above, not a claim that no related component has
ever appeared in the broader literature. Two of the near-misses
— [15] and [18] — post-date or parallel the works most often
cited for the individual elements, and are the two a reader is
most likely to raise.
a) The closest prior work, and how this paper differs
from it.: The evaluation philosophy proposed here is not
unprecedented in the wider literature, and we state the dif-
ference precisely rather than claiming a first. Four lines of
work are adjacent. [35] and [41] already evaluate learned or
heuristic controllers against an achievability reference, but the
reference is a MILP optimum for a particular finite instance;
it certifies nothing about an arbitrary deployment geometry,
and it cannot be computed without solving the instance. [40]
derives a rigorous geometric feasibility construct, and [39]
uses a feasibility upper bound to separate feasibility limits
from control-induced sub-optimality in a learned policy; both
concern a single coverage requirement, neither concerns K-
redundancy, and neither is combined with a persistent, energy-
constrained, failure-recovering control problem. Most closely,
[38] argues explicitly that coverage ceilings should be com-
puted before any learning experiment and quoted alongside
every result, and evaluates PPO against them — but for
drone-mesh interception, where the quantity being bounded
is interception coverage rather than K-redundant persistent
coverage of a fixed sensor set, and where the bound is closed-
form per configuration rather than a covering bound that scales
with N and K. The distinction claimed here is therefore not
“nobody has ever used a bound”. It is that the bound used must
certify the thing being claimed: a covering-theoretic lower
bound on N for K-redundant coverage of a bounded region,
an achievability ceiling computed for the same geometry and
the same redundancy requirement, and a metric that stays non-
degenerate when the bound says the instance is infeasible. That
is what the framework of Section III-G supplies, and the three
elements are used together rather than one at a time.
b) Three absences that the framework addresses.: A sep-
arate search over the same 2023–2026 corpus was conducted
for the specific claims that the framework makes, and the
absences are reported here because they are the substance
of the contribution rather than a side observation. First, no
paper in the corpus provides an infeasibility certificate for
a persistent-coverage instance in UAV swarms or mobile
sensor networks: the infeasibility-certificate literature that does
exist — for mixed-integer programs and for task-and-motion

A third absence concerns the mechanism that the results of
Section VIII leave as the leading candidate for the shortfall, the
credit assignment of a shared team reward. Explicit per-agent
advantage estimators do exist: the counterfactual advantage
of COMA [22], the difference-based estimator of DAE [23],
the per-agent value-iteration estimator of GPAE [24], and
the advantage-decomposition line of HAPPO/HATRPO [25].
Their argument against a shared team advantage is the credit-
assignment one: COMA observes that a global temporal-
difference error “does not explicitly reason about how that
particular agent’s actions contribute to that global reward”,
and GPAE states the objection in MAPPO’s own terms,
that the shared team advantage “ignores the agent-specific
impact on the joint outcome”. The limitation must be stated
fairly, because the shared team advantage is not known to
fail: MAPPO and independent PPO [27] show that a shared
reward with a centralised or a local critic can be a strong
baseline, and MAPPO’s own evidence for that is confined
to the standard cooperative benchmarks. The difficulty is that
the per-agent estimators have been evaluated overwhelmingly

ergodic convergence rates, and coverage reliability under sen-
sor failure — and the metrics used here are not novel in
isolation. What is claimed as new is the pairing: the non-
degenerate metrics are introduced together with the certificate
that determines whether they can be non-zero, so that a reader
can tell a policy failure from an infeasible instance without
knowing in advance which case applies.
III. SYSTEM MODEL
A. System Architecture
The system contains N active UAVs, one reserve UAV,
M fixed IoT sensors, a ground data sink/base station, and
S charging pads distributed within the operating region Ω.
UAVs provide sensor coverage through a range-limited air-
to-ground link and form a multi-hop communication network
among themselves. Sensor data reaches the sink through the
UAV communication graph whenever the graph is connected.
Figure 2 shows the architecture: the sensors, the UAVs, the
range-limited communication graph, the reserve UAV’s recov-
ery role and the shared actor that is deployed locally.
For tractability, the UAVs fly at a common nominal altitude
z0, so the decision process operates in the horizontal plane
while the altitude remains part of the physical state. Let
pi(t) = [xi(t), yi(t)]T denote the horizontal position of UAV
i and qd = [xd, yd]T the position of sensor d.

The critic sees the joint state, so it is a function of the
coverage deficit and can represent it; but the state does
not carry the per-sensor coverage counts nd(t) directly, so
the critic has to infer the deficit from the geometry of the
UAV and sensor positions. That distinction matters for the
credit assignment: a critic that could read nd(t) would face a
different problem from one that must reconstruct it, and the
difference is not visible in the reward. The same asymmetry
appears on the actor’s side, and it is the reason the broadcast
summary of the deficit is part of the observation model.

by the cell population makes the value global, so the agent
learns both where the deficit is and how large it is, and the
encoding is independent of M. The base configuration uses
G = 4, and the resolution sweep of Section VIII-A measures
G ∈{0, 4, 8}.
Two properties of this observation are not cosmetic, and
both are load-bearing for the shared-parameter design of
Section IV-A. The first is the identity. Parameter sharing is
sound only when each agent’s own observation identifies it,
so that a shared network can still specialise [21]; the first
version of oi did not satisfy this condition, and the conse-
quence was measurable rather than theoretical: in a symmetric
deployment every agent received an almost identical input,
the deterministic policy collapsed to nearly the same action
for all of them, and the swarm translated as a rigid body
without ever dispersing. The implication is specific to an action
space of displacements, which is the one used here: identical
displacements translate the configuration rigidly and so freeze
its shape. In an action space whose symbols index agent-
local targets, the same symbol would send different agents
to different places, and dispersion would be possible after
all. The second is the bearing to the charger. Without it the
observation carries the cost of the flight to a pad but not its
direction, and a learned policy cannot express the return at
all. We assume that the infrastructure which owns the charging
pads also broadcasts their positions, which is a communication
assumption rather than an oracle.
A third term — a broadcast summary of where the coverage
deficit is — was added a priori, on the argument that an
agent which knows how many sensors it covers but not
which are deficient has no gradient signal for deployment. The
measurement of Section VIII-A does not settle that argument
for the better: the summary makes no measurable difference
to the coverage at any resolution tested, so the argument for
adding it is neither supported nor refuted by the score, and
what it does change is the shape of the swarm’s motion.
The summary is therefore kept in Eq. (4) and reported as
a null result rather than quietly dropped, and we keep the

the reason is worth stating here rather than there, because the
two criteria are easy to confuse. σ compares an area to an area,
while K-covering a bounded region is a covering problem: the
four corner points of the square are more than 2Rcov apart, so
no disc can serve two of them, and the packing bound of the
next section then requires N ≥4K = 8 for this configuration
— the same configuration that σ passes. The bound above is
necessary rather than sufficient in a second way as well, since
it ignores coverage-disk overlap and the discreteness of the
sensor layout; scenario S6 of Table XI therefore sweeps Rcov
directly to characterize the transition.

G. Feasibility Certificate for K-Coverage
Before any policy is trained, the configuration must be
shown to admit a feasible solution. Two different requirements
have to be separated here, because they have different cer-
tificates: the requirement that every point of the operational
region Ωis K-covered, and the requirement that every one
of the M sensors is K-covered. The second is what the
experiments measure, and the distinction is not academic: the
corner argument that settles the first does not settle the second.
The packing lemma. Let A be the set of points to be K-
covered and define the packing number
P(A, R) = max

|X| : X ⊆A, ∥x −x′∥> 2R ∀x̸ = x′ 	
.
(11)
Then A cannot be K-covered by fewer than K P(A, R) discs
of radius R. The proof is one line: a disc of radius R contains
at most one point of X, because two such points would be
within 2R; so the discs that serve the K coverings of each
point of X are pairwise disjoint across distinct points, and each
point consumes K of them. This is a first-principles covering
argument — no disc covers two corners because they are more
than 2Rcov apart, and each corner must be covered K times
— and it is the only form of it that applies to an arbitrary
point set.

6.72 m, cover it K times with 4K discs. So N = 8 is not
merely sufficient for the region; it is exactly sufficient.
Sensor-set bound, and what the corner certificate does not
say. The sensors are not at the corners, so (12) does not
transfer to them. It would transfer if the sensor set contained
four sensors whose coverage discs were pairwise disjoint, and
a sufficient condition for that is one sensor in each of four
corner caps of radius below 5.00 m: two sensors in adjacent
caps are then at least 80−2r apart, and their discs are disjoint
while 80 −2r > 2Rcov = 70 m, the adjacent pair being the
binding one (a diagonal pair is 80
√
2−2r apart). The condition
is sufficient and not necessary — a packing of four sensors
more than 70 m apart can occur anywhere and not only near
the corners — but a random draw essentially never meets it:
a cap of that radius is 0.31% of the square, and a uniform
draw of 20 sensors lands one in each of the four caps with
probability 9.3 × 10−6. The applicable bound is (11) applied
to the realised sensor set. Measured over 30 random draws
(analysis/feasibility.py), the packing number has
mean 2.133 and range 2–3, so the bound is N ≥4.27 on
average and N ≥6 in the worst case, and N = 5 is excluded
for 4 of the 30 draws (13%). On the scenes on which the
teleporting oracle was measured it reaches CK = 0.990
at N
= 5, so the sensor requirement does not obstruct
N = 5 there; what that measurement does not do is certify
feasibility for the remaining draws, and the correct statement
is a probabilistic one, not a certificate. We state this rather than
the convenient one: the configuration is provably infeasible for
the region, and probably infeasible for a minority of sensor
draws.
The corrected configuration is feasible for both require-
ments. N = 8, K = 2, Rcov = 35 m satisfies (12) with
equality and the construction above, so every sensor is K-
covered for every sensor layout, not merely for the ones that
were drawn. The teleporting oracle of Section III-G confirms
it, reaching CK = 1.000 with a connected placement.
The area-surplus criterion certifies nothing. The metric
σ = NπR2
cov/(K|Ω|) equals 1.503 at N = 5 and exceeds one,
and the configuration is nonetheless infeasible for the region.
The reason is that area is a measure condition and covering
is a pointwise one: N discs can be piled over a small patch,
satisfying σ > 1 while most of Ωis uncovered, and conversely
a clustered sensor set can be covered with σ < 1. In particular
σ ≥1 is necessary for K-covering the region and is not
even necessary for K-covering a sensor set, and it is never


=== PAGE 10 ===
sufficient: at N = 7, K = 2 it is 2.10 and the region bound
(12) still excludes the configuration. A feasibility certificate
has to be a covering argument.
What the degenerate metric does, exactly. Let F be the
set of configurations in which every sensor is K-covered and
the communication graph is connected. The service-continuity
metric of Table X satisfies
F = ∅
=⇒
SC(π) = 0 for every policy π,
(13)
because SC(π) > 0 requires the trajectory to visit F at some
instant. The converse does not hold: a poor policy on a feasible
instance may also score zero, so observing SC(π) = 0 does
not prove infeasibility. The statement is therefore about the
best achievable value maxπ SC(π) and not about the value
any particular policy realises: a poor policy on a perfectly
feasible instance also scores SC = 0. When F = ∅the metric
is uninformative, and the time-averaged coverage deficit of the
same table is not, which is the point of reporting it alongside.
Corrected, feasible deployments: N = 8, K = 2, Rcov =
35 m (provably feasible for both requirements, and tight
against the region bound) or N = 5, K = 2, Rcov = 45 m,
for which four discs at the midpoints of the region’s sides
and one at its centre cover every point of the region at least
twice, the worst second-nearest distance being 44.72 m against
the 45 m offered. The second of these is not an argument but
a measurement: trained and evaluated under the protocol of
Section III-O — 25 episodes and 8 training seeds, the same
evaluation scenes — the alternative deployment is feasible for
the learned controller, and it does better there: with five UAVs
and a 45 m coverage radius the learned controller reaches
0.757 against 0.674 for the reported eight-UAV deployment, a
difference of +0.083 on the same training seeds and the same
evaluation scenes. The rule baselines were not measured at that
operating point, so this establishes feasibility for the learned
controller and not the superiority of the deployment. The
certificate identifies a deployment the original configuration
could not use, and on this instance the deployment it identifies
is the better of the two for the learned controller. All trained
results below use the reported eight-UAV deployment, and the
comparison is reported here because the framework produced
it.
Achievability
ceiling.
A
teleporting
placement
oracle
(analysis/feasibility.py) places the N UAVs any-
where, at no motion cost and ignoring energy, and upper-
bounds the coverage fraction CK of any policy, because the
per-step coverage fraction of any trajectory is bounded by
the best static placement. It therefore separates “the policy is
weak” from “the task is infeasible”, and it is the ceiling against
which the reported coverage is read. Two limits on the claim
are worth stating. The oracle is an upper bound on CK and not
on the service-continuity metric, which additionally requires
the requirement to hold at every instant of a kinematically
constrained trajectory; and it does not certify that a feasible
trajectory achieving the certified coverage exists. That last
point is checked rather than assumed: the construction of (12)
is admissible under the simulator’s own safety filter — its
communication graph is connected, it has no articulation point,
and its eccentricity is 3, within the H-hop rule — so the
certified configuration is reachable by a policy and the ceiling
is comparable with what a policy can achieve. The normalisa-
tion by the oracle is, at this configuration, the identity, since
the ceiling is 1.000 for every sensor layout; its information
is that the task is coverable at all with N = 8. Since the
construction is itself admissible under the safety filter, the
constrained ceiling is the same 1.000: the constraint removes
no headroom, so there is no second ceiling to compute, and the
normalisation by the oracle is meaningful at this configuration
rather than vacuous. At the corrected configuration the value is
CK = 1.000 and it is attained for every sensor layout, because
the construction of (12) covers the whole region, so the ceiling
is deterministic rather than a random variable over layouts.

metrics.

metric
“fraction of time all sensors are K-covered and the graph

1
T
P
t(1 −CKt), which is graded:
it gives partial credit for a near miss, where the binary flag
gives none, and it is the better-behaved quantity as a training
signal. We note that it is, exactly, the complement of the
coverage fraction CK, so it is a change of convention rather
than an independent measurement, and that it is blind to
the connectivity half of the requirement. The second is the
maximum refresh time, the longest run of consecutive steps
with any under-covered sensor, which is not a function of CK:
a controller can hold a high average coverage while leaving
one sensor dark for a long time, and the refresh time is what
detects that. It is the maximum refresh time, rather than the
deficit, that carries the information the binary flag cannot.

I. The Radio Model, and What It Gates
The graph of (14) and the coverage condition of (7) are
both geometric, and both are gated by a radio model: a UAV
counts towards a sensor’s coverage, and two UAVs count as
adjacent, only when the link between them carries a usable
service rate. The gate is what makes the discs physical rather
than notional, and it is stated here because the two conditions
above are otherwise read as purely geometric.
The air-to-ground path follows the Al-Hourani model [31]:
for a UAV at altitude z0 and a slant range d3 to the ground
node, the elevation angle θ = arcsin(z0/d3) gives the proba-
bility of an unobstructed path,

and the path loss blends a log-distance law for the clear path
with one for the obstructed path,

is a property of the scene and not of the step, and the inter-

physical link.
The received power is Ptx 10−P L/10, with Ptx = 0.5 W at
f = 2.4 GHz, and the noise floor is the thermal noise of a
20 MHz channel with the receiver’s noise figure. The signal-
to-noise ratio selects an achievable rate from the IEEE 802.11
OFDM MCS table [33], and a link is usable when that rate
is at least 6.5 Mbit/s, the lowest rate in the table. Writing
rateid for the rate that the access link from UAV i to sensor

and the radio is the budget, and which of the two binds

measures the link margin at the two operating radii and finds it
wide, so the feasibility certificate of Section III-G and not the
radio is what constrains the fleet. Second, because the gate

Two properties of this model are easy to state and easy to
implement incorrectly, and both were implemented incorrectly
in the first version of the simulator, so both are pinned by tests.
First, the return is a physical transition and not a decision
available to the policy: the simulator makes it, so that the
reward, the metrics and the charging arbitration can all see it.
If the simulator does not make it, then a learned policy has
no way to express the return at all, the arbitration is never
entered, and the reserve mechanism has nothing to recover —
the three mechanisms this paper proposes are then present in
the model and absent from the experiment. Second, a UAV
that is docked and charging has its rotors idle and draws only
the avionics and communications baseline; if it is billed the
hover power, the pack loses more energy to the rotors than
the pad puts back, no UAV can ever recover, and the charging
coordination is unusable. A UAV whose pack empties away
from a pad is out of service: it can no longer fly, and it must not
continue to count towards coverage or towards the connectivity
graph. Figure 4 shows the battery and failure state machine:
the transitions between flying, returning to charge, charging
and failing, and the point at which the reserve UAV takes
over.

L. Safety Constraints
The environment enforces
∥vi(t)∥≤vmax,
pi(t) ∈Ω,
∥pi(t) −pj(t)∥≥dsafe, ∀i̸ = j.
(25)
An action is masked if it violates a locally predictable hard
constraint such as workspace bounds, speed, minimum separa-
tion, or invalid charging. The energy rule deserves a sentence
of its own, because a weak version of it is a mechanism rather
than a detail: a UAV that may depart with a flat battery will
fly until its pack is empty, and an exhausted UAV is removed
from the active set, taking its share of the coverage and of the
communication graph with it. The mask therefore requires a
UAV to retain, after the move, the energy to reach a charging
pad plus the reserve margin, computed from where the UAV
would be. The rule is one-sided in the UAV’s favour, because a
UAV that is already below the threshold must still be allowed
to move towards a pad; blocking it there would strand it cer-
tainly. Connectivity is handled differently, and the distinction
matters. The policy is not assumed to predict connectivity from
one-hop observations; it receives the local bridge-risk feature
ρi and the team reward penalises connectivity fragility, so
nothing in the learning signal claims a global guarantee from
purely local information. The simulator, however, is a safety
filter: it evaluates the prospective communication graph for
every candidate action and masks any move that would leave
the swarm unable to remain connected, including the H-step
lookahead of Section IV. The guarantee therefore comes from
the safe-filter architecture, in which the filter has access to
the true state, and not from the policy’s own foresight. The
distinction is the standard one between learning which action
to take and being told which actions are admissible.
M. Failure and Recovery
A failure event changes Fi from 0 to 1 at the detection
instant tf. One reserve UAV is maintained with sufficient
energy for deployment when feasible. After a detected failure,
the reserve is activated and the active UAVs continue using
their decentralized policies. The recovery time is defined as
τf = inf {τ ≥0 : nd(tf + τ) ≥K, ∀d} ,
(26)
when recovery is achieved before the evaluation horizon. If
recovery is impossible under the available fleet, the event is
reported as an unrecovered failure rather than assigning an
artificial recovery time.
A second mode of loss of an active UAV is exhaustion rather
than failure: a UAV whose pack empties while it is away from
a charging pad can neither fly nor serve, and it is removed from
the active set. Such a UAV is out of service rather than failed,
and the same reserve mechanism can re-seat it. This distinction
is not cosmetic. If an exhausted UAV were left in the active
set it would continue to count towards coverage and towards
the connectivity graph while being unable to do either, and the
reported coverage would be optimistic by exactly the number
of sensors such a UAV was covering.
A recovery-time guarantee is therefore conditional: the
reserve mechanism can reduce the time required for reconfig-
uration, but it cannot mathematically guarantee restoration for
arbitrary sensor layouts, fleet sizes, or multiple simultaneous
failures. This distinction is important for a realistic system
model.

a) The energy-threshold term, and why a consumption

t

mission: flying 30 m to a charging pad costs about 480 J,
which is 1.6% of a 30 kJ pack, so the consumption term
contributes about 0.0016 to the cost, whereas the consequence
of not going — a UAV that cannot reach a pad leaves the
swarm, stops covering, and may fragment the graph — is
paid late and by the team. A controller that is only told
what it has spent therefore has no reason to turn back before
the consequence arrives. Bt is the mean fractional shortfall
below the return threshold of (22), i.e. the quantity the
observation already carries as the return-urgency feature, and
it is the term the paper’s own metric table asks for when it
lists “minimum battery level, and threshold violations” under
Energy. Section VIII reports a controlled measurement of the
effect of this term and of the alternative hypothesis that the
energy constraint is simply too tight for the episode length.
Table VI separates the two kinds of constraint: the hard ones
the filter enforces on every candidate action, and the trade-offs
the reward asks the policy to make.

The control interval is chosen so that the relative displace-
ment between two consecutive steps, 2vmax∆t = 2 m, is
smaller than the safety distance dsafe = 5 m; a coarser step
would allow a closing pair to cross the separation constraint
between two samples. The charge increment is quoted per step
and is therefore scaled with ∆t. The resulting charge time
is shorter than a real constant-current pack of this capacity
would require, because a real pack would not complete a
full charge within a tractable episode; this is stated as a
modelling assumption rather than a physical prediction, and
it means the cost of charging contention in the energy results
of Section VIII-B is a lower bound. The nominal altitude is
consistent with the coverage radius: a 74◦downward sensor
at 50 m yields a footprint half-width of 37 m. The two
power entries are distinct: Pelec is the total avionics and
communications budget, whereas Ptx is the radiated transmit
power, which is bounded by the 1 W (30 dBm) regulatory
ceiling and is two orders of magnitude below the avionics
budget. The chosen vmax = 5 m/s is conservative but not
arbitrary: Luna et al. [20] report a real three-UAV coverage
mission flown at 5 m/s cruise and 20 m altitude, and Datsko
et al. [19] measure a range-optimal cruise speed of 8.39 m/s
for the airframe they study.
a) The initial deployment and the episode length are
experimental choices, and they are stated as such.: Two pa-
rameters of Table VII deserve an explicit justification, because
the results are sensitive to both and a reader should be able to
see why they were chosen.
Initial deployment. The swarm starts as a connected cluster
in one corner of the region, not as a deployed formation.
The reason is measurable: a centred ring deployment already
covers 17 of the 20 sensors at t = 0, so every controller —
including one that never moves — scores CK = 0.850, the
achievable range is roughly [0.85, 1.0], and the comparison
cannot separate the methods. The clustered deployment is
connected at t = 0, so the connectivity invariant remains
checkable from the first step, but it covers only 3 of the 20
sensors, so the controller has to deploy across the field while
holding K = 2 redundancy. This is the standard arrangement
for a persistent-coverage benchmark, and the pre-deployed
arrangement is retained as scenario S9 so that the sensitivity
is reported rather than hidden.
Episode length. The episode is 2000 control steps, i.e. 400 s
of flight. At the 400-step episode used in an earlier revision —
80 s of flight, which is 13% of the pack’s 600 s endurance —
the pack never depleted: the return-to-charge transition never
fired, the charging arbitration was never entered, the reserve
UAV had nothing to recover, and the three mechanisms the pa-
per proposes were never exercised. A sweep over the candidate
configurations (analysis/energy_regime.py) shows
that at 2000 steps the energy constraint binds — 213 return-
to-charge transitions and 0.4 stranded UAVs per episode under
the Reactive heuristic — while the mission remains achievable.
The report’s 10 000-step target is a different question, and the
results here are explicitly for the 400-second episode.
Within scope are spatial K-coverage, range-limited UAV
connectivity, battery depletion, charging contention, single-
UAV failure recovery, collision avoidance, and decentralized
motion-policy execution. The primary model intentionally
abstracts small-scale multipath fading, detailed aerodynamic
dynamics, obstacles, wind, battery aging, GPS denial, sensor
failures, and multiple simultaneous UAV failures. These can
be introduced as subsequent stress-test layers after the base
control problem is validated.
b) Consistency of the physical parameters.: The audit of
Section VIII-F also records the derived physical quantities, so
that the modelling choices are explicit rather than implicit. The
endurance implied by Bmax and Phover is 30,000/50 = 600 s
(10 min); the power ratio Pmove/Phover = 1.5 is conservative
against the 1.09 measured by Datsko et al. [19] for energy-
optimal multirotor flight; and the charge increment of 2×10−4
of the pack per step corresponds to a full charge in 1000 s,
i.e. a 3.6 C rate, which is above the 1 C typical safe charge
rate of hobby LiPo and is therefore an explicit modelling
assumption rather than a physical prediction. Two further
observations matter for the interpretation of the results. First,
the separation constraint is enforced at the sample rate: two
UAVs closing head-on at 2vmax have a braking distance of
v2
close/(2a) = 25 m at a = 2 m/s2, five times dsafe, so the mask
guarantees sample-time separation and not braking. Second,
the energy budget of the reported episode is tight rather than
generous. A pack of 30,000 J at the moving draw of 80.1 W
lasts 1873 steps of continuous flight and nothing else, so the
fleet can sustain the 2000-step episode only at a duty cycle
of about 89% against the Ereserve margin, and the charging
rate of 0.0002 of the pack per step is a 3.6C charge, which
is an explicit modelling assumption of this work and not a
physical prediction; the consequence is that the quantity the
charging machinery has to arbitrate is genuinely scarce, and a
controller that does not manage it will strand its UAVs. A third
observation concerns the connectivity constraint: at N = 8 on
an 80 × 80 m field the inter-UAV graph is not always dense
— measured over a 2000-step flight in the deployed regime,


=== PAGE 15 ===
the mean node degree is 3.63 of a possible 7, the graph is
complete in only 12% of steps, and nodes of degree ≤1 —
leaves of the graph, which are not articulation points but mark
how thin the swarm’s connectivity is — occur in 23% of UAV-
steps. Connectivity is therefore a live constraint throughout the
mission and not only after a failure, which is what makes the
H-step mask and the reserve mechanism load-bearing rather
than decorative. All four quantities are reported rather than
silently adjusted, because changing them would change the
measured results and the results are the claim.
IV. PROPOSED ML ALGORITHM
A. CTDE MAPPO
The proposed algorithm uses parameter-shared MAPPO.
During training, the centralized critic observes st while every
actor uses oi(t). Figure 5 shows the loop: the environment and
the control loop, the training-only feedback to the critic, and
the transfer of the learned actor to decentralized execution.
During deployment, the critic is removed and each UAV
evaluates the same shared policy:
ai(t) ∼πθ (ai | oi(t)) .
(30)
Parameter sharing is appropriate when (i) the environment is
equivariant to agent permutations—identical observation and
action spaces and identical transition/reward structure—and
(ii) each agent’s own observation breaks the permutation sym-
metry, so that a shared network can still specialise (Foerster et
al. [21]). Condition (ii) does not require a literal index: relative
coordinates to the other agents break the symmetry just as
well, because they distinguish the agents. What it does require
is that no two agents in the same physical situation receive the
same observation, and the consequence is a statement about
the hypothesis class rather than about optimisation: if oi = oj
then a shared policy is a function and πθ(·|oi) = πθ(·|oj),
so no amount of training can make the two agents differ.
The first version of oi did not satisfy condition (ii) — it
distinguished the agents only through their individual position,
battery and mode, which in a symmetric deployment are nearly
identical across the swarm — and the measured consequence
was that the deterministic policy chose nearly the same action
for every UAV and the swarm moved as a rigid body, so the
shared-parameter claim could not be sustained on the evidence.
We therefore treat 1i as part of the model rather than as an
implementation detail, and Section VIII reports the controlled
comparison. The known limitation (Fu et al. [28], Theorem
4.2) is that a shared policy provably cannot learn an optimal
policy for non-symmetric tasks such as the XOR game; this
does not apply here because the swarm is homogeneous.
If grounded or docked UAVs with heterogeneous roles are
introduced, parameters must not be shared.
For a collected rollout, the temporal-difference residual is
δt = Rt + γVϕ(st+1) −Vϕ(st),

A fixed-length rollout ends either in a genuine terminal state or
in a time-limit truncation, and the two must not be conflated.
At a truncation boundary the last state is not absorbing, so
the advantage recursion must cut without treating the state as
terminal; the correct treatment is to bootstrap the temporal-
difference residual from V (sT ) rather than from zero [34].
The size of the error is explicit: replacing the bootstrap by
zero changes the value target by −γ(γλ)T −t

more than zero and upward when it is worth less, and the
sign follows the sign of the continuation value. The claim is
about the value target and not about a fixed direction of policy
improvement, since a mis-estimated advantage near zero can
push an update either way. The bootstrap is unbiased for V π
only in the idealisation that the critic is exact and the truncation
is exogenous; with an approximate critic it inherits the critic’s
error at the boundary, scaled by γT −t. Conflating the two
nevertheless injects a systematic error, and it did so in this
work: the simulator initially reported the end of the mission
time limit through the same flag it used for a genuine dead end,
so every episode boundary was bootstrapped from zero. The
simulator now reports termination and truncation separately
— the mission time limit is a truncation, and only the loss
of every UAV is a terminal state — and the rollout consults
that flag rather than inferring termination from the episode-
end flag. The distinction is pinned by unit tests, one of which
asserts that a time-limit episode is reported as a truncation
and not as a termination, and another that asserts the rollout
reads the environment’s flag rather than re-deriving it. The

a) Value

Value normalisation is one of the components the
MAPPA/MAPPO literature identifies as load-bearing, and it
was missing from the implementation while the earlier revision
of this report asserted it. It is now present, and the details mat-
ter. The critic is trained to predict the returns in a normalised
space defined by running statistics of the return distribution,
maintained as an exponential moving average with β = 0.99:
bRnorm
t
=
bRt −µ
σ + ϵ ,
(36)
where µ and σ are updated from the current rollout’s returns.
The consequence is easy to get wrong: the critic’s raw output is
then the normalised value, so the temporal-difference residual
of Eq. (31), the advantage recursion of Eq. (32), and the
bootstrap at a truncation boundary must all un-normalise it
before use, as V (s) = σ ˆVϕ(s) + µ. Reading the raw critic
output at any of those three points is a silent scale error in
the advantage estimates: the training loss still decreases, the
entropy still falls, and the policy is simply trained against the
wrong signal. The implementation therefore exposes a single
accessor for the value and the test suite asserts that the rollout
uses it rather than the raw output; a second test asserts that
the value-clipping auxiliary term compares two quantities in
the same space, since the recorded old value is in the original
scale.
The advantage is normalised as well, by the mean and
standard deviation of the batch. We also implemented a per-
agent variant, in which each agent’s advantages are normalised
over its own history rather than over the pooled batch, and we
report the measurement in Section VIII: with a shared team
reward every agent’s advantage sequence is nearly identical,
so the per-agent normalisation is close to a rescaling and does
not change the credit assignment, which is the limitation of
shared team rewards rather than a normalisation choice.
b) The credit assignment is a property of the re-
ward, not of the normalisation.:
With a team reward
and

: the factor that weights
every agent’s score is the same number for all of them, so the
gradient cannot distinguish an agent whose action helped from
one whose action was irrelevant. Giving each agent its own
value function does not repair that: it re-centres and re-scales
the shared team signal per agent, so the advantage is no longer
a single shared number, but it cannot decompose it, because
the advantage’s dependence on the other agents enters only
through the aggregate reward and through the observation,
which are symmetric in the other agents. Redistribution of
credit requires a per-agent reward, a joint-action critic, or a
counterfactual baseline. This is the credit-assignment objection
that the per-agent estimators make explicitly: COMA [22]
observes that a global temporal-difference error “does not
explicitly reason about how that particular agent’s actions
contribute to that global reward”, and GPAE [24] states the
objection in MAPPO’s own terms, that the shared team advan-
tage “ignores the agent-specific impact on the joint outcome”.
We state the limitation rather than the conclusion, because
the limitation is not a failure: a shared team advantage is a
strong baseline on the standard cooperative benchmarks [3],
[27]. What the literature does not contain is an evaluation of
the question on a persistent-coverage task, and Section VIII-D
reports one: the same learner with the advantage made per-
agent, and nothing else changed.
B. Action Feasibility Mask
Before the sampled action is executed, the simulator eval-
uates the predicted next position and applies the follow-
ing checks: workspace bounds, maximum speed, minimum
UAV separation, charge validity, and connectivity-preservation
constraints. If a candidate movement would disconnect the
communication graph, it is masked in normal operation. The
H-step rule is a statement about the mover’s eccentricity,
not about the graph’s diameter and not about robustness: it
prevents a UAV from drifting to the end of a long chain, since
a node at the end of a chain of length greater than H has an
eccentricity greater than H and may not legally act from there,


=== PAGE 17 ===
and it does not by itself prevent articulation points, which the
separate articulation test forbids — a path of seven nodes with
the mover at its centre satisfies the rule and has six articulation
points. The rule also constrains only the node that is acting,
so another agent may extend a chain and raise the first agent’s
eccentricity without violating that agent’s own check, and in
a dispersed graph no legal move may exist for some node
at all. A rule expressed as a hop radius therefore restricts
the topology more than it protects it, as the ring example
above shows. During an active recovery event, the connectivity
rule remains a hard constraint unless the simulator enters a
predefined recovery mode in which temporary reconnection is
required by the recovery objective.
This separation between policy learning and hard feasibility
is important. The neural network learns how to trade off
several feasible actions, while the safety layer prevents the
network from selecting actions that violate non-negotiable
physical constraints.
The masking is applied at the logit level, before the softmax,
so that the policy that is sampled from, the importance
ratio that is computed against, and the entropy bonus that is
regularised are all the same masked distribution.
a) The filter does not leak, but it does restrict.:
Two
properties
of
the
filter are
measured
rather
than
assumed.
First,
the
graph
is
connected
at
every
step
in which the active set is unchanged: over 2000 steps
driven by the learned controller, the graph was discon-
nected on no step in which the active set was unchanged
(analysis/mask_admissibility.py). A connectivity
availability below 1.000 in the results therefore coincides with
UAVs leaving the active set — a failure, or a pack that empties
away from a charging pad — and not with the filter failing,
because a removed UAV takes its share of the coverage and
of the graph with it. Second, the filter excludes configurations
that a covering argument would admit: the 8-node ring is
connected, has no articulation point, and is a valid covering
family, but its eccentricity is 4, so the H = 3 rule rejects every
move that would preserve it. The safety filter thus shrinks the
reachable configuration set, and a controller that needs to move
into a rejected family is stuck; we report this as a property
of the filter and not as a property of the task. This is the
mechanism that Huang and Onta˜n´on [30] show to correspond
to a valid policy-gradient update rather than a biased surrogate:
masking is implemented as a state-dependent differentiable
transformation of the action-probability distribution, which is
exactly what setting the masked logits to −∞before the
softmax does. We note the limit of that result, which was
stated explicitly in the same work and is repeated in the
UAV action-masking literature [36]: the validity argument is
formulated for a single policy, and extending it to a centralized
critic with heterogeneous per-agent masks requires the critic’s
training distribution to be consistent with the induced joint-
action support. We therefore apply the identical mask to the
rollout distribution, the stored log-probabilities and the update,
and we verify this by construction in the test suite rather than
by assumption.

C. Failure-Aware Execution
When a failure event is detected, the environment removes
the failed UAV from the active graph, activates the reserve
UAV if the reserve is available, and updates the local obser-
vations. The reserve UAV uses the same shared actor after
insertion into the mission. The other UAVs also re-evaluate
their local bridge-risk and coverage information. No prediction
of the failure event is required; the controller reacts to the
observed state change.
D. Mapping from Model to Algorithm
The algorithm is deliberately aligned with the system model.
Sensor positions produce the coverage quantities in (7)–(10);
neighboring UAV positions produce the communication graph
in (14); battery and action information produce the energy
state in (20); charging requests enter the assignment problem
in (24); and failure indicators activate the recovery process
in (26). Thus, every actor input corresponds to an explicitly
defined state quantity and every learned action has a defined
environmental effect.

outs, initial UAV positions, initial battery levels, charging-

A practical implementation can use a multilayer perceptron
for the shared actor and centralized critic with normalized
numerical features and masked action logits. If fixed-length
neighbor features are insufficient, a permutation-invariant
pooling operation or a small attention encoder can be added
without changing the underlying Dec-POMDP formulation.
A recurrent policy should be introduced only if experiments
show that instantaneous observations do not provide sufficient
temporal information.
F. Training Hyperparameters
The initial training configuration follows the values in the
project presentation. These values are starting points for the
implementation and can be tuned on a validation set without
changing the system formulation. Table VIII gives them.
G. Implementation Plan
The implementation follows the three-stage validation strat-
egy presented in the project plan. The objective is to validate
the swarm-control logic before introducing detailed wireless-
channel complexity. Figure 6 shows the stages and what each
one adds.
Phase 1 contains geometric UAV motion, persistent K-
coverage, connectivity, battery dynamics, charging coordi-
nation, failure/recovery, a heuristic controller, and MAPPO.
Once these components are stable, Phase 2 introduces wireless
communication and network-level measurements. Phase 3 then
adds PHY-aware communication. The same actor observa-
tion/action interface is retained across phases so that increasing
simulator fidelity does not require redesigning the learning
problem.
a) Execution status.: Phases 1 and 2 have been executed;
Phase 3 is scaffolded but not yet run with the learned policy.
Phase 1 is implemented in ml_impl/ with a test suite of 134
cases that pins every reported equation, and the simulator has
been exercised over 8 training seeds. Phase 2 is implemented
with INET 4.6 and OMNeT++ 6.4 on WSL2 with a Simu5G
1.4.3 stack; the UAVIoT network configuration runs to com-
pletion and produces scalar and vector outputs, and a dedicated
802.11 physical-layer scenario was built for the validation of
Section VIII-F. The three-stage structure is retained not as a
description of a plan but as an audit trail: it records which level
of fidelity each reported number was produced at, so that a
reader can tell an analytic result from a simulated one and a
simulated one from a measured one.
Two things are worth recording about what Phase 1 actually
cost, because they bear on how the Phase-3 results should
be read. First, the phase is not complete in the sense of
the plan: the first implementation of the Phase-1 simulator
satisfied every equation of the report and every test, and the
coverage numbers it produced were meaningless, because the
motion step never applied a move. The defect was found by a
diagnostic — the swarm’s spread never changed — and not by
the equations, the tests or the loss curve. Second, the physical-
layer scenario of Phase 2 produced frame counts that did not
respond to the transmit power, and the negative control is what
exposed it; the instrument was then rebuilt around a statistic
that does respond, and the rebuild showed that this statistic is
still not a usable instrument for the claim it was wanted for
(Section VIII-F). Both episodes are reported here rather than
in a footnote, because a reader deciding whether to trust a
result from this pipeline should know that the pipeline’s own
diagnostics, and not its unit tests, are what caught the two
most consequential errors in it.
V. COMPARISON MODELS
The comparison design preserves the practical baselines
from the project presentation and adds recent learning-based
methods required for a meaningful research comparison. The
practical baselines test whether any adaptive coordination is
useful; the MARL baselines test whether the proposed CTDE
MAPPO design provides advantages over other learning for-
mulations.
The fixed, greedy, and reactive controllers correspond di-
rectly to the practical alternatives already identified in the
project plan. The two learned baselines are implementations
of the method families the comparison table names, not
reproductions of the cited papers: an independent value-based
learner and a masked PPO with a local critic. Both run in the
same simulator, on the same observation, with the same action
mask and the same team reward as the proposed method, so
that the only differences are the learning machinery; where a
literature method would require a different input representation
or native action space, the adaptation is documented rather
than presented as an exact reproduction. Vanilla MAPPO is

a) Which of these the paper reports.: Of the metrics
above, this paper reports the persistent K-coverage, the con-
nectivity availability and fragility, the service continuity, the
time-averaged coverage deficit, the maximum refresh time,
the energy, charging and movement quantities, the reserve
activations and the stranding count, the plasticity of the shared
actor, and the degradation of the coverage with N and M
through the scenario matrix. Three are not reported: the outage
severity during a recovery interval, the distribution of the
recovery time, and the inference-time scaling. The collision
and out-of-bounds counts are prevented by the safety filter
rather than measured by it, and the separation constraint can be
violated by up to one step of motion when the joint projection
reverts a move, so we do not present a zero in a column we
did not instrument as a measurement.
A. Evaluation Scenarios
Nine scenarios vary the dominant environmental factors
independently before they are combined: sensor density, fleet
size, battery capacity, the number of charging pads, Rcomm,
Rcov, the time of a single-UAV failure, a combined-stress
configuration in which energy scarcity, pad contention, weak


=== PAGE 20 ===
connectivity and a failure occur together, and the initial
deployment. Each scenario has two variants, and every variant
is run.
a) The evaluation protocol, stated exactly.: Every con-
troller is evaluated on the same scenes with the same initial
conditions, and the sampling of a deployed policy — Eq. (30)
specifies ai(t) ∼πθ(ai | oi(t)), so the controller samples —
is seeded from the evaluation seed alone. Three consequences
follow, and they are properties of the protocol rather than of
the controllers: an evaluation is a function of (policy, scene);
every controller sees the same sampling stream on the same
scene, so a difference between two controllers is a difference
between policies and not between the luck of the draw; and
every number in this paper can be recomputed from the stored
policies.
A learned controller is trained several times and reported as
the mean over those training runs, with the seed-to-seed spread
of the coverage. The rule baselines are deterministic: they have
no seed-to-seed spread, and their spread over the evaluation
scenes is reported separately. The two sources of variation
are reported separately in Section VIII, because they behave
differently: the scene-to-scene variation is common to every
controller and cancels in every difference, while the training-
seed variation does not.
The single-component arms are paired: every variant is
trained on the same training seeds as the full configuration,
at the same training budget, and differs from it in exactly one
component. A difference is therefore measured on the same
training runs, and it is reported as a confidence interval on that
paired difference rather than as a comparison of two numbers
against a threshold. We report the resolution of each arm —
the smallest effect it could have detected — because a null
result from an arm of a given width is a statement about
that resolution and not about the component. The principal
conclusions are based on the task-specific metrics in Table X,
not on the raw reward curves.
The ablation experiments remove, one at a time: the
connectivity-criticality reward term, the degraded-service re-
ward term, the energy-cost term, the under-coverage term, the
reserve-UAV mechanism, the charging arbitration, the action
mask, and each of the three observation terms. This identi-
fies whether each proposed component contributes an effect
that this protocol can resolve. In particular, the comparison
between the full proposed framework and vanilla MAPPO is
necessary to distinguish improvements caused by MAPPO it-
self from improvements caused by the domain-specific system
design.
Three candidate explanations for a shortfall against the
strongest controller in the comparison — the unprivileged
reactive rule — are named here, before the results, because
the arms of the next section test them one at a time: the
content of the local observation, the energy model, and the
size of the training budget. Each is tested by a single-factor
intervention that changes that one thing and holds the rest of
the configuration fixed, and each is reported as a confidence
interval on the paired difference, with the resolution at which

VII. EXPERIMENTAL DESIGN MATRIX
The evaluation varies the dominant environmental factors
independently before combining them. Table XI maps each
experiment to a specific research question; every row is run,
and the results are reported in Section VIII.
VIII. RESULTS
All experiments use the corrected, feasible configuration
N = 8, K = 2, Rcov = 35 m on an 80 × 80 m field
(Section III-G), the clustered initial deployment and the 2000-
step episode of Section III-O. Every controller is evaluated on
the same scenes with the same seeds, and the rule baselines
and the learned controllers are trained on the same budget.
The teleporting placement oracle reaches CK = 1.000 on this
configuration; it is the ceiling against which every coverage
number below is meant to be read, and it is what makes
the comparison meaningful: the oracle establishes that the
configuration is coverable, so a controller that falls short of
it falls short as a controller and not because the instance was
infeasible.
Two things are true of this configuration, and we report
both. First, the task is not hard at the parameters the project
specifies: a deterministic reactive heuristic that assigns UAVs
to uncovered sensors reaches CK = 0.953 while maintaining
full connectivity. Second, the learned controller does not reach
that figure, and the arms below bound how much of the gap
each candidate explanation can account for. Three candidate
explanations can be tested with controlled arms — the content

of the observation, the energy model, and the credit assignment

way they come out, with the resolution at which each was
